text:
I declare open this hearing of the Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs Legislation Committee inquiry for the 2026-27 supplementary budget estimates. I'd like to begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the lands on which we meet today and pay our respects to their ancestors and elders, past and present. I extend this respect to all Aboriginal and Torres Islander people who might be joining us today.

The Senate has referred to the committee the particulars of proposed expenditure for 2026-27 for the portfolios of Home Affairs and the Attorney-General and other related documents. These are supplementary budget estimate proceedings, and the outcomes to be heard during today's estimates are from the Home Affairs portfolio. The committee has set Thursday 5 November 2026 as the date by which written questions on notice are to be provided to the secretariat. The committee has also decided that answers to written questions on notice should be returned to the secretariat by 5 pm Thursday 17 December 2026.

Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session. This includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that in giving evidence to the committee they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence to a committee. Officers and senators are familiar with the rules of the Senate governing estimates hearings. If you need assistance, the secretariat has copies of the rules.

The Senate by resolution in 1999 endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings. Any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in the estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise. The Senate has also resolved that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution prohibits only questions asking for opinions on matters of policy and does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted.

I particularly draw the attention of witnesses to an order of the Senate of 13 May 2009, specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised. Witnesses are specifically reminded that a statement that information or a document is confidential or consists of advice to government is not a statement that meets the requirements of the 2009 order. Instead, witnesses are required to provide some specific indication of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of information or the document. This will be incorporated into the Hansard.

The extract reads as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

As chair, I'll be particularly vigilant in ensuring the cultural safety of First Nations people and culturally and socially marginalised groups.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I welcome Senator the Hon. Jenny McAllister, representing the Minister for Emergency Management. I call officers from the National Emergency Management Agency. Good morning, everyone. Minister, would you like to make an opening statement?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Yes, please.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Please proceed.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text:
Thank you for the opportunity to address the committee. The high-risk weather season is underway, and significant weather events are already affecting communities across Australia. Overnight, I understand it's been confirmed that a Queensland man has died in floodwaters. This will be a very distressing time for his community, for his friends, for his family, and I think all senators present would acknowledge that distress and offer our condolences to that man's community. The conditions are expected to intensify over the coming months. There will be an increased risk of fires across northern and south-eastern New South Wales, South-East Queensland, north-eastern Tasmania, parts of Western Australia, South Australia and Victoria, and large parts of the Northern Territory. Daytime and overnight temperatures are forecast to be above average nationwide, increasing heatwave risks and accelerating the drying of vegetation. Forecasts like this underscore why our government's investment in emergency management and risk reduction remains critical.

The National Emergency Management Agency, NEMA, continues to work with states and territories to help communities prepare for, respond to and recover from disasters, and we work with our partners across Australia to strengthen preparedness. Disasters are becoming larger and more complex and more costly. Early action does save lives, strengthens communities and helps government and emergency services support Australians when they need it most. Anticipation and preparation can make all the difference when conditions deteriorate. I acknowledge the leadership of Minister McBain and the work of NEMA in this space.

Over recent months, NEMA has engaged with jurisdictional crisis response and recovery agencies. They've delivered the annual preparedness summit and national preparedness exercise. They've provided sector-specific briefings and finalised the disaster reference booklet for federal members of parliament, which I hope everyone here has accessed. Together, these efforts strengthen planning and preparedness, build national resilience and reduce potential harm to communities ahead of each higher-risk weather season. This work is complemented by new national capabilities that are designed to help ensure Australia is ready.

A core aspect of our national readiness is AusAlert, Australia's new national warning system. It uses the latest technology to send emergency messages to compatible devices—I should say they are to mobile devices. AusAlert gives Commonwealth, state and territory agencies access to cell broadcast technology. This is considered best practice for telephone based warning systems—it is used in more than 35 countries. Following the successful national test in July this year, AusAlert is now available and ready for use. NEMA is working with jurisdictions to finalise operational arrangements.

Looking forward, Australia faces a rapidly changing risk environment. The Albanese government is focused on ensuring that our nation is prepared and ready to respond. This summer Minister McBain and the team here at NEMA will continue working diligently to support communities during these more-demanding operational months. The government wishes to acknowledge the emergency services workers, first responders, local councils and many volunteers who will undoubtedly be on the ground protecting lives and communities in the face of extreme weather. On behalf of Minister McBain, I thank everyone here for the opportunity to speak today. To everyone working across Australia to keep our country safe, I thank you for your continued efforts.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Thank you, Minister. We certainly associate ourselves with your words of condolence at the beginning, too. Mr Hetherington, would you like to make an opening statement?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text:
I would. Thank you, Chair, and members of the committee, for the opportunity to make a statement. The National Emergency Management Agency supports communities during emergencies, and helps Australia prepare before disasters occur. In recent months, we've worked with governments, industry, community organisations and emergency management partners to strengthen preparedness and national resilience.

A key milestone was our fourth annual national preparedness summit, which brought together more than 300 representatives from government, emergency services, industry and the not-for-profit sector. The summit focused on strengthening readiness ahead of the high-risk weather season, sharing lessons from recent events and testing Australia's ability to manage complex and compounding crises. Since establishing our national crisis exercise capability, NEMA has delivered 11 national-level exercises to strengthen preparedness and coordination, identify emerging risks and support continuous improvement. Preparedness is not just confined to exercises; NEMA has also delivered national preparedness briefings and leadership engagements across government and key sectors. This work helps ensure that those responsible for keeping Australians safe have the information, relationships and plans they need before emergencies occur.

While preparedness remains a significant focus, NEMA continues to support responses to domestic and international events. Between 1 April and 9 October, national plans were activated nine times, including for natural hazards, biosecurity incidents, overseas assistance operations, overseas repatriations, and space debris re-entry. During this period, NEMA coordinated 11 requests for Australian government non-financial assistance, and convened 26 national coordination mechanisms to support coordination and share the situational awareness. During this period, NEMA coordinated 11 requests for Australian government non-financial assistance and convened 26 National Coordination Mechanisms to support coordination and shared situational awareness. Even during what is traditionally the lower risk weather season, our Crisis Coordination Team was active for 170 of 192 days. This reflects both the breadth of NEMA'S responsibilities and the sustained demands on its coordination capability across all types of hazards.

Recent work has included deploying a planning team to the Northern Territory to support the response to elevated bushfire conditions and coordinating the response to H5 avian influenza alongside the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry. We also supported the response to space debris in Queensland and coordinated the repatriation and quarantine of Australians following the MV Hondius hantavirus incident. Overseas, NEMA supported Australian assistance to Nepal following the catastrophic flooding and landslides. Australia's aerial firefighting deployment to France was also conducted during this period.

Recovery also remains a significant focus for the agency. Since July 2025, assistance under the Disaster Recovery Funding Arrangements has been activated for 78 disaster events affecting 237 local government areas across Australia. NEMA continues to work closely with states and territories to support communities as they recover and rebuild.

As Senator McAllister mentioned, AusAlert, Australia's new national cell broadcast public warning capability became operational on 1 October. It has strengthened the ability of emergency management agencies to deliver targeted warnings directly to people in affected areas. Community trials and a successful national test provided confidence in the capability before it went live. Our focus is now on supporting national adoption, finalising implementation arrangements with jurisdictions and ensuring personnel are trained to use the capability effectively.

We'd also like to update the committee on payroll improvement work within the agency. In recent months, we've strengthened payroll, governance and administration and progressed remediation planning. We have also prioritised the transition of our payroll services to the Department of Industry, Science and Resources Shared Services Hub. This transition is intended to strengthen payroll controls and to support a more sustainable payroll environment into the future. While this work is complex, our focus remains clear: to ensure our staff are paid in line with their entitlements and on time, address any identified discrepancies and put in place arrangements that provide greater assurance and confidence for our workforce.

Finally, I'd like to acknowledge the results of our 2026 APS employee census. The results show that NEMA employees remain strongly connected to the agency's purpose and committed to serving the Australian community. They also identify areas where improvement is needed, including change management, internal communication, wellbeing and leadership alignment. Bullying and harassment also remains an area that we want to focus on throughout the course of the next few months. We're analysing the results further to inform targeted action in the areas identified for improvement, and we remain committed to fostering a safe, respectful and inclusive workplace. Chair, the demands on Australia's emergency management system continue to grow in scale and complexity. NEMA remains focused on strengthening preparedness, supporting communities and building the capabilities Australia needs when crises occur. Thank you, and we welcome questions.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Thank you very much. We'll proceed to questions and begin with Senator McDonald.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Thank you very much, Chair. Good morning to you. I want to ask you how many staff are currently housed with NEMA? What's your FTE?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: In ASL terms, we are about 380 ASL. You'll see in our budget—I'll just ask the acting COO to find exact numbers for you. But we're about 380 ASL in our 2026-27 PBS. You can see that we have a budgeted ASL of about 425. I think in headcount terms, we're probably closer to 390 or so people. But if I'm incorrect, I'll be corrected by our COO.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Senator, that's correct. If I'm looking at an ASL until 31 August 2026, the actual ASL is 380.8. If I'm looking at an APS headcount perspective as of 31 August 2026, it's 405.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: On notice, can you give me a break down of where abouts in the country those bodies, the 405, are based, please.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Yes, we can, Senator. In broad terms, the vast majority are here in Canberra. We have an office in Brisbane, and we have outposted and staff in every jurisdiction, but smaller numbers, obviously, outside of Canberra. We can provide that on notice.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Thank you. As you know, when a natural disaster hits a community, it's the council that is on the front line, it's the council that the community turns to for first response and it's the council that is often responsible for maintaining so much of the infrastructure in a community. In recognition of this, can NEMA provide concrete assurance to local government that councils will not be left worse off financially as a result of the new disaster recovery funding model?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: What I would say is that, in the first instance, there are no changes to the Disaster Recovery Funding Arrangements for this upcoming high-risk weather season, and we've been very clear about that from the outset. As for the reforms, we're still working through those, but the intent was never to provide less of a resource or less funding to local government areas. The nature of the relationship around disaster funding is between the Commonwealth and states, but I can assure you that the intent was not to reduce resources available to those people on the front line of recovery.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: On 5 June this year, the Albanese government announced that it would be negotiating changes to Australia's longstanding disaster recovery funding arrangements and replacing them with the new disaster recovery funding framework. To provide clarity on this, can NEMA give this committee a comprehensive update on the progress and status of these ongoing negotiations with the states and territories and the local government sector when it comes to establishing the new disaster recovery funding framework, and can that update include relevant next steps, such as working groups, meetings, upcoming milestones and timeframes? In the interests of time, I am happy for that detail to be provided on notice.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: We can. I will pass to Mr Minack in a moment to walk through some of that. But as you say, on 5 June, we announced reform of the disaster recovery funding arrangements and, since then, have undertaken what has been a very comprehensive set of engagements, both bilaterally and multilaterally and both at the ministerial level and at officials level, across all jurisdictions—we can walk through some of that—as well as received, I think, something in the order of 260 written submissions around the reform. So it's been a comprehensive engagement thus far. But I'll pass to Mr Minack just to walk through the elements of the reforms as well as where we're at, what has already been announced and what remains to be done, if that's useful.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I'm just conscious that we have a deadline of 10 o'clock and I have a lot to get through, so perhaps we could keep it succinct and provide the detail on notice, please.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Just in terms of engagement, since the announcement on 5 June of the proposed framework—that was always out for consultation—we've done a series of engagements both at a jurisdiction and a state, territory and local government level. We've also had key leadership meetings in the sector in terms of ANZEMC, which is the Australia-New Zealand Emergency Management Committee, being all the senior officials, of which ALGA is a representative. There have also been the ministerial meetings, of which ALGA is also a representative. In terms of submissions, we received 266, of which 130 were from local council, and we've also established a local government advisory group, which has met twice. Again, to your point, that's specific acknowledgement of the important role that local government plays in terms of delivery of both recovery and resilience measures on the ground. That's a key focus in terms of engagement and, clearly, it will be a key focus of engagement going forward. From a personal perspective, we have also presented to all the local government associations around Australia again to get feedback in terms of the proposed reforms, and that will be ongoing.
witness_position: First Assistant Coordinator-General, Policy and Governance

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: That is what I want to know. I don't want to know what has happened to date, as we are all aware of what has happened to date, with the massive outcry from councils and states around the country and the government now walking back some of those announcements. I want to know what is happening going forward, and I'd like details about who sits on that local government representative group and what the plan is to continue to engage and land this beast.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: We can give you a list of who sits on that local government advisory group, and I will say that it is representatives from all jurisdictions. In terms of going forward, we're certainly intending to meet with local councils, local government associations, and state and territory jurisdictions. As for where we are with the reform process, obviously a key announcement was made by the Treasurer and the minister around cost-sharing arrangements, counter-disaster operations and activation thresholds. That is a component. There are a number of other elements, in terms of standardised packages, risk-reduction activities et cetera, on which we still need to engage with key stakeholders and, specifically, local councils.
witness_position: First Assistant Coordinator-General, Policy and Governance

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: In particular, one of the core issues that councils have called out, repeatedly and unanimously, has been the need for streamlining and reducing the complexity associated with administering the recovery arrangements. Additionally, as noted by Mr Minack, a key piece of the work going forward is to work with councils to identify where now are the obstacles that they have been facing with evidence requirements and claiming processes through their relevant state or territory et cetera, as appropriate, and looking at ways to try to streamline some of that going forward.
witness_position: Deputy Coordinator-General, Disaster Resilience and Recovery

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Again, you've provided very little detail of what is happening. You have given lots of 'we are going to consult', but perhaps you could provide on notice the details of that local government group, how often it will meet and what its milestones of success are. Please provide the same regarding your consultation with states and territories and those other groups, regarding what the milestones are and what set meetings there are.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: The challenge that the officials have is that you've asked them not to provide detail right now, in the interest of time, and you now offer a criticism because of the lack of detail. To shortcut this, Senator McDonald, perhaps I can say that the engagements, including those with state jurisdictions and local government, have been extensive to date. I think the way that NEMA has proceeded with this does involve deep consultation with partners. Disaster management is absolutely a team sport. We usually are not in the lead in a disaster situation, as it is for state and territory to take the lead. We need to cooperate with states and territories. We also need to cooperate with local government, which plays a key role, as your questioning indicates. That reality is reflected in the consultation process that, to date, has taken and is taking place, and I am absolutely confident that will be reflected in the consultation process going forward. Officials, I think, are willing to provide, on notice, more of that detail that you have requested.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I would like to hear the officials talk to milestones, dates and commitments, as opposed to further consultation, which, as we know, the councils and states have responded to, unanimously, with a rejection of what the government had proposed, which is why the government has had to walk back that 50-50 split. That goes to my next question. Based on NEMA's disaster management reform discussion paper and the government's recent decision to abandon the proposed 50-50 cost-sharing split with the states and territories, what key reform priorities for the DRFF remain under active consideration and consultation?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text:
As my colleagues have mentioned already, there are quite a number. We responded, in the first instance, to the things that people raised with us as the areas of most concern. Fifty-fifty cost-sharing arrangements, counter-disaster operations and activation thresholds were the three key areas where people made submissions and raised concerns. Frankly, rightly, the government addressed those three areas of concern first and made the announcements that you have seen. The remaining areas, which Dr Charker has started to illustrate, include things like streamlining the processes.

As you would appreciate, there are quite a lot of evidentiary requirements associated with the disaster recovery funding arrangements that land with local governments, and that's an area that we want to streamline as much as we possibly can. We want to reduce red tape to accelerate the way in which funding arrives and is subsequently assured for local governments and for state governments. That's one area. We are still working through what standardised recovery packages look like. We really want to provide certainty to communities who have experienced or are experiencing disasters or crises and are in recovery so that they know what's available to them and there's no question about whether they can or cannot do a certain thing, and whether that will be supported by the federal government. So we're still working through that process. They're probably the two big elements, amongst others, which I'll pass to Dr Charker to comment on.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I would just add that there's also the whole issue around betterment. When an asset is damaged in a disaster event, sometimes there's a strong case to build it back to a more resilient standard so that, when future events occur, it's either less damaged or, ideally, not damaged. That is an important issue that councils have raised, as well as states and territories. There was an initial proposal put on the table back in June about what a possible resilient infrastructure scheme or betterment scheme could look like. Again, we've received some good feedback across governments, both local as well as state and territory. Currently, we're working through what some alternatives could be, and we'll continue to do that.
witness_position: Deputy Coordinator-General, Disaster Resilience and Recovery

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Senator McDonald has indicated she has further questions, but I am going to share the call around and come back to Senator McDonald. Senator Darmanin.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I have some questions about Disaster Ready Fund round 4 projects for the mighty state of Victoria. Speaking of the importance of local government in recovery and resilience, Moira Shire Council secured funds for the Barmah Flood Resilience project. I wonder whether you could give us some detail around the project and speak about its importance and impacts for the community in that region.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: In terms of the assessments, the DRF round 4 has been completed, and the minister is in the process of making progressive announcements. To date, we've had successful projects announced for Victoria, followed by Queensland and, this morning, the ACT. The Victorian projects in total represent $17.72 million of Commonwealth investment. Part of the DRF also requires a co-investment from delivery partners or proponents. That resulted in an extra $19 million, bringing the total investment for Victorian resilience and readiness projects to $36.8 million. I've got a few examples. What particular one are you asking about?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: The Moira Shire with the Barmah flood.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Phase 1 of the Barmah Flood Resilience project is going to undertake flood mitigation works to replace the culvert seals and flap valves and install penstock structures at multiple locations throughout Barmah. These upgrades will reduce water leakage through road culverts and ensure safer pumping of floodwater from within the levee system. So this will strengthen the levee system to better protect the Barmah community from future flood events. Obviously, that will protect assets but also improve access in and out of that area. As for the dollar value of that, there is $100,000 for that project and a matching co-contribution of $100,000, which together amount to $200,000. So it is building on existing mitigation works. There are a few other examples for Victorian projects, if you would like to hear about them.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Yes. Perhaps you have a list. I am interested in the area around the Ruffy community centre in the Strathbogie Shire Council. Do you have information on that?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I'm not sure whether I have that with me.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I understand that is around the new design of the Ruffy community centre.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Yes, we do have it. Again, the 26 January bushfires destroyed Ruffy's recreation reserve and the Tablelands Community Centre, which are the community's main places for gathering, recreation, and coming together after emergencies. This project delivers community engagement, a master plan and a detailed design to rebuild these facilities. This will ensure that the centre is accessible and resilient to future disaster, and it will reduce the community's recovery burden by providing a pathway to reconstruction and recovery. That'll be $163,000 from the Commonwealth and co-contributions of $184,000, giving a total of $348,000 for that project.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Did you just say that, in terms of its resilience into the future, the considerations around that concept of betterment that we have just heard about are included in that design work?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Yes, certainly. Again, the design work and the discovery of this will ensure that facility is going to be more resilient for the future, help the community to recover and also help handle the community during an event as well, so they will be the important features. Again, I'm happy to take on notice to provide other examples, as we do have others. The minister, again, announced the construction of a flood levee along Racecourse Creek in Bendigo. That's a significant investment of around $6 million from the Commonwealth, matched by about $6.2 million from the co-contributors, which gives a total investment of $12.2 million. That's going to reduce the flood risk to over 500 homes and 60 businesses in that Bendigo area.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I was going to ask about the projects that have been successful in the Rochester, Bendigo and Castlemaine areas. Are there any others outside of Racecourse Creek that you can take us through?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Yes. We have the projects for Rochester and Elmore District Health Service. One is the construction of a levee to protect the Rochester hospital from flood events. This will mitigate flood impacts like those experienced in the 2022 flood, which caused the hospital to be evacuated, close for two years and incur millions in damages. The project outputs will include levee design and construction and integration of resilience measures. That's going to be funded to the tune of $1.7 million from the Commonwealth, with matching funding from the state and territory of $1.9 million, which will total $3.6 million for that project.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I have another question for you. The ones that I've asked about and that you've talked about have really been about flood mitigation and response to bushfire. Do you have an overall comment, in terms of the totality of projects across Victoria, regarding whether they specifically look mostly at those types of natural disasters, or is it a mix? Can you give us a bit of a flavour about that?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: It certainly is a mix. Of the total funding for the Disaster Ready Fund, a portion was for infrastructure, and another portion was for things ranging from planning, research, flood modelling—

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Community support?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: community support and all that type of thing, including community knowledge and readiness. So there's a range of projects, and we can certainly take on notice to provide a full suite of those. By the way, just to be clear, we've published all the projects on the NEMA website as well. They will be added to progressively as further announcements take place.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: That is excellent. I will direct my community to the website for a lot more detail.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I might just add to the end of that answer a little about the infrastructure nature of some of this, through our work in the hazards insurance space. It's important that we get the right mix of projects as well. The community resilience piece is absolutely critical. The delivery of some of these larger infrastructure levee related projects is the sorts of thing that the insurance sector looks at, in terms of driving down premiums and providing greater availability of insurance. So that's one of the considerations that we also have when we look at the impacts.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: That's very helpful.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Senator Payman.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: My line of questioning goes to my question on notice at the last estimates in May, where I asked about the cost of the creation of the AusAlert system. NEMA responded by saying that the total expense of delivering AusAlert 'is not for publication due to it being commercial-in-confidence'. I refer to Minister McBain's press conference on 26 February this year. A copy of the transcript of that press conference is available from the Home Affairs website, and I have a copy of it. During that press conference, Minister McBain said that 'to date the government has invested $132 million to build and test the system'. Has Minister McBain breached an understanding that the cost of AusAlert is commercial-in-confidence?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: No, I don't believe so at all. I think she has mentioned an investment of around $132 million, and I don't think that includes all the costs associated with sustainment. We can walk through some of those things. In our budget papers, you will see that we have 'not for publication', as there remain commercial sensitivities with the telecommunications providers that we're engaging with.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I understand, but I'm sorry. The question that I put on notice was quite clear. Are we saying that this information isn't commercial-in-confidence?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I might pass to Mr Dasgupta to walk through the costs around AusAlert and what we have and have not published, and hopefully that will provide that clarity for you.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: The investment, as an overall figure, amounts to $132 million. That is because it includes expenses from multiple agencies, such as the department of infrastructure, which was managing the CBC contracts, and NEMA, which was managing the CBE contracts. The initial expenses started with Home Affairs before the establishment of NEMA. A number of these CBC contracts with telco providers are commercial-in-confidence because of their sensitivities, and that's why they are not on AusTender. Hence none of the budget papers mentioned the financial details of the AusAlert budget measures; they were mentioned only in an overall way.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: So it cost less than $132 million, but you're not willing to tell me how much it actually cost?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: No. I think what he's saying is that the overall investment is about $132 million. But once you start to disaggregate the $132 million by agency, with people knowing that we are managing the contracts for a particular component of AusAlert, it will become evident how much we're spending on certain elements of it. That is where the commercial sensitivity arises. So the quoted figure of $132 million that you have seen in the minister's media statement is accurate.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: What is the latest estimate of expenditure on AusAlert, now that we know the minister has publicly mentioned that the investment was of $132 million?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: At the moment, I would still go with the $132 million being the estimated investment figure. Because the voice module that was announced is, again, commercial-in-confidence at the moment, I would still go with the $132-million investment figure.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I just don't understand why you wouldn't share how much it has cost. I'm not asking you to tell me who applied for the tenders or was involved in this. I'm just asking how much the expenditure was. Clearly, it seems as though you won't tell us what the actual cost or amount was for this particular component, and, when we're here in supplementary budget estimates, trying to figure out how much this cost, that's not really helpful for us. Is there a figure that you can provide that's not the $132 million? This is very vague.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I think it's quite normal for government to withhold expenditure estimates when we're about to enter into a negotiation because, amongst other things, providing an estimate of expenditure gives a potential vendor an indication of how much you're willing to pay. In essence, that's one of the reasons for such information being withheld. You have asked for more information, and I think we can take that on notice and examine what additional information could be appropriately provided that would not trip over some of the commercial-in-confidence issues. I'm reluctant to do it on the run at the table, but I think we can have a look at it and see what's possible.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Just a point of clarification: if the $132 million figure was made public in February, why wasn't it included in the question on notice that I put to you guys in May?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: That was the estimated investment. However, as you know, the build was still not complete—we are still going through the voice module—and, if we were to start adding more figures, again commercial sensitivities would occur. So we will take it on notice and then see what we can provide.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I think you can appreciate that it's a bit of an unhelpful answer, when I received an answer to a question on notice, saying that it's commercial-in-confidence after the minister had stated a figure already.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Senator Payman, is this BE26-0995? I'm just trying to check that we're all talking about the same thing.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Yes, it is.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: That's the correct one.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text:
It was question 4, to be exact:

What was the total expense of creating the system?

Thank you for taking that on notice. On notice, can you also please identify all contract notice IDs relevant to the delivery of AusAlert. Also, NEMA's website states:

In the 2026-27 Budget, the Australian Government announced funding over 3 years from 2026-27 to sustain the AusAlert system.

What's the value of this funding for each funding year?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Again, you will see in our budget papers that that's not for publication, and that's what I was referring to at the outset of the question. There are ongoing sustainment costs associated with the system that are still commercially sensitive, so the extent to which they're in the public domain hampers our ability to work with the telecommunication providers in a commercial way. We will come back on notice with more detail. The investment of $132 million is right at a point in time, and, 'There is more to come,' is probably part of the answer. So we are still working through a voice module et cetera. I appreciate that, when these responses have been given, they are at a point in time.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Senator McDonald.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I will again flag that I have a lot of questions. If government members on the committee have questions, perhaps they could direct them to government members outside of estimates; otherwise, I will have to go over time. I'm just flagging that.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: We're usually pretty good at sharing the call and managing time, but we appreciate that you've got lots of questions. Senator McDonald, you've got the call.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: In the joint media release between the Treasurer and the Minister for Emergency Management on 9 October, the government stated that it would be 'revising funding activation thresholds'. Can NEMA advise the committee what the revised activation thresholds will be and confirm that 'large disaster-prone regional councils with a smaller rate base, extensive road networks, dispersed communities and recurring disaster impacts' will not be financially disadvantaged by any changes being considered.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text:
I can assist with that. The current Disaster Recovery Funding Arrangements that have been in place for some time have an event based activation trigger point of $240,000. In consultation with all states and territories and local governments, all the states and territories agreed that has been too low. It has been in place for many years and has not been indexed. The government then, in June, proposed an initial reform position of new trigger points of either $2.7 million for the larger jurisdictions, being SA at that time, New South Wales, Queensland, Victoria and Western Australia, or $1.65 million for ACT, Tasmania and the Northern Territory. As has been indicated by Mr Hetherington and Mr Minack, following extensive consultation and very strong views received from local, state and territory governments that those thresholds were then seen as too high, in October the Treasurer and the minister advised a revised set of trigger points or activation thresholds, being either $1 million for New South Wales, Queensland, Victoria and WA, or $0.5 million for ACT, South Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory.

It's important to note that, across the eight jurisdictions in this country, states and territories, in turn, have their own arrangements with councils. So whilst, as the interim coordinator-general has pointed out, these arrangements are between the Commonwealth and the states—they are funding arrangements for cost sharing between the Commonwealth and the states and territories—it is open to states to have, and in fact many states currently have, additional activation thresholds set enormously differently for different councils based on rate bases and other considerations on top of that, which are not set by the Commonwealth.
witness_position: Deputy Coordinator-General, Disaster Resilience and Recovery

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I might just add to that, as I think it's important. The way we envisaged those thresholds was that there has to be a certain amount of damage—it can't just be a heavy rain shower—before you're eligible for Commonwealth assistance. We don't think about those costs as being passed on to a local government, as that's a state and territory apparatus that's in place. Under the new thresholds, if Queensland had an event that caused more than $1 million worth of damage, we think that would meet the activation threshold, and it's not the Commonwealth's position that those costs be passed on to local government. As Dr Charker has outlined, there is a range of different arrangements across every jurisdiction where those costs are passed on, based on a bunch of factors, including rate base et cetera. But that is not a feature of the system that is controlled by the federal government.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Could you provide, on notice, any modelling that has been done to support the first activation level and now this updated activation level or whether it's just a negotiated number?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Yes, we can take it on notice. In very broad terms, the first set of activation thresholds were based on some modelling done by the Productivity Commission some time ago and updated for price, and the second set of activation thresholds are similarly price updated based on historical numbers. We will take that on notice and come back with some detail.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: While councils appreciate retaining the ability to claim costs under counterdisaster operations, what recovery measures will be included in this?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: With the retention of counterdisaster operations and support for cost sharing associated with that, we'll see, as per the Treasurer and the minister's announcements, the same measures that are currently included in counterdisaster operations. CDO is a broad bucket. It includes, for example, but not exhaustively, aerial operations for fire activity. It includes sandbagging for flood activity. It might include evacuation of people. It might include clearing pathways for ingress and egress of people's properties or other facilities. It is a really broad bunch of activities that can form part of counterdisaster operations, and the government has indicated that will be retained.
witness_position: Deputy Coordinator-General, Disaster Resilience and Recovery

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: On notice, could you please provide that list of measures. We had some commentary around the 15 per cent resilient infrastructure scheme or the betterment funding. I see that it would provide the states and territories with access to additional resilience and betterment funding of up to 15 per cent, which would be cost shared 50-50 with the Commonwealth. Given that the discussion paper said the 15 per cent ceiling was the starting point for engagement, can NEMA clarify where this engagement is up to currently, whether the 15 per cent is being reconsidered and what the feedback from state and local governments has been about the adequacy of the 15 per cent.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text:
Generally, the views have been, firstly, welcoming of some fairly predictable, standardised way to approach betterment. One of the challenges for the current system has been that different states and territories have or seek varying levels of access to betterment, and the proposal for this resilient infrastructure scheme was a way of saying, 'How can we standardise and make available to all states and territories a predictable source of betterment expenditure?' That's the issue that we're trying to grapple with. The questions then come: What size should that be, and how should that money be apportioned? Should it be a certain amount of a given asset? For example, if a bridge were damaged, should it be some proportion of the amount that it costs to fix that bridge, on top, or if a series of assets were damaged in a particular event—bridges, roads et cetera; that is, a program of work—should that amount be some proportion of that cost?

The initial position put forward in June was, as you noted, for a 15 per cent amount for an eligible public asset that was damaged. The feedback that has been received from states and territories and some councils has been, in some instances, that 15 per cent is not enough for betterment. In other instances, states have sought more flexibility to manage a suite of assets that was damaged rather than betterment for an individual asset. That feedback has been provided to us through all the engagements we've outlined and the written submissions we've received, and we're reviewing that, and that will be a matter for further government consideration.
witness_position: Deputy Coordinator-General, Disaster Resilience and Recovery

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text:
I'll put some more questions on notice with regard to that. I asked you earlier about the disaster reform advisory group with the local councils. On notice, perhaps you can provide when the group was formed and who it reports to it and, in addition, what councils sit on the advisory group; how its membership was decided and whether there was a process for the selection criteria; whether it has a terms of reference and, if so, whether that could that be tabled; and how often it has met since it was established, when its next meeting is scheduled for and whether minutes for its meetings can be provided. Also, in terms of a timeframe, could you provide on notice how long this advisory group will be active for and, given the importance of disaster recovery funding reforms, how the government will ensure that councils can have the opportunity to provide input into and are informed of outcomes from the disaster reform advisory group.

I want to turn now to the closure of Disaster Relief Australia. Specifically, we know that Disaster Relief Australia was liquidated on 29 May 2026, only two days after the last Senate estimates with NEMA on 27 May. DRA was a national not-for-profit organisation that consisted of thousands of veterans and volunteers who utilised their training, skills, expertise and commitment for turning up for Australians at the worst of times. Given that we have recently commenced a severe high-risk weather season, what nationally scalable and rapidly deployable boots-on-the-ground recovery workforce now exists to replace the proven capability that was provided previously by Disaster Relief Australia?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I might quickly pass to Ms Carroll to talk about some of the capabilities that we can field, but I would say at the outset that it is true that we won't have a DRA-style capability for this next high-risk weather season in the format that you have seen with DRA. We're considering options, working up some thinking around what that could look like into the future. But that's not to say that there's no capability that can be brought to bear across the next high-risk weather season. I might pass to Ms Carroll to walk through some of those things, including stockpile and the like.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Firstly, from the outset, I would like to say that, really, the liquidation of DRA is disappointing. They were highly regarded and deployed a number of times, particularly for clean-up, logistics, planning and management of spontaneous volunteers. Certainly, there are some challenges going forward. We are doing a piece of work to see what a future capability will look like, but obviously, in the meantime, we are doing some work to make sure that we address some of those risks and gaps. I will pass on to Karina Menday, the Assistant Coordinator-General.
witness_position: Deputy Coordinator-General, Emergency Management and Response

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: As you say, for the season, we're working really closely with states on how we can support them with a whole range of recovery and response activities. That includes things like deploying liaison and planning officers into states if that is helpful. We also have capabilities, such as the National Emergency Management Stockpile, which states can call on if they need that type of capability.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Just to clarify, that's not people, though, is it?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: There are two elements to it. We have the physical stockpile, which has the things in warehouses that are ready to deploy—

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: On notice, please provide what that list of things or inventory is.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Absolutely. We've got an updated list that we can table today. The other thing that the NEMS capability has is a panel arrangement, which is a little bit like a virtual supermarket. It has a whole lot of emergency-services support that states and local government can call on as well. There are capabilities there around recovery, planning and logistics, being the kind of support that states or local governments could access, if they needed to, at fixed prices and from already procured and checked organisations.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: On notice, perhaps you could provide that list, because I'm still seeking to understand what is being put in place to replace the capability of DRA.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Absolutely.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Senator McDonald, we will return to you. We will go to Senator David Pocock. However, before we do, we have some media in the room who are seeking permission from the committee. Permission is given, with all the usual rules applying. Senator David Pocock.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I've got some serious questions about the results of this year's APS Employee Census, after reading through them. Maybe we should start with the performance of the Senior Executive Service. Forty-six per cent of respondents said that the SES do not work as a team, with just 24 per cent saying that they do. That's 31 per cent worse than the APS overall and 25 per cent worse than just last year. What's going on? What's happening at NEMA?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text:
I touched on some of the census results in my opening statement—I appreciate that you weren't here for that—and called out this leadership piece. Clearly this is an area on which we're going to focus across the coming months. We're in the process of working up our action plan on the back of the census. I think a few things are driving that. Firstly, I would say that it is not a capability question for our Senior Executive Service employees. The results around people's perceptions of their own senior leader are really quite high and remain high. Teams generally have a good view of their own leadership line.

As you rightly point out, the concern is whether we're working together as a team, and I think there are a few interrelated findings in the census. Change management and communications are two areas where we know we need to do better. Clearly, what the workforce has not been seeing is the engagement across the SES to deliver shared outcomes in the way that they want to see it. Some of that is about how we communicate with the workforce. In recent weeks, we have undertaken a very detailed analysis of these results to make sure that we could properly target our action plan to address what is a real concern of our workforce. The cohorts in which we see the biggest impact associated with SES leadership are our EL1s and EL2s and, in some measure, that relates to clearly articulating the goal and priorities of the organisation and communicating how it is that we're working across the organisation to deliver on those shared outcomes. We have not done that to the satisfaction of our workforce. So, as we consider what our action plan looks like, there will be a series of very tangible actions associated with this particular part.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Thank you for accepting that there is a problem, as that is obviously the first step in trying to address it. Clearly, the former coordinator-general is no longer with the agency. What has been the rate of executive turnover in the past four years?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I might just see whether the Chief Operating Officer has those figures. Just while he looks for those, contextually, as you know, there has been some instability in the agency. In the context of when the survey was done, there was changeover in leadership at a number of levels, including at a deputy level, and the impending departure of the former coordinator-general. Also, throughout that same period, the payroll issues, which we've discussed here previously, came to light, amongst other things. So, throughout the period of the survey being undertaken, there was a general level of instability in the organisation that, although not being the sole driver, contributed to this. As for SES turnover, I'll pass to Sanandan.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I do not have the SES turnover, but I do have the overall staff turnover.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Perhaps you could give me the overall now and then take on notice the SES.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Yes. For the 12 months of the 2025-26 full financial year, the ongoing separation rate is 23.77 per cent.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Do you know how that compares to the APS average?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: It's higher.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: There are no surprises there. In your response to my first question, you mentioned direction and lack of direction. I was shocked to read that 36 per cent of respondents said that the SES 'do not clearly articulate the direction and policy for the agency'. You are incredibly well paid executives. How is it that NEMA does not articulate the direction?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I think it's more nuanced than that, which is why we have invested the time we have in getting behind the data.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: It may be nuanced, but that's a fairly stark finding.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Indeed, but I come back to the point I made before. That is that line teams have a great deal of confidence in their SES, and that's also evident in the outcome. So they're confident that their leadership has the capacity to direct, prioritise and lead the teams. It is this cross-organisation issue that has come to the fore in the context of this census result, and we need to work through that. The sense that we organisationally understand what all the priorities are and that we're all pulling in the same direction is part of the missing piece here.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: That seems to point to the fact that you've got some good people in there, and people respect and like working with them, but clearly the top needs to take responsibility here. Why haven't you been coordinating the SES and providing more direction?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I'm the person who is accountable for that. In the first instance, I've had some visibility of these census results for a while. We have already started making some changes to make sure that the SES cohort is working more clearly as a team. We've instituted a weekly sync that brings every SES officer together so that we can talk collectively about what the priorities are of the organisation. Out of that, they take that information back now to their teams and communicate not only their own priorities but also the priorities of the organisation. That's a simple mechanism that we've put in place. We'll continue to build on those sorts of mechanisms. As I said, our census action plan will have a great focus on this, and that will be made public in the coming weeks. I think, in mid-November, you'll see our census action plan. We just want to do a bit more work on that and test it a little bit with the workforce to make sure that it's hitting the mark for them, before putting it out. But there will be a series of really tangible things.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: So you're doing weekly catch-ups to try and get on the same page. You'd hope that was happening previously. So that's one change. What else are you doing? Surely that can't be the only thing that you're doing about this.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Yes. As I said before, part of what we saw in the census was comms. We've been running a series of all-staff meetings. We do a series of meetings called 'short and sweet' on key topics, and we've been making sure that they are well attended by SES officers. We've been doing more regular staff stand-ups with people. We've been putting out weekly reports from the Chief People Officer, or they may be fortnightly or monthly reports. So we're amping up all of the elements of communication. Recently—this is a good point too—we did a whole-of-EL2 cohort. One of the big cohorts in our workforce is the middle management layer at EL2, who on a day-to-day basis are really out there delivering for us. We've pulled together a workshop of all the EL2s and worked through a range of these issues with them, talking through very openly any concerns that they've got. So, in the first instance, we are starting to expand that communication piece. As I say, in our census action plan, you will see some very tangible additional measures that we are going to put in place.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: That's good to hear. Some of that sounds good. I hope that it's not just more meetings, though, because I think that creates its own set of problems. I just want to touch on retention. You have said, 'People may think we don't have direction but, actually, people really like the person that they report to.' But 44 per cent of respondents said that they wanted to leave their position as soon as possible or within the next 12 months, which is much higher than the APS average, and just 14 per cent of respondents want to stay at the agency for more than three years, which is much lower than the APS average. What you're talking about, though, doesn't point to problems of that kind that you're talking about. You're saying that people really like the person to whom they're reporting, but they just have some concerns about the top. That, to me, points to an agency that's really struggling culture-wise. How are you going to address that?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I would exchange the word 'like' for 'they have confidence in'. Rather than their necessarily 'liking', I think the way they're framed is that they've got confidence in their senior leadership. I'd suggest that there are a few factors at play that speak to the numbers that you've just called out. As I've said, context is important. It's been a rough 12 or 18 months for the organisation, just in terms of leadership change, payroll issues and poorly communicated change management, and those things feature in the way that people respond to the census. There's no question about that. Also, across the breadth of the organisation, we are an operational organisation, so it is the sort of place where people will come in and, for a period of time, work hard and for long hours, so some turnover for us is actually healthy. Not only do we need to maintain the right level of capability and expertise but equally, as an operational organisation, we do appreciate that people will come in, do a bit of a tour through the place and then move on. I am probably most concerned about the number of people, as you have called out, that want to leave within the next 12 months, and I think, honestly, some of that is related to their experience in the organisation over the last 12 months or so. One of the things that we are doing to improve culture, for example, is making sure that people have a better understanding of the work that is conducted in the constituent parts of the organisation. On Dr Charker's side of the house, you've got that resilience and recovery work; and on Ms Carroll's side of the house, you've got, effectively, emergency management response. Those things are dedicated to the same outcome at different times on the continuum. So we're doing a lot of cross-training between those two parts of the team, and I think that's going to have tangible results on not only our capacity to surge but also, in due course, the culture of the organisation. Cultural change, though, is a longer term proposition. Obviously, we are hoping to see positive results in the next census. We will do our own spot check probably in about February to see whether or not the things that we are putting in place are making a difference. But I think it is a longer term proposition to get to where we need to be.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I take your point that, with delivery, there are deadlines, pressures and so on, but I just want to ask about wellbeing and support, because NEMA ranks 103 out of 112 agencies. My office has been approached by a number of people with stories of bullying and harassment, and very poor culture in the agency. Also, last year, 15 per cent of respondents to the APS Employee Census reported bullying or harassment at NEMA, which is 50 per cent higher than the APS average. You have said, 'We need more direction and it's a high-pressure environment, so that probably accounts for the churn.' What accounts for bullying and harassment? How are you going to stop that? That's totally unacceptable.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I agree; the number is way too high. You never have an organisation that has zero cases of bullying and harassment. Our job has to be to drive that down as much as we possibly can, but in the right way and not because people don't want to report it. What we have seen is an increase in reporting of bullying and harassment, which paradoxically, for us, is heartening, in that people are trusting in the systems and feel confident that they can report bullying and harassment, but the number remains way too high and is another area of focus in our census action plan. Again, we've done a bit of a deep dive into the data to try to identify where that's occurring, and there'll be some targeted action around that. But at a general level, we have put in place greater capacity for people in the organisation to navigate our policies and understand what their entitlements are. We rolled out a capability called Ombpoint, which is a confidential service that our employees can go to. That is not EAP but in addition to EAP, and that helps them to understand how they can report and what supports are available to them, if they do experience bullying and harassment. But will you get no disagreement from me. It's absolutely an area of focus for us going forward, and we'll be putting in place measures to try and drive that down, as I say, appropriately, without stymieing people's capacity or desire to report those things when they do occur.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I have more questions, so I'll wait for another opening.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Senator Polley.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I have some questions to ask in relation to the Disaster Ready Fund. These relate to Tasmania and the integrated fire camera network. I wonder whether you could not only give us an update on the project but also outline the critical nature of its role in the bushfire season?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I'll ask Ms Cartwright to talk about that project. I'd just note that, as has been my previous testimony, we're yet to announce round-4 outcomes for Tassie, and that will happen imminently. But this project relates to one of the earlier rounds, and I'll ask Ms Cartwright to talk about it.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Yes, it's round 3, so it's pretty important.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: The Tasmanian Integrated Fire Camera Network project received $1.439 million in Australian Government funding under, as you rightly point out, DRF round 3. The remaining $2.187 million is being provided by the proponent, Sustainable Timber Tasmania, and its delivery proponents. The project will enhance Tasmania's early fire detection capability by integrating new and existing camera networks into a centralised online portal using AI enabled technology with human verification. The project is currently in planning and design, with the technical designs, frameworks and protocols being established. The project is due for completion in June 2028.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Another successful project was around building flood resilience in key areas of Glamorgan Spring Bay on the east coast of Tasmania. Can you give us an outline of and an update on the work that's been undertaken to achieve these improvements in resilience?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: The Building the Flood Resilience in Key Areas of Glamorgan Spring Bay project received approximately $504,000 in Australian Government funding under Disaster Ready round 3. The remaining $63,000, approximately, is being provided by the proponent, the Glamorgan Spring Bay Council. The project will improve flood resilience in Glamorgan Spring Bay by implementing effective infrastructure improvements and repairing management strategies. It will also trial river monitoring devices to provide early warning of flooding, and it will improve community awareness and preparedness. The project is in the stage of initiation. The grant agreement has been executed, work on the communication plan is due to begin shortly, and the project is due for completion in June 2028.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: When will round 4 be announced?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: The outcomes for three jurisdictions have been announced so far. The outcomes for Queensland and Victoria were announced last week, and the outcome for the ACT was announced this morning. The outcomes for the remaining jurisdictions will be announced over the next short period of time. As they are announced, we also publish, on the NEMA website, a list of the full suite of successful projects. We'll work with our lead agencies, and they will also handle their own communications with the proponents. That website also includes the first three rounds. So you've got all states in the first three rounds and the three states that have been announced in round 4, and they will be added to progressively as the further announcements occur over the next couple of weeks.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I'd just add that we have to work with jurisdictions around timing as well, so we'll settle those.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I also have a question that concerns WA. Can you update the committee on the Disaster Ready Fund project from round 3 that looks to mitigate the risks of seawater into South Carnarvon?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: The Mitigate the Risk of Seawater Inundation of South Carnarvon project received $5.58 million in Australian Government funding under Disaster Ready round 3. The remaining $625,000 is being provided by the proponent, the Shire of Carnarvon, and its delivery partners. The project aims to extend, upgrade and heighten the town's surge wall and coastal levee system to mitigate the risk of seawater inundation. The project is in planning and design stage, with concept designs and preliminary reports being completed. The project is due to be completed in December 2028.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Senator McDonald.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Just turning back to Disaster Relief Australia, there is something that I want to understand. You've identified a couple of existing groups that may or may not have the capacity to step into the shoes of the thousands of veterans who were previously undertaking the work of disaster recovery. Given that the government has stated that it will not be relying on the ADF following natural disasters so that Defence personnel can remain focused on their primary role of protecting and strengthening Australia's national security, how do you reconcile that and NEMA's capacity to deliver boots on the ground?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Senator McDonald, I might start and then ask officials to supplement my answer. I think your characterisation of the government's position is not entirely accurate. In fact, the government has always said that Defence will be available when required. We have also said that we need to make investments to supplement the capabilities that are available to local communities during and after a disaster, because Defence should not be the first port of call in every instance. It was on that basis that we made the investment that we did in Disaster Relief Australia. As I have done previously, I do want to acknowledge those volunteers who provided their commitment and effort to that organisation. I saw some of those volunteers and the work that they did, and I heard from local communities who benefited from that work. I think everyone in this room thinks that the people who committed to that organisation were good people, trying to do good things for their communities. We made a very substantial investment, and it was always on the basis that organisation become financially self-sustaining.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: But how, Minister?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Senator McDonald, perhaps I could just conclude, after which you can ask another question if you would like to. You've already heard from officials that they are actively considering options to further develop capability of this kind. The officials are not in a position to get ahead of a decision of government, but they have indicated to you that we recognise that this is an important area of policy work and they are undertaking that work.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I will table a press release from Senator the Hon. Murray Watt in which he says that the independent findings of the Defence Strategic Review recommend that the Australian Defence Force should 'only be used as a last resort' and 'will not be available for disaster recovery as normal'.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I don't think that's inconsistent with what I have just said. We have always indicated that they will be available; it's just that they ought not be the first point of call. That's why we have made the investments that we have in disaster recovery, being investments that were not made under the previous government. We have built a substantial national capability to supplement what's on offer from states and territories and, indeed, from local government.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Minister, that's the point that I think is contested. That is, under the coalition, the funding for Disaster Relief Australia was funded. This government stopped that funding and is now seeking advice from government on how to replace exactly the work that Disaster Relief Australia did: the capacity, the expertise of the volunteers, and the ability to harness Defence-trained veterans to go into places that are not well-served by the sorts of alternate organisations that might be flagged. I think that is the kind of capability that cannot be replaced by humans going into human situations to restore trust. At every estimates, we talk about how great Disaster Relief Australia was. I'll give you an example. In Townsville, an elderly man, who was over 80 years of age, rang me and wept because Disaster Relief Australia had provided a lawnmower for him to go and mow the lawns of widows of veterans and, with the demise of Disaster Relief Australia, he could no longer offer that service. That is a very small human example of the disaster that has occurred since the government allowed Disaster Relief Australia to fold.
