I can't understand how it would ever be the point of government that Disaster Relief Australia would be some standalone organisation when, like Defence and so many other government organisations, of course it should be funded by government. There is no other body who is going to fund it.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Senator McDonald, that was obviously a very long statement. Perhaps I can deal with a couple of matters. You are incorrect in saying that the government ceased funding. The government continued to provide resources to Disaster Relief Australia. On 31 December 2023, that organisation reported that milestone 2 of the agreement had been achieved. That was—they said; what they told government in 2023—that they had established a sustainable funding model, including staffing and financial diversification, to support long-term organisational viability. That was the advice to government. We've been through this in previous estimates. But in November 2025, NEMA received serious allegations regarding management of Disaster Relief Australia, including the possible misuse of Australian government funding—

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Which, when tested, was proven to be unfounded.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: and, Senator McDonald, you will appreciate that any responsible public sector organisation on receipt of serious allegations of that kind needs to address them. NEMA commenced a formal investigation under the Commonwealth Fraud and Corruption Control Framework. In the final report delivered on 26 May, there was not enough evidence to substantiate allegations of fraud and corruption against DRA, and NEMA then instructed the Business Grants Hub to release their milestone payment.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: And it was too late.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: On 29 May, a creditors' meeting was held, where it was decided that the organisation would be wound up.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: The government failed.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Senator McDonald, you may wish to assert that, upon receipt of serious allegations of fraud, the government should ignore those and continue to pay an organisation. I think most reasonable observers would say that is not a reasonable position.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: You're talking about an organisation that can't pay its own staff properly and has spent millions of dollars on consultants to be able to pay staff yet still fails to do so, which then does not continue to allow payments to be made to Disaster Relief Australia to keep the lights on and says, 'We're investigating fraud', where no evidence has been found to substantiate such a claim. Anybody who has run a business knows that the very predictable outcome was that organisation would fold, along with the thousands of volunteer veterans and the organisation's expertise. Now the government seeks to fill that hole by finding somebody else to do the work that the government had identified already that Disaster Relief Australia was doing such an exceptional job in delivering, as agreed by everyone, and it was government's failure to understand cash flow and the very basic commitments of business that allowed it to fold. That's a statement, and I don't expect you to respond to it.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I will respond to it, Senator McDonald, because I can inform the committee that the government will continue to apply the Commonwealth Fraud and Corruption Control Framework—

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: But the—

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: May I finish my answer? That is a non-negotiable position for this government. Should you be elected to government, you may take a different approach. You may consider that the Commonwealth Fraud and Corruption Control Framework isn't important. That's up to you, and I encourage you to go to the Australian people with that position. This government takes fraud and corruption allegations seriously, and we do have to deal with them. But it is the case that very substantial investments were made in Disaster Relief Australia, and we do acknowledge the very important work that was done by the volunteers who worked within that organisation.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: It's unacceptable.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Senator David Pocock.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I want to come back to the underpayments and payroll issues that we've been talking about during the last few estimates. Initially, NEMA execs tried to tell the Senate that it was limited to one or two staff and, clearly, it's not. At last estimates hearing, you told us that you were continuing to engage consultants to help with the payroll issues. How much has been spent on consultants to date?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I might pass to the Chief Operating Officer just to walk through some of those details. But while he finds those figures, perhaps I can give you an update since last estimates. As has been said, we have continued to consult with the workforce. We've looked at some of the enterprise agreement terms and conditions that we think were driving potentials in inaccurate pay outcomes. We've sought legal advice around those to settle the application of those enterprise agreement terms. You'll recall from, I think, previous evidence that we had some issues around the way people were reporting concerns in payroll. It was going to multiple inboxes—sometimes to personal inboxes, sometimes to Home Affairs and sometimes to us—which I think was one of the key failings in understanding themes that were emerging in payroll concerns. We have since rolled out a singular—

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I'm sorry, but do you not have an HR?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I'm coming to what we've done. We do have HR, but we are a shared service with Home Affairs. Home Affairs manages our payroll system. Historically, what has happened is that you have had staff who have sent queries to the payroll system in Home Affairs and to our HR area—they have sent them to individuals they know in our HR space—and we have not had that singular view of the issues that are impacting on payroll.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I'm sorry to cut in here again, but you've got, what, 120 staff in NEMA?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: There are about 400 staff in NEMA.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Why is there not just an email to all staff saying, 'If you have payroll issues, email this email address'? How did we get to this point?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: There is very much now a clear singular point for—

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Why is it taking so long? We're paying execs half a million bucks or so.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: There are a few things in a run-up like this. Firstly, you have a workforce who know about shared services arrangements. They may have contacts and colleagues who work in Home Affairs, for example, in the HR area. They may have colleagues whom they know in our HR area. So, notwithstanding comms going out to people about, 'Report your HR payroll concerns here', people will choose a multitude of paths in order to do that, particularly—

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Especially when it doesn't seem as though they're being taken seriously. But can we just go to the number first?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Senator Pocock, I understand that you might be a little frustrated.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: He is chewing up my time.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I appreciate that, but officials at the table are entitled to answer questions without interruption.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: The question wasn't about this, though. It was about the number.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: You also can't direct officials in how to answer your questions. If we could please proceed with your asking questions and giving the official at the table the time to respond, I'd be grateful. I then would have to intervene less.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: The question was: how much has been spent on consultants to date?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: This is as of 31 August, exclusive of GST. We have paid KordaMentha $300,000 for payroll remediation work. We have paid KordaMentha $252,164 for payroll review work. We have paid KPMG $372,500 to do the internal audit compliance review. So all these add up to a total figure of $924,664.12, exclusive of GST.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Is everything sorted now? After spending almost a million dollars, have payroll issues been sorted, or are there still ongoing, unresolved issues?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: There are still some ongoing, unresolved issues.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: How is that the case?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text:
It's very easy to oversimplify what it takes to address a payroll issue of 400 people over multiple years, where terms and conditions across each pay could be different. I don't want to give you the impression that this is a simple matter of 'just go in and fix a single individual's pay'. There are a multitude of allowances that are available to people and a multitude of different terms and conditions, and there are about 110 business rules that have been in place over an extended period. So it is a complex endeavour, and that would be the first point that I'd make. What I was talking about before was the progress that we have made to date. We have assured ourselves that we have an agreed understanding of the terms and conditions in our enterprise agreement. We have worked through—and part of the KordaMentha work was working through—where there were discrepancies between our payroll system, the system that makes pay to people, and our terms and conditions in the enterprise agreement. We have made the difficult decision to take our payroll services to a shared service provision under the Department of Industry, which services, I think, about 17 clients across the Commonwealth, in order to set up a payroll system that is properly aligned to our enterprise agreement going forward. We're in the process of transitioning our payroll services across to our new service provider to make sure that, going forward, we don't have any of these problems; and that every time there's an update to our enterprise agreement, that is done accurately and as it relates specifically to NEMA. So, in setting up the future, they are available to us. That was the first port of call. An enormous amount of effort has gone into that, in order to understand the system, any discrepancies in the payroll services, how to properly configure our payroll system going forward and how to transition to a new provider, which will take place in the next couple of months.

Having fixed the problem going forward, we then can turn our mind to the remediation of past pay issues. A couple of options are available to us, and we are still assessing which of those is the most effective and efficient use of Commonwealth resources. It could be taking a newly configured payroll system, washing all the historical data through that system and then determining where there are discrepancies between what it should have been and what it was. That's one option, and that's a big undertaking. Alternatively, through analysis of parallel payroll processing, where we run payroll in the new system and compare that to the old system, it could be homing in on particular areas and creating a standard loan model to do that. So I'm trying to give you the impression that a lot of work has happened, and this is not a simple endeavour just to resolve.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: If you are going to have to do that to figure out how to solve it, what did the million dollars get us? You knew that you had a problem and you still know that you have a problem, and now you are proposing two different solutions to figure out how much underpayment or overpayment occurred, but we've shelled out a million bucks to get us to this point.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Indeed, and I remain comfortable that expenditure has been value for money. The KPMG report was the first insight into the systemic nature of it, which report we've released in a question on notice to this committee. In that report, they did a thorough analysis of all the various issues that could be impacting on payroll. That was an important piece of work to get done so that we could understand the magnitude, or size and scale, of it. As to the work with KordaMentha, they've been assisting us in leading to the resolution. So the configuration of systems has all been a part of that work, which, as I say, is no small endeavour.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: What is the scale of it? What's the total overpayments and the total underpayments?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Currently, from a remediation perspective, that work will happen once we move to the new payroll system, but, as KPMG had identified—I'll just open the—

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I think from memory it was something like a $1.7 million potential overpayment and a $1.6 million potential underpayment.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: It is $1.86 million which is underpayment, and $1.537 million overpayment. This is a potential over and underpayment. It's not a remediation outcome, because the KPMG report mentioned you will have to undertake a detailed analysis of the remediation process, looking at pay rules for each employee. This is only a—

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: It's a statistical estimation of overs and unders. It's not something that you can take action on an individual's pay profile.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: So for $370,000 KPMG basically just said, 'You have a problem'? They didn't say—

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text:
From a KPMG perspective, they highlighted the areas where there were differences, sort of, which were raising these overs and unders. As a result of that, we have undertaken a number of steps to address the concerns. As an example, firstly, we started with an enterprise entitlements position paper, which was circulated to the staff so that there was a common understanding of the employee entitlements. So that was the first thing which happened.

Then, as part of the KordaMentha first payroll review, we now have a single HR query portal system, which was launched in September. As an example, if I go into the HR portal system, from 9 September till 22 October we have received 138 queries. This is new progress which has been made. Out of the 138 queries, as at 22 October 134 queries have been resolved. Four remained in progress. Out of 138, 83 related to payroll matters, where the questions were around payroll related inquiries related to processing of overtime payments, time off in lieu, restriction allowance, higher duty updates, assistance with timesheets. Out of that, only one matter related to a potential underpayment issue, as it was a query about application of a meal allowance during overtime. A further inquiry concerned a request for accrued TOIL to be paid out and was an entitlement administration matter rather than an identified underpayment. Progress has been made, so we are addressing these queries.

Further, we are also updating on a regular ongoing basis, which is the monthly update to the Fair Work Ombudsman, how we are going. We are providing monthly updates to the CPSU and monthly updates to all staff by the Chief People Officer. The Interim Coordinator-General and the Deputy Coordinator-General, EMR, are having stand-ups with the CCT and NSR staff.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Do you mind tabling that KPMG report, please?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: We already have in a question on notice. We've released the report in full to you.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Minister, can I get your take here? The Senate has been asking questions for a long time on this. There are still $1.86 million underpayments and $1.53 million overpayments. How is this acceptable? Your government comes down really hard on the private sector. Clearly our payroll system is incredibly complex. The award system has to be simplified. What does the government have to say when departments can't get it right but we're cracking the whip with the private sector on underpayments and overpayments? Is this acceptable?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Our government considers that paying employees correctly and on time should be a priority for all of our departments. We're supportive of the work that Mr Hetherington and his team have been doing to remediate the issues that have been identified.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Wage theft is illegal in the private sector, but it seems like in the public sector, a year later, a million bucks in consultants and people still haven't been paid what they were owed.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Our expectation is that people should receive the correct pay, and we are, as I've indicated, supportive of the work that's being undertaken and that officials have spoken to you about at length this morning.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Is there a date at which people will have been paid for work that they've done?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I will take this as the final question before I rotate the call.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I'll ask Mr Hetherington to update on the point at which we expect this to conclude.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: We expect this to be finalised within this financial year. You'll see that we've accounted for this in our financial statements. We've declared it as an issue. We've created a provision to make good payments for staff in this financial year. That's available in our annual report. To your point—all of the effort that we've described and the expenditure that we've described is in order to make sure that we are compliant with the law. I take that very seriously as the accountable authority. This is a matter for the agency to resolve. Minister McBain has made it very clear to me that she expects this issue to be resolved as quickly as is humanly possible. But I make the point that it is complex and that I need to get it right. If I rush and we don't get this thing done properly and we don't set it up for the future, we will find ourselves with pay issues on an ongoing basis. We've been absolutely transparent with the staff. We've been transparent with this committee. We've been transparent with the Fair Work Ombudsman. I have been transparent with this committee, and we will continue to be transparent with all of the stakeholders in this until we get it right. I make that commitment to you.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Senator McDonald.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Reflecting on the line of questioning from Senator Pocock, it strikes me that if NEMA were held to the same standards that Disaster Relief Australia was, then the government would withhold funding to your organisation until they were satisfied that you were not breaching the law and you were paying employees properly. Who's held accountable to the same standards that we hold small businesses and other government contractors to when their payments are withheld? Will you just continue being paid?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I don't agree that the two things are comparable. We're not talking about a case of fraud or corruption in respect of payroll. I appreciate that it is an issue that we need to resolve and that we are currently not compliant with the Fair Work Act in that regard, and we are working to resolve that. But we are not talking about allegations of fraud which were received with respect to the DRA.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I think millions of Australians who are frustrated by government waste would disagree with you and ask why there will be no boots on the ground at the next flooding event in—pick a place in Australia; Far North Queensland—but the NEMA staff will continue to be paid despite not holding themselves to the same standards that we hold other organisations to.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I realise this was a throwaway line, but I don't want to leave that unattended. Our government is absolutely committed to being a good partner to Queensland and to all of the other states and territories that we work with to respond to disasters when they arise. Our government has made substantial investments to uplift our national capability so that we can do that. I wouldn't want your remark to be interpreted as there being a lack of support during the higher risk weather season. In fact, you've heard this morning about the steps that have been taken, working with our government partners and our private sector partners, to prepare for exactly those scenarios that we know and, regrettably, that we can expect to increase in frequency and intensity in the coming decades.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Your statement is comforting, but I fear that the thousands of boots on the ground that were provided by DRA are now not being filled. I've asked questions on notice about the emergency stockpile, but I fear that we have lost capability that is not being replaced, and unfortunately who is right will be proven out by the next disaster and whether or not people turn up to do the work that we know was done so capably by Disaster Relief Australia.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: The government continues to invest in ensuring that we do have the resources that are necessary to support communities. It's a very different approach to the approach that was taken by the previous government, when requests for resources were rejected, including during a very significant fire season.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Talk is cheap. It'll be whether there are boots on the ground. My question now is about the Northern Australia NAFI app, North Australia and Rangelands Fire Information Service. What funding has the Commonwealth committed to NAFI for 2025-26 and each subsequent financial year?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I'll pass that question on to Karina Menday, the Assistant Coordinator-General, but just to summarise that we do think that NAFI is a very important database that obviously provides that information about current fires, history, mapping of fires, burnt areas and really assists with Indigenous fire rangers and land management owners in managing fires into the future. It's a very important database in terms of the work that they do in that part of the world.
witness_position: Deputy Coordinator-General, Emergency Management and Response

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: In the 2025-26 MYEFO, the Australian government provided $1.48 million to NAFI over two years and, in addition to that, $0.35 million to the Business Grants Hub in the industry portfolio to manage the grant on our behalf. That funding is through to 30 June next year.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: So there's no further funding after that?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: At this point it's a matter for government.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Is that funding secured under a formal agreement with Charles Darwin University?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: That's correct, yes.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: So that was $238,000 that you paid to the Grants Hub to administer that funding?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: It's $0.35 million, and that's over the two years.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: So that's $350,000 over two years is paid to the Grants Hub to administer that?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: That's correct.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: What would you expect the Grants Hub to do for $350,000?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: We work with the Business Grants Hub because we don't have a grants management capability in NEMA. When Business Grants Hub establishes a new grant, there's a fair bit of cost associated with creating a new grant.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Contract, photocopier, maybe send an email?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Not quite, and detailed questions on what Business Grants Hub does should be directed to them directly. Setting up a new grant does take a bit more time than just creating new programs under a particular grant.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: But it's not a new grant. How long has NAFI been funded for?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: NAFI has been funded since 2013, but through successive different government departments that have been responsible for it at different times.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: $350,000—$175,000 a year for somebody else to do a job, which is manage bushfires. Extraordinary!

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: As Ms Menday said, those questions could be directed to the business—

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I absolutely will, but I can't believe that you'd sign off on that. I don't want to get stuck on this, because I've run out of time. I will ask the Grants Hub. We know that in February 2026 ABC Rural reported problems with NASA's ageing Terra satellite could result in gaps of 10 to 12 hours in detecting fires. What has been done to point to a new satellite system?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: We became aware of those reports as well and have worked really closely with NAFI to understand what that capability gap might mean. We also talked with other relevant government agencies, including Geoscience Australia and the Space Agency, to understand what those needs are. It's not an Australian-owned asset, so there's not a great deal that we can do. More detailed questions could be directed to Geoscience. But certainly we're continuing to work with NAFI and other partners to understand what those capability gaps might mean.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Does the southern Australia fire monitoring system use Terra as well?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Are you referring to the National Bushfire Intelligence Capability?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: What's it called?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: NBIC.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: NBIC?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: NBIC, yes. NBIC is a national capability, and NBIC does complement the work of NAFI, so it draws on information that NAFI provides and uses that data to then undertake its work. The two services complement one another. NAFI is a very operationally focused service. It's used by land managers, it's used by Indigenous ranger groups and it's very focused on information about bushfires that are happening at the time or historic kind of burn data. NBIC is more of a capability that analyses and then models how we're dealing with bushfire hazard into the future as well. It will take into account climate change predictions and things like that.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: So it's using Terra as well? It's using the same satellite system?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: It's using NAFI data.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: So given that this is the one tool that, as I talk to station managers and farm operators across Northern Australia, they tell me is the only useful thing that government provides for them, I hope that government will look to re-funding this project and potentially funding it adequately so that they can utilise a satellite system that doesn't have a 10- to 12-hour gap, which could be the difference between losing homes, infrastructure and livestock. I will move on from that. I want to return to the AusAlert system. I'm interested that it's been proclaimed as a success. I had seven staff in my office in Townsville on the day of the alert. Half of them didn't receive an alert. I went through and checked that they had the most up-to-date software, that they had updated their codes, that they were using phones that were compliant, and that they were hooked up to Telstra. They ticked all of those boxes, and only half of them received a notification. I wonder if NEMA has any capacity to understand who didn't get a message? How can you proclaim this as a success when 50 per cent of my office didn't get a message?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: I'll ask the team to walk through some of the success measures and what the capability does and doesn't do, to the second part of your question. We know on the day we declared 94 per cent of cell towers broadcast the message. When we reviewed that technical data after the event, for those towers that were available—telcos will sleep towers or towers will be in repair—99 per cent of available towers broadcast that message. In addition to other technical data we've received from telcos, we then did a survey, a representative survey, of about 4,052 people across the country to get a better sense of the experience throughout the national test. It indicated strongly something like 80 per cent or 85 per cent of people reported having received the message, so had compatible devices in order to do that. We know that a like jurisdiction started out much lower than that. New Zealand started out with something like 30 per cent compatibility and has grown over time. We've started at a much higher bar than that.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: What percentage was Australia's?

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: So 86 per cent of people reported receiving that message in a representative survey. An incredibly high number of people were expecting to receive that. 95 per cent of people knew that it was a test, knew that they didn't need to take action, and so the comms campaign that was around that was highly successful. That, in addition to the community-based trials, where we had the opportunity to test a wide variety of different circumstances and devices, gave us great confidence that we were ready to go live. We also received something like 20,000-odd submissions online of people reporting their experiences. We are going through the process of theming some of those things. I would be interested in digging into the particular circumstances of your staff phones, because that does not gel with the rest of the data that we're seeing, to be perfectly honest, and also doesn't gel with the reports we've had from jurisdictions around it as well. So it would be interesting to look into that.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Surveys are always self-selecting, aren't they? I'm out of time; could you provide that information on notice.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Thank you so much for answering all of the questions for the committee this morning. I expect you'll get a number of questions on notice.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Yes.

agency: National Emergency Management Agency
text: Thank you for your patience and for staying longer on the program than we had you scheduled. Thank you for all of the work that you do. You are now released.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I now welcome Senator the Hon. Murray Watt, representing the Minister for Home Affairs. I also call officers from the Department of Home Affairs, including the Australian Border Force and the Illicit Tobacco and E-cigarette Commissioner, for cross-portfolio, corporate and general matters. Minister, do you have an opening statement?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I do not, other than to say there is nowhere on earth I would rather be.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Secretary, do you have an opening statement?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I do.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Please proceed.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text:
I want to begin by expressing my horror at the abhorrent attack on the member for Indi, Dr Helen Haines, last week. Violence of this kind has no place in our community. My thoughts are with Dr Haines, her family, her staff, her friends and her community at this very difficult time. We are working hard with colleagues across the Home Affairs portfolio and Finance to engage with parliamentarians to ensure we understand their concerns and needs and to provide all possible assistance.

I would now like to reflect briefly on a few key highlights of the department's achievements since I last provided an opening statement to this committee in February 2026. I've spoken previously about the devastating antisemitic terrorist attack at Bondi Beach. That attack has continued to shape our work. Since February we've supported the listing of Hizb ut-Tahrir and White Australia as prohibited hate groups. We've coordinated the government response to the interim report of the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion. We appointed a full-time Counter Terrorism Coordinator, Mr Brendan Dowling. We've progressed reforms to the National Firearms Agreement in support of the launch of the National Gun Buyback Scheme, and we've ensured all interim report recommendations are complete or on track to be completed by the end of the year.

This work has taken place alongside escalating conflict in the Middle East, rapid changes in the threat and technology environment, major reforms to cybersecurity and sustained operational pressures, all of which have placed demands on our organisation and our people. We've also supported government on a suite of significant migration reforms, delivered our migration and humanitarian programs in full, significantly reduced our protection visa caseload, increased citizenship finalisations by 45 per cent and more than halved our citizenship caseload.

The ABF commissioner will speak in more detail to the ABF's achievements, but I wanted to note in particular their enforcement successes. Over the reporting period they have seized or prevented the importation of 15.7 tonnes of illicit drugs and precursors, 2.25 billion illicit cigarettes, 593 tonnes of loose-leaf tobacco and 13.2 million vaping products. We've also supported the introduction of 20 portfolio bills to the Australian parliament, with 14 receiving royal assent in the same period.

All of this took place in the context of a voluntary redundancy round which saw us lose more than 700 staff in a tight fiscal environment to ensure we operated within our budget. Last week we tabled our 2025-26 annual report. I'm proud to say that we met or substantially met more than 90 per cent of our targets and delivered a financial result for 2025-26 that saw a small operating deficit of 0.4 of 1 per cent of our total budget.

I have spoken publicly about the combined impact of these factors on our staff and how that was reflected through our census results this year. Many of our indices declined from the high levels recorded in 2025, which was disappointing but not surprising in the context of this very tough year. Importantly, the longer term trajectory since 2023 indicates that we remain on track to improve as an organisation. While some indicators fell slightly over that period, important measures showed strong growth. The proportion of employees who would recommend Home Affairs as a good place to work increased from 57 per cent in 2023 to 65 per cent in 2026. Likewise, the proportion who felt inspired to identify new, better ways of working increased from 41 per cent to 50 per cent. Overall, the majority of our census results have improved over the past three years. That said, we take the 2026 results seriously. Our staff have been clear about where we need to focus and we're listening.

The past year has tested us. It has also demonstrated the strength, resilience and capability of our people. I want to thank all of our staff for what they have achieved together. Finally, as we did in May, we have ensured that all necessary witnesses are available in outcome 1 to respond to questions relating to Bondi and the royal commission.

text: The department statement said that the environment had changed post Bondi and therefore a need for sustained leadership presence. What specifically changed for the role, given the threat level hasn't changed?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text:
Again, let me answer in the general but in a way which I hope will be helpful. We sometimes find ourselves in a position, as I said, where we're not able to respond to or to agree to a very specific request, but we will work with the person on what other arrangements might be possible. In terms of the change, we were not long after a very horrific terrorist attack. We had changed our arrangements internally in the department. The teams were under very significant pressure and remain in that situation. If I can again speak generally, one of the concerns that we have in a situation like that is whether or not the particular flexible arrangement of compressed hours is able to be managed. When someone works compressed hours, it means that they do a standard number of hours spread across a smaller number of days. For example, a standard number of hours spread across four days—not five. The salary that's attracted is the same for those four days of compressed hours. This means that, if someone were part time for four days, normally we would be able to act someone in the role on the fifth day so we had sustained leadership presence, but that's not available to us without additional cost to the department, to the taxpayer. Compressed hours is a particular form that carries with it a number of characteristics that we need to manage.

The other thing that we need to take into account with compressed hours is the fact that most SES do not work a standard number of hours. Many SES are working in excess of those standard hours and therefore might often be working the same number of hours per day as the employee on compressed hours but working five days instead of four. I'm sorry, I'm getting quite technical here, but they're all the considerations that we take into account when we assess whether or not we can accommodate a specific request. As I said at the outset, if the specific request isn't one which we can agree to, we will always work with the employee on alternatives.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And no SES in there?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: SES aren't technically part of the voluntary redundancy scheme. That applies to staff employed under the enterprise agreement. We did, though, make available to SES staff the opportunity to indicate if they wish to take an incentive to retire, which is the equivalent for SES, and we assessed that on much the same basis. Is this a role that we could either manage without or reorganise around? In each case we were clearly responding to the individual's interest but looking at the organisation's interests in making those decisions.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: How many of those incentives were offered and how many were taken up?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Six were accepted and, I think, seven were offered.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I wonder if now is a good time to share the call.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: One further question on this, perhaps on notice: in what areas were those SES offers accepted?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I might need to take that one on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Shoebridge.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Given the time, rather than traversing some of the questions that we've heard about restructuring, I might just move to a couple of discrete issues about answers to questions on notice. One of the first issues is that what we find repeatedly is, for example, when we put questions on notice in the May sessions, we will wait three, four, five, six, seven months and then get an answer that comes in. The answers that come in give us data up until the end of March. I could point you to 30 examples of this. We ask a question in May, we get an answer in September and the data is backdated to March. By the time we get that answer in September, it's pretty much useless, because six months have moved on and it's not timely. I'm trying to understand from a department's perspective why this happens. Perhaps some of it is the delay in matters being with the minister's office. If so, if you know that a question hasn't been answered, is there a process where you can update the draft answer that's sitting with the minister's office so that the answers can actually be timely and helpful?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I will get the experts in the area to help me, but my understanding is that we set a date. In order to be able to answer the questions, we say we will do these questions as at a particular date. To my knowledge, we have never contemplated a process of revisiting it if they are not lodged.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The issue has become kind of chronic because of the delay. We will come to where that delay happens later. It appears that a lot of the delays are in the minister's office in that questions are being provided to the minister's office by the department. Are you tracking when the minister actually signs off and answers them? Does that responsibility lie in the department, or is it solely a matter for the minister once you put a draft across?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I would need the team to answer the tracking question, but I believe we do keep a record of when they're actually lodged. It doesn't quite go to the question of timing, but we have actually lodged 99 per cent of the 1,202 questions we received in May.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: When you say 'lodged', what do you mean?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Lodged with the committee.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: With the committee? That may well be the case, but of course now we're in October. For example, we were seeking answers about the number of partner visa subclass 300 and 309 visas provided. That answer came in September, well past the deadline for provisions, and the answer referenced March data. We know that, as at September, when we got the answer, you would have had the end of financial year data. What I'm asking is: when you know that delay has happened, when you know that the data is then stale, is there a process in place where you, knowing your questions haven't been answered, can actually update the data so it's actually useful? This process is meant to be useful. Your obligations here are to provide as much assistance as you can. This seems like a space where, given the delay appears to be in the minister's office and not yours, you could update those answers.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I indicated before that I am not aware that a process of that nature has been contemplated. I understand the perspective you are coming from. From a departmental perspective, that would be doubling the workload of responding to the questions, because we would do it once and then we would do it again.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: But the work would be purposeful, because the answers you give would actually be useful, and it would be far better to actually spend a little bit more time and make the answer useful than what we're getting currently—stale, out-of-date data because of the incredible delays.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm acknowledging your point, but saying that at the time they're being prepared they're being prepared with relevant data. Were we to update them before lodgement, that would be the department responding twice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: At the time I buy milk, it's fine. If I leave it in the fridge for six months, it's undrinkable. This is the same issue. You've bought the milk, you've given it to the minister's office and it's turned into yoghurt. We would like a timely answer. Could I ask you to take on notice whether or not there are systems that can be reviewed to ensure the answers are purposeful and useful for the parliament's use and therefore the public's?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Extra points if you include jokes about milk!

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes, I was hesitant to take it on notice for fear that you would feel that was—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In this case, I promise I won't take offence. I won't make a yoghurt joke. In this case, I think it's entirely reasonable to take it on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I will take it on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We now might go to some of the delay that has become apparent in the answers. Minister, you will recall on the last occasion, I think there were some 40 questions that were answered at 8 pm the night before, sometime between 8 pm the night before, and 9 am in the morning of estimates. Do you remember that exchange, Minister?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I remember us discussing questions on notice pretty much every estimates hearing.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. Just to refresh your memory, what I will ask is: for each of the 40 questions that were answered between 8 pm last night and 9 am this morning that were finally put on notice, when did the minister get the proposed answer by the department and when was it provided to the minister's office? Ms Foster, I recognise your reticence today, partly because we had this exchange where you said, 'We can take that on notice for you.' I remember that moment.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I believe we have answered that question.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text:
You did, and the answer that came back was:

The answers to questions on notice that were provided to the Senate Standing Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs Secretariat on Tuesday, 26 May 2026 and Wednesday, 27 May 2026 were first provided to the Minister's office between 17 November 2025 and 12 May 2026.

Minister, I know this isn't your portfolio, but can you seek an explanation from the minister about why a draft answer sat on the minister's desk from 17 November 2025 and wasn't provided until 26 or 27 May?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I can take that on notice, yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Minister, in your ministerial responsibilities in terms of your responsibilities to the parliament, do you think a more than six-month delay in a matter having sat on a minister's desk, even though you've been given the pre-chewed answer from the department, is consistent with responsible government?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm not going to give an opinion. You would be aware that, at estimates, opinions are not provided. As I've repeatedly said to you, Senator Shoebridge, every time we have this discussion, the government, whether it be ministers, public servants or ministers' offices, does everything it can to respond to the exponentially growing number of questions on notice that it receives. In this portfolio, at the budget estimates this year in May, 1,211 questions on notice were asked just in that one estimates session, the highest that have ever been asked. To give you a comparative figure, three years earlier, in May 2023, 864 were asked. When we are seeing a 50 per cent increase in the number of questions on notice, in addition to the doubling of orders to produce documents, that is jamming up the system. I have recognised previously that, while the Greens are contributing to that increasing number, primarily the increasing number is coming from the coalition and from one coalition senator in particular, Senator Hume, who has consistently submitted over 70 per cent of all questions on notice that are asked at each estimates. This has consequences, I'm afraid.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Minister, I can't conceive of what reasonable explanation there can be for a draft answer sitting on the minister's desk from 17 November 2025. It's been drafted by the department with its expertise and assistance. I cannot conceive of what possible satisfactory explanation can be given for it then sitting for six months in the minister's office, being dusted off once a month and not being provided.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I've taken that on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Minister, you would have heard my questions to the secretary about circumstances where the delay has made the data stale. In those circumstances, is your government open to having a quick exchange with the department to ensure the information that's been provided to the parliament is timely?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I also heard Ms Foster take that question on notice, and I think it's appropriate that she has the opportunity to respond. On behalf of the government, a substantial reason for what you argue are unreasonable delays is the sheer volume of questions on notice that we are having to answer. I know it must be frustrating for you that answers take longer than you would like to be provided, but we can pick out isolated examples—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I gave 40 examples.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We can pick out isolated examples of draft answers that have remained with ministers' offices for a period. It's not as if they're the only ones they're dealing with. There were 1,211 just from the last budget estimates.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm not here to answer Senator Hume. I was asking about the 40 questions. Those are not isolated examples. Of course, Minister, if your government committed to actually providing timely and direct answers in the course of these proceedings and giving the data that's requested, the answers that are requested, in the course of these proceedings rather than taking so many questions on notice, you would save yourself a lot of work. It's much simpler to simply tell us the answer in these proceedings rather than have it churn its way through the notice process. That commitment from your government would go a long way to addressing this.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's why in my experience—as someone who sits through pretty much every day of estimates and every night—the overwhelming number of questions that are asked at estimates hearings are answered during the hearing. Of course, there will be questions that require a level of detail that those appearing at the table don't have or where discussions need to be held as to whether a public interest immunity needs to be claimed. There always will be questions that need to be taken on notice. I know from your point of view that you don't want your answers being slowed down by Senator Hume, for example, asking 10,657 of the 14,400 questions on notice that were asked at budget estimates, but we can't show preferential treatment to one senator or one party over another. There are thousands of these. It would be in everyone's interests if these processes—questions on notice, orders to produce documents and all of the other processes that are available—are used in a more responsible and targeted manner.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think we come back to the point that there is a potentially mutual frustration here in the delays in answers. With all respect, I will take issue with your view that the questions are largely answered in proceedings. That is not my experience, and I do not think it is the public's experience when they watch these exchanges. At the end of the day, the public deserve this process to work. They deserve timely answers. This is public money that your government is spending. Ms Foster is paid by the public. Ms Tressler is paid by the public. Mr Berlis is paid by the public. And you, Minister, are paid by the public. To retain trust with the public, timely answers about where money is being spent and about how policies are directed is critical. I know that we've seen the Secretary of PM&C and others offer critique and share some of the frustrating engagements that we have, but, if you're talking about making the process work, and we're committed to restoring trust, can I urge you to do whatever you require on that side of the table to take fewer questions on notice, to answer questions simply and fairly, and let's make it a joint project in restoring the trust.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We are happy to do that. We equally would request senators to use a little bit more judgement about what is actually required to be put on notice. To give you some comfort, Senator Shoebridge, in this portfolio, of the 1,211 questions that were asked on notice at the May estimates, only nine are outstanding. Of the 860 questions that were asked in February this year, only three are outstanding. It is a very small proportion that remain outstanding of a large and exponentially growing number of questions that are asked.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I would also remind senators that we do have to ask some questions in Senate estimates rather than just make statements.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'll take that on notice!

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Payman.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sorry, just one further point—it is not only, of course, the questions that are asked in the hearing on notice. Ms Foster has just pointed out to me that, of the 1,211 questions on notice that were asked in this portfolio in the May estimates this year, 1,033 of them were submitted after estimates as written questions, which means that, for all of your claims that we continually take questions on notice, that works out to about 80 questions that were taken on notice in the hearing out of 1,211.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In terms of hearing that 80 questions have been taken on notice in the course of these hearings, you may think that's a small number. It's a—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Let's count the number of answers that are given, like the one I just gave right that second.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You say potayto; I say potahto.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I feel like this is entirely unhelpful. Senator Payman, you have the call.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: On that previous line of questioning, I understand that Ms Warner's position was made involuntarily redundant. Was her role considered not essential?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We have not had any involuntary redundancies through the program either at SES or at staff level. The process for SES is that they can either seek or be offered an incentive to retire, and the choice about whether to accept that incentive to retire lies with the employee.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Is anyone working in that role or a comparable role right now?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: My understanding is yes. If that's incorrect, I will correct the record.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Ms Warner submitted an FOI for documents relating to her return to work. The released FOI includes 17 documents. I'm curious to understand why the department claimed that the volume of documents was so immense that they needed more time and delayed the request.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I don't have the details of that. If the FOI team or decision-maker is here, I would invite them to assist; otherwise, we will try and get you an answer on the timing and the reasons for that.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Is your FOI team here?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm not sure whether it will be the FOI central team or the decision-makers who would be in another outcome.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I will continue with that line of questions. You can take them on notice. The department redacted significant portions of the documents released while citing public interest grounds. How can personal information of an individual which was requested by that individual for their own information be against the public interest?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Again, that would require a detailed examination of the documents. That's not information I have available to me, so we may have to take your questions about the process on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The department also claimed public interest redactions on the basis of impacting officers' willingness to give advice. However, the FOI guidelines specifically state this is not sufficient ground to not release on its own. Why didn't the department follow the FOI guidelines?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm very confident that the department would have attempted to and believed it was following the guidelines. Let me take that on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Does the department often fail to adhere to the FOI guidelines when responding to FOI requests?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: As I said earlier, my understanding is that we always seek to and intend to comply with the FOI guidelines.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Ms Warner submitted an internal review request and received a response citing, in effect, that the department was too busy to meet its statutory timeframes for the review. How many FOI internal reviews does the department currently have?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I might ask the head of the FOI area to join me for that kind of generic departmental advice. A general statement is that we have an extraordinarily high number of FOI requests. We have quite a significant team assigned to processing them. I obviously have to make judgements about the various responsibilities that I have and how to allocate resources to that. We put as much into the FOI processing as we can, but we do struggle to meet the timeframes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: How many FOI internal review requests does the department currently have?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think we have seven internal reviews at the moment, but if that's incorrect I will correct the record.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: How many FOI internal reviews has the department failed to review within the statutory timeframe?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I would have to take that on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Where the department can't meet the 30-day timeframe, does it still complete the reviews and notify people?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We do. It is our practice to continue to service the FOI request even when we don't meet the statutory timeframes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Wonderful. But you will get back to me on how many haven't met that timeframe?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Duniam.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I only have one more set of questions for the corporate section. Back on the voluntary redundancies, there was a cost of those voluntary redundancies of $70.5 million. What is the projected saving per annum?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In the first year, the projected saving is $90 million, and then that accumulates over time.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Is that $90 million net or inclusive? Would it be $20 million in the first year? On notice, if I can have perhaps the projection over the forward estimates of that saving.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Certainly. As you know, the reason for undertaking the program was to ensure we could meet our staffing costs within our allocated budget.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Indeed. Could I confirm that firearm and gun buyback questions are outcome 3?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: One.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We will come to that shortly. On the OpenAI unauthorised access matter that we have, I know that will be a—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Outcome 1.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes, outcome 1. What is included in terms of estimates of cost for replacement legacy systems et cetera?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: For the department?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We can certainly ask our deputy secretary for technology to join us and talk through how we're approaching this in the department.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Maybe we will have a quick chat about that, but we might come back in outcome 1 to some more substantive questions. I'm interested in what is happening in Home Affairs.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The Home Affairs angle is a cross-portfolio set of questions, so it would be most sensible to do that now. When we come to our role more broadly for cybersecurity, that's outcome 1.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Perfect. I do have questions for you in that area. The review that was undertaken, I presume, uncovered databases and IT systems that required updating within Home Affairs and agencies?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In relation to the OpenAI incident, we're not able to comment publicly on our responses to those cyber incidents. It creates information that's available to cyber threat actors that can increase risk.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Work was undertaken in response to that. I do not want to know which databases were the subject of this, but were databases or IT systems identified that required some form of remedial action?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Is your question specifically in relation to OpenAI?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That was a point in time, a catalyst event, if you will. It caused most people to reflect and think there are updates required here across government and probably commercial or private entities as well. Without it being in response to specific events that occurred as part of the Services Australia unauthorised access, there was a body of work undertaken across government around reviews of security, robustness of databases and IT systems. Has this happened in Home Affairs? Were systems identified? Has work been undertaken, and, if so, at what cost?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The direction was issued by Home Affairs with its whole-of-government hat on, but clearly Home Affairs, the department, was one of the recipients of that direction. Like all other government departments, we are reviewing all of our systems. We were directed in that direction to undertake a stocktake of legacy systems. The work we are currently undertaking is in progress. We don't have an estimate of cost yet, unless Ms Walker wants to correct me. The very first point that Ms Walker made is that we will need to assess, once we have completed the stocktake, what can be shared publicly and what will be damaging in terms of giving an advantage to our adversary. However, we're not yet at the point where we know the answers, can make that assessment and can therefore answer you, but the process is absolutely underway.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I will come back to the whole-of-government approach being undertaken by Home Affairs and then of course through relevant agencies, but, in terms of the stocktake that you're currently undertaking, when do we expect to have that done?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: There were two different deadlines: one was for systems of government significance, which are the most critical systems for government—and my memory is that was end of December—and then I think it was end of March for all other systems.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I understand we have one more block of questions from Senator David Pocock.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I have some questions about cybersecurity and access to frontier AI models. What access does Home Affairs have to so-called frontier models?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We will have all the experts here in outcome 1 to cover cybersecurity. Whilst I understand you're asking specifically about Home Affairs, it's actually a policy question rather than a departmental question. As soon as we go to outcome 1, we can cover those issues.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I asked because OpenAI have said that it has offered Daybreak access to Services Australia, the Victorian Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, the New South Wales national parks and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, but I didn't see Home Affairs on that list. I thought this was probably corporate. I would be happy to wait for the next section if it can't be answered here.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Across the Commonwealth, ASD is taking the lead on how departments are working with and using frontier AI models in terms of our own systems. The question would probably also be useful to be directed there.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: If any of the officers from outcome 1 can assist, I will invite them to join us; otherwise, I think we will be shortly moving to that outcome. Chair, when there is a change of call, Ms Hartigan wants to correct the record on something.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Do you want to take the opportunity to correct the record now before we move to the next outcome?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. The question I answered before was how many internal reviews we have currently on hand. I said that there were seven internal reviews, and that is actually the figure that has been received in the period 1 July this year to 31 August. On hand, in total, we have 82 internal reviews. There was a question about how many of those have not been complied with in the statutory timeframe, assuming there have been no extensions of time, and that number is 73.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Thank you very much for clarifying the record. That now concludes the questions we have in the cross-portfolio area. Officials in this area are released, with our thanks.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We will now move to outcome 1. Senator David Pocock.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Obviously, in the wake of the Medicare hack and what has been happening overseas with Hugging Face and other incidents, we now apparently need access to frontier models to protect ourselves from frontier models. OpenAI has announced this Daybreak program, where they are giving Australia $10 million worth of credits for Daybreak. What access does the Department of Home Affairs have to Daybreak?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think the point people have been making is that the Australian government, as Ms Walker said, through the Australian Signals Directorate, is working with the frontier AI companies to try to get access to the most contemporary intelligence to understand how the models work and then to apply those learnings both for government and for industry.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: What access do we have to those models at the moment?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The Department of Home Affairs doesn't have access to the frontier AI models, but clearly the director-general of ASD has said that they are working with the frontier models. The question is probably best directed to ASD to give you the sense about access, application and use.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Has Home Affairs requested access to frontier models?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I don't believe so, but we can take that on notice if that's incorrect or if Ms Walker has a different view. The basic premise is that the director-general of ASD has said on the public record that they are working with the frontier AI companies. That's the area of technical expertise in government that they're sharing with other agencies and departments.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You don't have access to OpenAI's Daybreak cyber program?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Not in the Department of Home Affairs.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Why is that? They told the committee that Senator Duniam is the deputy chair of that they have given access to Services Australia. Surely Home Affairs should have access to Daybreak?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We are securing our systems, but not to my knowledge do we have access to Daybreak.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Have you contracted anyone to assist with cybersecurity in the department?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We will ask Ms Walker to come back to the table. I wasn't quite sure where your questions were going. It's sort of crossing over both outcomes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Are we contracting anyone to help with cybersecurity in the Department of Home Affairs, given the information that you would hold and given what we've seen with these agents?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Within the tech group and in Home Affairs, we do have a number of contractors who support us in general with cybersecurity. We have established a frontier AI taskforce within the tech group as a direct result of the changed threats in the environment, and we are working across the group to strengthen and understand the new threat.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Who are those companies? Are any of them sovereign Australian companies, or are they all—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I would have to take that on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Has the frontier AI taskforce requested access to Daybreak?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Not that I'm aware of.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Maybe on notice you can come back on that. Minister, given what we saw with Medicare, why haven't you asked for access to Daybreak?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Across the Commonwealth, we're following the process led by ASD.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Minister, I might get your take on all of this. We have a US company that's hacking government websites, and its response is that it will give us access and some credits for this Daybreak cybersecurity program to potentially protect ourselves from its own company. Surely, as a Five Eyes member, supposedly the closest ally of the US, this is something that we should be demanding anyway? Why are we treating these companies like sovereign nations?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The government, through the Prime Minister, initially made our position very clear to OpenAI that we thought what had occurred was unacceptable. As you've heard from the officials, there is work still underway within government, being led by ASD, to deal with this incident. In my view, not only have we made our position clear but we're taking action to deal with it.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Has the government accepted OpenAI's offer of access to Daybreak?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I don't know personally. I'm not sure whether any of the officials could add anything there.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Does anyone know?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We're trying to find out. As Ms Walker said earlier, the Australian Signals Directorate is coordinating the engagement with the companies and the priority of different government agencies for different technologies.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's not what OpenAI told the Senate committee. Its representatives said that Services Australia, the Victorian Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, New South Wales national parks and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare have Daybreak access—supposedly the ones that they hacked—and then they talked about ASD and the Victorian Department of Government Services, which have it through the government trusted access for cyber programs. I'm slightly concerned that Home Affairs isn't across this and working at speed to put things in place to ensure you don't get compromised.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I hadn't quite understood the question. The agencies that have been provided that are the agencies that were impacted by the incident. It goes to my point that ASD is working very closely with agencies on what an appropriate response is. In this instance, it was those agencies that were impacted which needed access to that.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The other point to note at a policy level is that a small number of agencies need access to frontier AI capability, which can then be amplified throughout other agencies. For the vast majority of departments and agencies, commercial models are able to protect those agencies. I think that's a separate issue from access to the funding of Daybreak and where that might be provided. We have spoken at a policy level to OpenAI about Daybreak, its fund and how that might be applied, as well as any support that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic might be able to provide Australian government agencies. That's an ongoing discussion that we're having, both for Australian government agencies but equally for law enforcement.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The only other point I would add, Senator Pocock—and you've heard similar just now—is that having an agency like ASD, with its expertise, undertaking and leading the effort for a rigorous assessment of these sorts of models is a really important first step before any decision is made about greater involvement within government.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The background, though, is that the Medicare hack happened in June. We're now in October, and these models are being improved and released, it seems, every month or two. It seems to me there is some urgency here. Finally, in terms of the $10 million worth of credits, do you know how long that would last?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I have no idea.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I will put a few questions on notice and come back for ASD.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Duniam.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: On the same theme, why don't we go to the whole-of-government response to OpenAI. We've traversed those deadlines as they applied to Home Affairs. I presume that applies across government. Mr Hansford or Lieutenant General McGuinness, who's running the program in terms of the whole-of-government approach?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
