text: The National Office of Cyber Security did coordinate across government in consultation with affected organisations and other relevant agencies. The Australian Signals Directorate led the technical response and incident investigation. The Australian Federal Police were aware and connected at all times. The ASD and the Australian AI Safety Institute assisted with digital forensic investigation to ascertain more information, including whether government systems were impacted. In coordination, we coordinated two calls that included our state and territory counterparts as well as federal government organisations. In the second call we invited OpenAI, which was able to speak directly with those organisations in order to understand what had happened and the data that they had.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think your question might also have been going to who is coordinating the response.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm sorry. It was so I knew to whom to direct—the Lieutenant General or Mr Hansford within Home Affairs.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: General McGuinness was obviously speaking about the response to the incident. It's Mr Hansford's policy area that prepares the direction to agencies and then works with agencies on compliance.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Beyond the deadlines that Ms Foster referenced earlier in response to my questions around Home Affairs directly, are there other deadlines or specific points in time related to the work plan to have a whole-of-government response to this issue that we should know about?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Certainly. Our whole-of-government response actually started in 2025, when we put out guidance about the use of AI within Australian government systems. We've embedded in the Protective Security Policy Framework the policy around the deployment of new technology and how agencies must evaluate technology risk. That's embedded in the actual Protective Security Policy Framework. From a policy level, that requirement exists for every agency. There has been a series of directions that have been additive to the PSPF, whether that's on the legacy technology piece that the secretary mentioned—which we're managing and answering questions with agencies and obviously going through that process ourselves. That's the next big piece of work, with the two deadlines, as the secretary said: 31 December for the systems of government significance and then March next year for other internet-facing systems to get a sense of the legacy of Commonwealth systems. The reason we wanted to start there is to effectively look at what are the legacy systems, how can we better protect them, how can we quantify the legacy debt and how do we put in place a program of effort both to prioritise and respond and ultimately update, replace or better protect those systems in the future? We continue to do a whole range of work on AI generally in a policy context and learn from every incident.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It's been put to me, Mr Hansford, that at a cybersecurity conference at some point recently you had estimated that replacing vulnerable legacy Commonwealth IT systems would cost between $15 billion and $17 billion. Does that ring a bell with you?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sorry, the point I was making at the Protective Security in Government Conference is that, if you just looked at the cost of legacy technology, that is a very blunt approach and does result in a bill such as $14 billion, $15 billion, $16 billion—noting the work that we've got underway to quantify the legacy technology. That was clearly an example, not a specifically defined cost, that has been picked up by the Canberra Times. It effectively says that, if you approach the policy problem by just saying, 'Here's the bill,' it doesn't actually reflect legacy technology, how to quantify it, how to better protect it and how to stagger its replacement. Effectively, that is the point I was trying to make.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: But that was a back-of-envelope calculation?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think the actual quote is 'such as'.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I should use that more in my interviews that I get in trouble for! Is there an estimate, though? I know the work is being done, but surely there is some idea, even within Home Affairs, of what kind of cost we're facing to address some of these issues? Sometimes it will be a patch; other times it'll be an entirely new program, I gather.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The starting point is that the definition of 'legacy technology' is often misunderstood. People think it's just old technology, but it's actually unsupported technology. Actually trying to get to the quantum is the whole purpose of this work as you've rightly outlined. It is pretty clear that it will be a significant figure, but I think the most important thing is that, in order to get to the point of replacement, we have to quantify and better protect now. That's the work that has been accelerated and is included in the direction.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It's about making informed choices about what actually needs to be replaced, what could be done in a different way and what could be shut down. It's not simply a matter of going along and saying, 'We've got all these systems and we just need to upgrade or patch them all, and this is the bill.' It's actually an assessment about what does the technology estate look like at the end of this process. One of the really helpful things about the systems of government significance is it gives us a way of prioritising what is most important.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Are we confident that we will not have more exposures found, attacks, breaches or unauthorised access occur between 31 December and then indeed beyond that to March or the end of March next year?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, no-one could ever give you a guarantee that there will be no attempts of any cyber incident. If something is internet connected, it's at risk. Even the ASD threat report out today shows that AI is enhancing the attacks that we're seeing across the economy, which means that some of the basic cyber settings that have been in place for a number of years are so much more important. Thinking about and deploying AI in a different way is the area that agencies are looking at and grappling with. That doesn't mean that there won't be further attacks; there will be further disruptions. The kind of macro point is that we've thought about 24/7 access to systems for a very long time. What's happening in the environment means that, if you prioritise security over the system being provided, that might mean systems are down for a short period, which is why you have seen websites pre-emptively taken down to patch and then put back up as a prioritisation of security. I think we will continue to see that type of disruption into the future.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Please explain to me again those two deadlines. What was the body of work to be completed by the end of March?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Mr Neal will give you the specific details in the direction.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The March 2027 deadline includes the legacy stocktake for non-systems of government significance and the beginning and implementation of a technology risk management plan, which includes a target for legacy reduction, prioritisation strategies that support delivery, mitigation to address the risks and procedures to identify those areas to rationalise the technology estate. December is for those systems of government significance, as the Secretary has already mentioned.
witness_position: Acting First Assistant Secretary, Personnel and Protective Security

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Do we have a deadline to have all of these things dealt with, though? You've talked about identifying and stocktaking—very important, because then you know what you're dealing with—but there were elements of what you described just then in terms of mitigation and rationalisation et cetera. Do we have a point in time where the government is saying, 'We must now be completely secure'?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The reality is it's an iterative approach from here, and really there are three ways to address legacy technology. There's stopping, mitigating and replacing. The first instance is to stop those legacy technology pieces that have been identified in the stocktake that are no longer required. The element that is mitigation and replacement is kind of an ongoing piece. The reality of technology is that things that are supported now will become legacy in the future. In fact, we're dealing with an ongoing process that will need to be implemented by agencies from now in a continuous manner.
witness_position: Acting First Assistant Secretary, Personnel and Protective Security

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: There's obviously an urgency around this. The public concern around this is such that action must be taken. Government have said action will be taken. I'm just trying to understand by what time it is the intention to have these matters broadly resolved, noting it is an ongoing job. I don't think we can stand up tomorrow and say to the people of Australia, 'It's going to be a work in progress forever.' What is the government's intention to have these matters resolved in some certain or solid way? Is there a date, for example?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We will know more, both internally but across government, about what the nature of the challenge is when the stocktake has been completed and when people have been in a position to look at the different treatments that Mr Neal has just outlined. Our approach will be to use the systems that we currently have in place to prioritise treatment, whatever that treatment is, for the most critical and the most vulnerable systems. We will be giving our focus to the things that matter most, but it's not going to be possible, in a world of rapid technological change, to say at point X everything is perfect.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, I don't think anyone can expect it to be perfect, because as we advance so do our adversaries, and to the point that was made earlier—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The direction is not just a stocktake. As part of the direction, the stocktake is the first bit; the second bit is a legacy technology risk management plan, to pick up on exactly what Mr Neal said. It's not just counting what we've got; it's actually having the plan to remediate. The date for that is also 31 March 2027.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: A plan is good, but what about actioning the plan? There will be action items yet to be determined. I plan to ask you a whole heap of questions, but I'm not going to be able to do so today. I'm just trying to figure out what confidence Australians who might be tuned in to this for some bizarre reason will get from the timeframes that this process has for resolving issues where there are exposures or sensitivities around our systems.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We will be in a better position to answer that when we actually have worked with the agencies on those plans.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I won't be here for that, though. I will be watching from the other end then.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Darmanin.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Could you update us on your work under Horizon 2 of the Australian Cyber Security Strategy?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Horizon 2 was initiated by the minister back in June this year and really sets us laser-focused on three key priorities. One is strengthening people as our greatest defence. The minister often calls it the human firewall, but it's providing that support to citizens, in their homes, workplaces and businesses, to empower them to provide the right culture and the right organisational structures and institutional processes that support our technology. The second is a strong focus on our government and critical infrastructure, and it plays out in the designation of our systems of government significance. We will also be mapping our critical supply chain underpinning the critical infrastructure and key government systems, and then providing additional support in exercising those supply chains as well as providing additional tools to businesses to uplift themselves and exercise themselves. The third lens is really about the safe and secure adoption of emerging technology, that is, how do we embrace the opportunity of emerging technology, including frontier AI, in order to uplift our security and defences, but also preparing for post-quantum cryptography.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In terms of the human firewall, it sounds like, in terms of the strategy you talked about, it's exactly that: having humans well equipped and resourced as much as they can be. Can you talk a bit more about this one in particular and why this is important?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We know that when organisations are prepared, not just with the right technology stack but with the right culture, the right training, the right preparedness and the right exercises, they fare much better. This strategy is about resilience rather than preventing every attack. How are we strong enough to identify, to respond quickly and to recover quickly?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The focus really is on behavioural change, particularly with Horizon 2, to focus on small and medium businesses and not-for-profits, where we are seeing people need the most support. In terms of delivery of Horizon 2, to date we have delivered five of the 64 initiatives. That includes setting up a not-for-profit cyber uplift community of practice, and also working on an industry data classification framework as well as a smart device labelling scheme pilot program. The intention of that, again, is to make sure the general public can have confidence in the tech that they're buying, that it has inherent cybersecurity there, alongside that general uplift in terms of the basics of cybersecurity and how to protect themselves online.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: With those five out of 64 initiatives, how do you see it rolling out in terms of a time frame and that getting across to small and medium enterprises and NFPs, which is a very large community to work with?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'll get Mr Bell to talk about that in more detail.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It is an ambitious agenda, but the key part is the consultation we're undertaking with industry. As you mentioned, the small business and not-for-profit sector is incredibly large. One of the big focus points for Horizon 2 is actually getting into that scale. There are a lot of great programs out there around cyber resilience. As the coordinator noted, it is about resilience, but it's also about reach. Where we can increase resilience of a small business in the hundreds or the thousands, that's great work, but we are looking at the 2.5 million small businesses. Part of the work we've done through establishing the CyberSmart program—we had a recent town hall with industry to go through what CyberSmart will be—and part of the reason we're taking that sort of structural approach is to say, 'How do we look at standards that will apply to all small businesses at low cost in a way that's easy to implement and that is actually fit for purpose?' To answer your question around the timeframes, these processes, along with our other consultation, have already commenced and will continue to roll out over the next couple of quarters as we look to work towards establishing those standards.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Cyber Policy and Programs

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: On supply chain, I think General McGuinness talked about mapping that as one of the other pillars. Can you explain in a bit more detail some of the things the government is doing to strengthen supply chain resilience?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We're finding that there is a concentration of risk. We're trying to encourage businesses and industry to look at that risk. It's not necessarily a bad thing, but you need to understand the concentration risk and have plans in place to mitigate that. Some of the work we do—and that's led by the coordinator—is around exercising, but also just providing clear guidance and understanding of how to assess your supply chain risk, how to build up cybersecurity resilience within it, and ensure every member of your supply chain is aware of the risk, because you're only as protected as the lowest common denominator. The other thing we're doing more broadly is we have recently signed a digital resilience agreement with Microsoft. What that does is work with large hyper-scalers which most of industry and government use, to say to them, 'Here are the strategic risks we're facing. We want to work more closely with you and together build our resilience to some of these concentration risks.'

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Specifically with the supply chain mapping, we will map that critical dependency that we see across both critical government systems and critical infrastructure systems, and then we will provide scalable exercises for them to both exercise themselves but also to participate in more tabletop exercises within sectors and across sectors.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Across the economy, outside of perhaps the world of people who are more familiar with these concepts, what are some of the lessons that you've learned from the recent cyber incidents that you think should be known across the economy?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think the longstanding advice since I've been in this role is really the key actions that we promote under our Act Now, Stay Secure campaign, which include: having unique and long passphrases for every different account; always applying multifactor authentication when it's available; and rapidly updating your software, whether you're a business patching or installing new software when it becomes available. We know that these foundations still make a significant difference in building our resilience in our cyber posture. We also encourage Australians to recognise scams—to actually recognise—which has become easier with the technological evolution as AI can become more convincing. We are asking and giving our citizens additional resources to recognise those things. Importantly, the National Anti-Scam Centre recommends that we stop, think and protect. We need to just take that moment and, if you're unsure, not be so urgent. We know that our cybercriminals will try to force urgency, make us feel like we know them, that they're familiar and that we should respond. We actually finished up phase 4 of our Act Now, Stay Secure campaign in May this year. Once again, the campaign performed at or above benchmarks, with more than three out of five people who interacted with the campaign taking an action to make themselves more secure.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think you got an award.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That campaign did win a bronze award at the Effies as well. Those awards are about the impact that advertising and marketing actually have. That's the result of some great marketing and communications experts working with us to get that message out.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Duniam.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Ms Spencer, with the digital resilience program you were talking about—and you talked about signing a contract with Microsoft and working with hyper-scalers, the other large foreign entities—is there any work underway to work with, at different points in the stack, sovereign providers of services or goods that would assist? This idea of trying to catalyse an industry here in Australia—is that something Home Affairs is working on or thinking about doing?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I can jump in there. The Executive Cyber Council, which the minister chairs and which includes 32 of our largest industry leaders across the economy, has a number of initiatives through working groups. One of them is about promoting sovereign capability. In fact, in the next two weeks in the first week of November in Sydney, it will host the second showcase for our sovereign capability, ACE26. That will bring sovereign start-up cyber capabilities from around the country and allow them to showcase their capability. At the same time, we will bring the procurement folk of those large businesses across the country and government procurement together. We're doing a little bit of matchmaking as well as providing some uplift and running a conference on what capabilities exist. If I go back to our mapping of supply chain, we're also hoping that, as we provide additional scalable exercises online which businesses can take and then exercise themselves, they're supporting their own confidence in entering into the supply chain of these big businesses and of critical infrastructure. We have a range of initiatives across our strategy and across Horizon 2 that we hope will both build confidence and identify and promote sovereign capability.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: This is perhaps outside of your remit, but obviously something that you might have considered. Have you identified any barriers in the procurement rules around trying to procure sovereign?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I haven't to date, and that is a key question as we engage across our sovereign work group, which is industry for industry leading that working group. Some of the key questions we are always asking our industry partners are: are there policy or legislative barriers that prevent both uplift but also things like building that sovereign capability?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Turning to ISIS brides, is there any update on any status or information relating to Australian citizens and/or their families currently overseas who fought with or were affiliated with Islamic State? Do we have any further or new information related to anyone in that category?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: With the independent arrival of the last cohort of women and children, we believe that is the remaining Australians bar one from the al-Roj camp. There are a range of other Australians of counterterrorism interest who remain overseas.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: With regard to the bar one, that is the medical doctor who remains; is that correct? Or is he separate?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: When I said 'bar one', I was referring to the women and children. I should have said 'bar two', because there are two individuals associated with that cohort.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That includes the doctor?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It's one of the women and her child.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: With regard to the medical practitioner, whose name escapes me now, do we know if there are any activities being undertaken at present by third parties to facilitate the repatriation of that individual?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I am not aware of any efforts to repatriate. The Australian government is certainly not involved in any efforts to repatriate, but not to my knowledge.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: With regard to the remaining female and her child, is there any effort underway by third parties or any correspondence with government of which you are aware relating to the repatriation of those individuals to Australia?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The Australian government has no direct involvement relating to those individuals travelling to Australia. I am again not personally aware of any current efforts to arrange any sort of repatriation, no.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Mr Dowling, you referenced travelling to Australia. Is it your understanding that they are anticipating travel to Australia imminently?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, that is not my understanding.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Has any communication been received by the department in relation to these individuals and efforts that might be being made to assist their repatriation? Has any meeting occurred with individuals or with the minister?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: For all Australians of counterterrorism interest overseas, we maintain through our interagency bodies a degree of awareness or information-sharing that might tell us what people's whereabouts or intentions are, but none of those arrangements go to meetings with people or third parties in relation to potential travel arrangements.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: To go to the spirit of your question, the answer is, no.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That includes with the minister and his office?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: To my knowledge.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Perhaps, Minister, you might take that on notice?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: With regard to the individuals who have returned to Australia, have any further individuals been charged as a result of the ongoing investigations?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I believe, since September last year, of the people who have returned in that period, four individuals have been charged. Those, to my knowledge, have been reported on in the media after the AFP or the other law enforcement agencies charged. That is the extent so far, but that does not mean that individuals don't remain under investigation.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Different matters. What has been publicly reported is the extent of the charges that have been laid?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I believe so.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Have any of the court proceedings come to their conclusion?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think all of those court proceedings remain in train in relation to those who have been charged after return.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That would probably be best directed to the AFP Commissioner this evening.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes, indeed. Is this agency notified, kept abreast of, these developments as they occur? I certainly will ask Commissioner Barrett and her colleagues.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: As I think you're aware, we do have a range of cooperation and coordination mechanisms across relevant agencies. As court proceedings develop, as the secretary mentioned, the AFP lead in relation to the prosecution's work. They would keep us updated on developments.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We will resume this outcome after the lunch break.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We will resume in outcome 1. Senator Duniam.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm just trying to figure out where we got to. I think we talked about charges and where those cases were at but nothing further there. My question was going to be in relation to current arrangements related to members of either of the cohorts and what arrangements have been put in place in partnership with Victorian and New South Wales state governments around monitoring or related.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You're referring to the returning women and children's cohorts?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes, correct.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think the first thing is to say that those who have returned home of their independent accord have done so by their own arrangements. There are plans put in place to ensure that, on their return, agencies across the relevant states and territories and the Commonwealth can conduct whatever interviews may be required at that time and investigations can proceed. Obviously, I wouldn't comment on any operational details, but there may be people who are considered within that cohort who remain subject to police investigation by either the AFP or New South Wales or Victoria police through the joint counter-terrorism teams. Those cohorts also will be considered for countering violent extremism programs delivered through the National Support and Intervention Program if that's the appropriate mechanism to look at their reintegration into the Australian community. There may be other services that are provided if there is further support, which might go to health, welfare or employment services, but those would be coordinated by the states and territories.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Just on the countering violent extremism program, do we have an update on how many of those returning women and children have participated in that program?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I believe all have been considered for inclusion in the program. My advice from the state and territory authorities is that there has been constructive engagement, and many are engaged in a relevant countering violent extremism program. I hesitate to say that today everyone is, because there's a range of circumstances, including those relating to age of the person and other factors, which means that is fluid, but they have all been engaged to one extent or another in relation to those programs.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So they have participated. I know it's a voluntary thing. They are asked: 'Would you like to participate?' And from what you say, they have said, 'Yes, we would.' 'To some extent' is what I'm interested in.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I believe that's right—that, to varying degrees, all returnees have engaged to an extent in those programs. But what personal remediation is in place is highly variable. Under state and territory arrangements, everyone is considered through a panel as to what programs they're referred into, the length of those programs and what services are appropriate, so what ends up actually being delivered is highly variable.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So, as the first step, the request is made and a panel assesses what sort of engagement should occur; is that right?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Most states and territories—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: There are only two here, according to this statement.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's right. This is applicable in relation to New South Wales and Victoria. For participation in a program funded under the National Support and Intervention Program, those jurisdictions operate a multiagency panel which will determine—and I'm talking in broad about any participant, not just these cohorts at the moment—whether those services are appropriate for that person at that time. The police will usually be involved in those conversations. There can be reasons why that panel could determine that the CVE programs are not appropriate for that person, which might go to law enforcement activity or to the situation that person is in, in terms of education or workforce, or to that person's personal behaviour and whether there's any risk to practitioners as a result. So a considered decision is made as to what program is appropriate for that person, and if it is determined that a service funded under the National Support and Intervention Program is the right mechanism, then the engagement will happen with the participant to offer and encourage the availability of those services.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So everyone has gone through that determination. Does this include the children?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Of the people who have returned, some were as young as six years old on return. I'm not across exactly what arrangements would be in place, but I would suspect that a six-year-old wouldn't be considered under the CVE programs. It doesn't mean the state government isn't thinking about what is appropriate for that six-year-old, but it wouldn't be a countering violent extremism program.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It would be under some other arrangement that they deal with directly.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's right.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I don't want to labour this issue too much, but I'm just interested in, and you point out, the varying degrees. Some might turn up to their first meeting with a counsellor or—who knows—someone to assist them, and it goes right through to some form of full participation. Is there any visibility that you have of the extent of the engagement these individuals have had with the program?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I will take on notice what we're able to tell you about the extent of engagement, which will involve us talking to our state and territory counterparts.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sure. In general terms, if you can.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In general terms—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I don't want 'No. 1 did three sessions'.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes, which would be—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I just would like to know perhaps what the minimum has been, noting what you said about different circumstances.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That would be helpful. And have we got a measure of what success from these programs looks like?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Again, it is variable. Through the course of a year, we have several hundred people participate in countering violent extremism programs. Many more than dozens will enter. Dozens will exit. The aim of a countering violent extremism program is to have someone disengage from violent behaviours and violent tendencies. Where those tendencies are associated with beliefs—a perverted sense of what is right and wrong—then the practitioner or the person delivering the support will engage with those belief systems. Ultimately, what success looks like is that someone can exit the program with a sense that they have disengaged from a tendency towards violence. That can take three months; it can take three years. It can involve a lot of service delivery; it can involve less. The end of a violent extremism program doesn't mean the end of engagement. Someone might be referred to a subsequent service. So there's no graduation certificate, I guess. It tends to be a bit more fluid than that. But I think practitioners in the field—the people who are delivering the support service—do have a sense of what success looks like in terms of a participant having disengaged from those violent tendencies.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Okay. Do you, or does the department, receive updates on this? Given the community interest and the fact that it is administered under this joint arrangement, do you receive updates on this on the way through?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We do. We have a much more comprehensive data reporting portal that now operates, in which states and territories and delivery agencies input data as to a person engaged in the program—what types of reasons have been referred into the program, as in what beliefs and extremist tendencies they might have; what programs are being provided to support them; and when they exit from the program. That is not a longstanding program. I might ask Mr Goldie to join me, but I believe we've had that data portal in place for the best part of months or a year now, which, over time, will give us a far more comprehensive picture of what people's pathway through the programs is.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Okay.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The ASIC system that Mr Dowling is talking about commenced with the National Support and Intervention Program. It's been operating since 1 July 2025.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We might just clarify what ASICS stands for.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The Australian support and intervention caseload system. It came to me eventually.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sure.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We have a lot of acronyms.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You can thank him later for that spot test.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. Thank you, Boss! What kind of data we collect in that system is an iterative process, because we came from a much lower baseline, with our former programs that the NCIP replaced, so we're always looking at what useful indicators there are for us to inform our position as that national coordination and funding agency, as opposed to directing operational activity. Some of the things that we're looking to drill down into over the next few months and years are some additional indicators of the impact of a program on somebody's individual mental health outcomes and their engagement with education and support services so we can have a little bit more granularity around the individual impacts at a more national aggregated scale.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Understood. Excellent. I look forward to that information on notice around what participation has occurred in a generalised sense. That would be very helpful. I want to go back to the individual known as Tareq Kamleh, otherwise known as Dr Jihad, who has been covered in the media. Have any measures been put in place to prevent this individual's return to Australia or has any advice been sought on how to do so?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The individual in question is somebody who is, obviously, on our radar and on the radar of operational agencies in relation to activities that he may have engaged in overseas and what law enforcement response would be applicable. I'd have to take on notice or just be a little bit careful with information about what he's up to, what we think he might be intending to do et cetera.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sure. I'm more interested in what government might be doing to prevent the individual's return, if anything at all. I'm not interested in operational—what's he up to, where's he shopping and that sort of thing. It's more: what are we doing to secure Australia? If you're able to take that on notice, that would be good.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Just with other questions related to NZYQ, is that here or in outcome 3?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I always get confused.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So do I.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It's outcome 3.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Okay. We'll deal with that. Chair, I'll return the call.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Shoebridge.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I have questions about the Enhanced Border Security Partnership, the EBSP. Is that you, Mr Hansford?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It certainly is.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You would've seen that the EU have advanced their negotiations, I assume.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The EU has agreed a framework with the United States, which then will be implemented.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm having trouble hearing you.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I understand the EU has agreed a framework with the United States that will then be implemented 27 different ways in the EU context.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think the EU has proposed a framework, and they've put it out for consultation. The EU council have put out an explanatory memorandum and they're consulting on it.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. I think, following discussions and agreement with the US, that's the process they're moving forward with.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Can you update us on where negotiations between Australia and the Trump administration are on the Enhanced Border Security Partnership?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Certainly. I think the first thing to say is that, without the Visa Waiver Program, Australians would have to apply for a visa to the United States and provide relevant information. With that as context, we have been discussing with the United States. I personally discussed the Visa Waiver Program with the US between 25 and 27 August. In doing so, we talked about what model might well be able to support the continuation of the Visa Waiver Program. In doing that, we very much talked about our Privacy Act, the Australian Privacy Principles, the fact that a privacy impact assessment would have to be undertaken, the data that the US would require. Then, subsequently, in October, a team from Home Affairs went to the United States to continue the discussions about the expectations of the US under the Enhanced Border Security Partnership program, what that would mean for Australians and what data the US would require, noting that, without the Visa Waiver Program, the only other option for Australians to travel to the United States would be a visa. So we are talking about that in the context of the technology that's applied to that data. We're talking with the US about where that information might be hosted or, indeed, whether or not there's a different way to work the system, in terms of whether there would be a process where Australia could do the checking and provide a result to the US and then, where there's a result that requires more information, put an Australian in a visa scheme. They're all the things that we're talking about. To summarise, no agreement's been finalised; we're engaging with the US at the moment.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You didn't want to add anything, Ms Spencer?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No. That's all good.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Were either of you part of the team that, I assume, went to the US in October?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Neither of us, no.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Is anyone in the room part of that team?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Who did?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: One of my staff members who's now on another international engagement.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm sorry—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It's one of my staff members who is now currently overseas for meetings.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I thought you said, though, that a team went to the US.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sorry—an individual from Canberra, supported by one of our officers at post who's part of the Home Affairs team.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And that individual from Canberra is now where?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: On another overseas trip.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: On another overseas work trip?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's right.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text:
You will have seen the way in which the EU sought to provide a higher level of protection for what is called, in their agreement, special categories of personal information. And they are defined by the EU to mean:

… personal information revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions or religious or other beliefs, trade union membership, genetic data, biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person, and personal information concerning health or sexual life. An individual's name, date of birth, place of birth, nationality/citizenship, or other basic biographic identity information shall not be deemed to constitute in themselves special categories of personal information …

Are you aware of that, which has been negotiated, as I understand it, between the US and the EU, as a category of information that requires additional protections?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes, we're aware of that from the EU but also aware through discussions with other Five Eyes partners about the approach that they're taking with the US.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Is it the government's position in negotiations that that kind of information—and I won't read it out again, but it involves racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, trade union membership and a person's health or sex life—will not be handed over to the United States under the Enhanced Border Security Partnership? Is it intended to protect that?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We're focused on personal privacy protection and looking as far as we can to options that require consent from any Australian traveller.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, consent is one thing, but, if you've set in train and agreed to a process where there's an expectation that that kind of information—someone's racial or ethnic origin, political opinions or trade union membership—and the provision of that information is necessary for getting a visa under the Enhanced Border Security Partnership, then questions of consent become much harder to navigate for people, if the government's agreed to an arrangement where that kind of information is expected to be handed over. So is your only protection in relation to that intended to be one of consent? 'We're going to make these arrangements. If you want it, buy in, and, if you don't, tough luck.'

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, Senator. There's no agreement that has been finalised with the US. We're engaging with the US. I think, relevantly, the Privacy Act already provides that Australian information like biometric information is sensitive information and already has additional protection. So we've outlined that to the United States, particularly the requirements of our Privacy Act, and our discussions are ongoing.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text:
Well, last time we asked this—and I think it was May, some time ago—you said, Mr Hansford:

It is unclear at some elements about what the US is requiring, so that's why we're having the meetings to understand their specific requirements.

Well, since that evidence, you've had two rounds of meetings. You had the rounds of meetings that you were a part of, Mr Hansford, in late August over three days. Then Ms Spencer's team member and another went and had a round of meetings in October. So I'm going to ask you again: what identity elements, what information, are the US seeking under the EBSP?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Our discussions are still ongoing. You'd appreciate, Senator, that it's a complex area that we've got to navigate with the US. Every country comes to the US discussion with a different annual temporary visa refusal rate, with the acceptance of repatriation of its citizens and entering into an agreement in terms of lost and stolen passports—a whole range of different issues. That's the first element that the US considers. And then the practicalities, the laws, the privacy requirements and the access to things like criminal histories are all things that we're talking to the United States about.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, I'm not asking what you're talking to the United States about. I'm asking about what the United States is saying they want. As I said, last time you told us in May: 'It's unclear on some elements about what the US is requiring. That's why we're having the meetings.'

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's right.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Now, are you telling me nothing's advanced? You've had three days of meetings in August, you've had further meetings in October, and you still don't know. You've got no idea what it is the United States is asking for. Is that your advice?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No. We have much more fidelity about what the United States' requirements are, they have much more understanding about our legal framework and our technical limitations and opportunities, and we are advancing the discussions.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, you say you have much more understanding. That's the exact issue that I'm asking you about in my questions. What do you understand now, after these two rounds of meetings, about what information the US is seeking that you didn't know last time we had this conversation, Mr Hansford?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text:
A number of different things. The key requirements of the US are that—and kind of rightfully so—when you fill out the Visa Waiver Program, you're required to outline whether or not you have a criminal history. The first US argument is that people are filling that out and some people who do have a criminal history tick that, no, they don't. So the first requirement of the US is to validate from the partner country—in this case, Australia—whether or not that statement is accurate. So the first requirement of the US is to understand whether or not the individual travelling to the United States has a criminal history or not, and that's the relevant consideration for the US government on the Visa Waiver Program. So that's the first area.

The second area is about making sure that who is coming to the United States is the individual who has applied for the Visa Waiver Program. They're the two principal areas that we're exploring with the United States.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, is what the United States seeking a binary answer—yes or no—on criminal history, or are they seeking information about, if somebody does have a criminal history, the elements of their criminal history?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That is precisely what we are trying to negotiate with the US. There are many different models. One model is to provide the actual criminal history to the US. That's a model that other jurisdictions are thinking about with the US. Another model might well be to say, 'Yes, this person does have a criminal history,' and to then push them into a visa pathway, for them to apply to a visa for the US, by not providing the actual criminal history. They're all the things that we're talking to the United States about on how an Australian system might well work.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: But what is the United States asking for? Are they asking for the criminal history, the details in the criminal history? Is that the start of their negotiating point? Is that what they're asking for?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The policy that the US government is working towards is to validate whether or not what an individual has said on a Visa Waiver Program application is accurate.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes, but what are they asking for?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, in how we get to that outcome, I've found the US government officials that we've engaged—I personally engaged officials when they came to Australia but then, equally, with the team—are open-minded as to how that outcome might be achieved.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: But you can't be having conversations like we're having, where the US is never putting their position forward and it's opaque—you're trying to pin the tail on a jellyfish. I'm assuming the US is coming and saying, 'This is what we want. Can you provide it?' and then you're having a discussion. So, Mr Hansford, what are the US asking for? I'm sure they're not just coming here with a series of platitudes and outcomes. They're asking for information. What do they want?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: They are the two principal policy discussions and areas that they have asked about—identification and criminal history.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So they want the details of the criminal history.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, they want the policy outcome to make sure that, when an individual ticks that, no, they do not have a criminal history on a form for the Visa Waiver Program, that is then validated by the Australian government. That's the policy outcome that they're seeking.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, unfortunately, Mr Hansford, we're going to have to come back to this and try and get not the policy outcome—that's your answer, but it's not addressing my question. My question is: what information are they seeking? We will come back to that aspect.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sure.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: But you also said they want to validate that who is coming matches the asserted identity. I'm assuming that, in order to do that, they want certain information, and what the US has made clear in its negotiations with other countries is that that is biometric information. Are they seeking biometric information to determine that question?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator, if I may, they are seeking assurance of the information provided by the traveller or the applicant, and that includes both biometric and criminal history information. The means by which we provide that assurance is the subject of ongoing discussions between us and the US.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We are clearly going to have to come back to this, because you keep talking about a policy outcome. My questions are really, really simple: what information are they asking for? And I am quite certain that the US officials are not as oblique as the answers I'm getting here and they have actual demands for specific types of information and that's their negotiating point. We will spend as long as is needed to try and get some answers about what the actual US demands are, and we'll come back to it in the next round.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Thank you, Senator Shoebridge. Senator Duniam.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Coming back to the issue of Mr Kamleh, the doctor, I want to ask when the government, perhaps the department, first became aware that he was not actually deceased, as had been reported in 2017.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm aware of the media reporting. It's a tricky question to answer because I'm not sure we thought what the media reporting said they thought it was.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So we didn't think he was dead, as a government.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think, over time, agencies have done their utmost to maintain visibility of the whereabouts and activities of Australians who might be associated with terrorist groups. It is a very murky, opaque environment over there.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sure.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: At what point through the course of the several years we were certain or not certain about his whereabouts or state of health I couldn't tell you in exact detail.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sure. Did we think he was deceased?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I personally don't have direct knowledge over the course of all those years, so I couldn't answer that question.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Would it be in the information in the possession of your team or somewhere else in the department? These people are on your radar. There must be records kept of appearances on radar and disappearances, including perceived death.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Information relating to those individuals tends to be the product of information that might come from the operational agencies like AFP, ASIO and DFAT, which maintains, obviously, our embassy presence overseas and has some visibility of some of these cases as well. That gets aggregated through our interdepartmental arrangements. It's possible over the years that there has been information shared in that group in relation to this case. In fact, I'd say it would be. What that information said I couldn't recall and would likely be subject to pretty sensitive classifications.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: On notice, then, perhaps could you furnish me with some understanding of whether at all, at any point, it was the agency's view that he was deceased. And it may not be; it may be the case that he was always believed to be alive. But, if that was not the case, when did they first become aware that, in fact, he was not deceased and was still in that Iraqi prison—as best as you can see?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sure. We'll work with agencies and see what's possible.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Thank you. I might go, if I can, to the Bondi royal commission. That's here, yes?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It is, yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Excellent. I wonder whether you might be able to indicate to the committee how many of the interim report recommendations have been fully implemented.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'll ask Mr Chapman, who is leading our taskforce, to give you the detail.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I can confirm that, of the 14 recommendations contained in the interim report, all do remain on track to be delivered in December of this year. Currently, six of the nine public recommendations have been complete and two of the five confidential recommendations.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In total, how many are left outstanding?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Six.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: With regard to the implementation of those, my recollection is that some are related to state and territory agencies. Of those six, how many are in the Commonwealth's control to respond to and how many are outside of its control?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We have been closely consulting, via the Australia-New Zealand Counter-Terrorism Committee, to ensure completion. The only one that is out of the direct remit of the Commonwealth is recommendation 1, which related to procedures adopted by New South Wales police in respect of Operation Jewish High Holy Days.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: But the rest are ones you are working through to implement?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes, that's correct.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: What is our projected timeframe on implementing the balance of those recommendations?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We're confident that they will all be completed in December of this year.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'll go to the issue around the allocation of resources devoted to national security, particularly counterterrorism. There's been a lot of discussion around whether funding levels or resources have increased, decreased or been spread differently. Between when the terror level was lifted to 'probable' in August 2024 and the events at Bondi in 2025, did funding or resources increase for counterterror activities, or was it the same across that period?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Most of our financial records go to financial years, so the exact timeframes don't match to those events necessarily.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The 2024-25 financial year is reasonably close.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sure, sorry. And, as I think you flagged, there is movement in and out of function, which means it's quite difficult to compare over periods. But I can say for the Department of Home Affairs' counterterrorism and counter violent extremism function that over that period between 2024-25 into 2025-26, the divisional, or the centre's, budget increased and the staffing level remained relatively similar over that period.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So the funding increased but staffing levels remained relatively static—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: so what did the additional funding go to in that period of time?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Over that period we had the announcement of the counter-terrorism and violent extremism strategy—in January 2025, I believe.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Some activities under that strategy were funded for the department to deliver. We attracted some additional funding for those programs, including around countering violent extremism work and engagement with online platforms. Over that period, I believe, the special fund relating to activities of the Australia-New Zealand Counter-Terrorism Committee also increased. On the flip side, I think some of the functions relating to high-risk terrorist offenders moved in the department. So there were some ins and outs but an overall net increase to the budget.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Has the review of the joint counterterrorism teams' leadership integration, systems access and information sharing been completed?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It has been completed. From memory, we received the final review on 16 October, so a couple of weeks ago.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Are there any key findings you're able to enlighten us about out of that review?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text:
Sure. The intention is not to make the review public. It has been shared with all jurisdictions and relevant agencies who have an equity in the joint counterterrorism teams. I will give you some headline findings. The first is that the joint counterterrorism teams remain the core operational capability for counterterrorism efforts in this country. The review affirmed that they are necessary, that they are working, and that they have successfully been involved in dozens of disruptions over the time that they have been in effect. So, at their core, they are a functional and critical capability.

Some of the areas for recommendations go to variability in the leadership and resourcing arrangements around the JCTTs around the country. They have been built up over several years. They've evolved in slightly different ways depending on the jurisdiction. That could go to the leadership structure: is it the Australian Federal Police or the state jurisdiction that sits on top? It goes to co-location elements. It goes to training. It goes to the triaging and hand-off relating to cases that come to the JCTTs. What the review found is that some of that variability is expected due to the size of the jurisdiction—the smaller jurisdiction will usually have a slightly different arrangement—but what we can do better is learn from the jurisdictions that operate really effectively and try and build on that across the country. What that should lead towards, our shared goal—and I'll say this in advance of us having formulated a national position with our state and territory counterparts, but I think it's fair to say—would be that there is better alignment in practice where it's appropriate; that we have more consistent assessment of threats and a more consistent understanding of what the hand-offs from a JCTT to another part of law enforcement are; and that we address some of the information-sharing friction that can sometimes slow down information that should flow quickly.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I take it there are specific recommendations in the report. When will the report be made available? I know you have to work with counterpart agencies, but in what timeframe do we expect to see responses formulated and then enacted related to this?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text:
First let me just correct something. I think I said 16 October. We received it on 13 October.

The process from here is that the purpose, as recommended through the interim report of the royal commission, was that the review would essentially be delivered to police commissioners and the Director-General of Security to then determine how to act on those recommendations. As I said, jurisdictions were heavily involved in the consultation, in the development of the review. We have shared the final review with them. In the next two weeks, along with my counterpart, the Deputy Commissioner of the AFP, we are aiming to convene discussions with the states and territories to work through the recommendations, prioritise what we think will give us the most bang for buck, and then develop an implementation plan. I would say some of them are short term. You'd expect, if everyone agrees to implementation, aspects like leadership structure and training could be addressed over the coming year. One of the recommendations goes to developing a technology road map for JCTTs. That will likely be a very long horizon to say, 'Here's what we can do to improve the technology that's available to the JCTTs, including to share information, and here is a rolled gold end state that might be some years in working towards.'

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In rounding out there, did you say when the report will be released?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We don't intend to make the report public. It has been shared with the royal commission.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's alright. Anything else you can provide on that on notice would be fine.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: What we'll do is look at what information there is without compromising any of the operational aspects.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Understood. Thank you.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Shoebridge.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Mr Hansford, I'll try and be plain in my question. In the negotiations and discussions between you and the United States in August and Ms Spencer's team member and the United States in October, what personal information have the US said they want to be provided, under the EBSP, for visa waivers?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Name and passport number are the key areas that we're discussing with the US for their requirement. And—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That wouldn't have taken three days. If they'd said, 'We want name and passport number,' you would have said, 'That's fine.' That's the first 15 minutes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, it's the way to get to that information. They actually want validation of the name and passport number that an individual has provided on the Visa Waiver Program. How you check that with Australia is the subject of the discussion, including what technical system you might be able to deploy for that. And the same thing for criminal history: does the person who has put 'no' or 'yes' on the form actually have a criminal history? That's what we're negotiating. They're the two bits of personal information.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You see, Mr Hansford, you've jumped straight to the outcome. I asked you a quite different question: what personal information are they seeking under the EBSP? I don't know how I can say this more plainly. I can give you a list. The EU has a list of personal information. I can repeat that to you again if you want, if that would assist. Would that assist?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, it wouldn't, Senator.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, why—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Personal information—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So can you address my question, rather than the one you wish I'd asked?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Name and passport number, and the fact of a criminal history or not—they're the two areas. How we get to the second one is the subject of discussion.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, no. You said that they want the name, but then they want to be able to validate—that's my understanding—that the person who arrives will match the name.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's right. They wish to validate the personal information that an individual has provided in the Visa Waiver Program, including name and passport number, with the Australian government to make sure that the name and the passport number match; equally, the same thing for criminal history.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: But I am quite certain that the US is not proposing that an individual just simply put their name and passport number and an assertion about a criminal history. I've filled in these forms—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's what happens now, Senator.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I've seen the negotiations and the outcomes of the negotiations in Europe, and there's a raft of personal information that is also being provided. There are provisions about how, when the personal information is of a particular nature, there'll be additional protections in them. Are you saying that the United States have not asked for specific information, that they haven't asked for biometrics? Have they or have they not asked for biometrics?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator, if I may. As I said previously, they're seeking assurance of the information provided. So, exactly to your point, with the information that an Australian traveller puts in their application for a visa waiver—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: the US are seeking assurance of that information.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And for that purpose. Look, sorry, I'm just—could you please answer my question?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sorry—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Did the US ask for biometric information in their meeting with Australian officials in either August or October? Have they asked for biometric information?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: They are open to how we provide that assurance. That is part of the discussion we're having as to whether we provide biometric information or we provide, as Mr Hansford said, a yes or no, that information is correct. That is the crux of what we are discussing with the US at the moment.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So one of the options they're seeking is the direct provision of biometric information?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's right.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Alright. That took a long time to get there. It took an unnaturally long time to get there.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator, in Ms Spencer's defence, in response to the first question, she did try to indicate that they wanted to validate the biometric information and there were different ways of being able to achieve that.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I sat through it, Ms Foster. You really don't need to remind me of the answers that were given. But, if there's any other clarification that you want to give about what specific kinds of information the US has been seeking in these meetings in August and October and you're aware of that, please do tell me now.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator, I was just indicating that I believe Ms Spencer had given you consistent answers.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Are you aware, Ms Foster, of any specific categories of information the US has been seeking?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, Senator.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Alright. Thank you. So biometric information is one of the categories that's on the table. What about political opinion? Was that raised at any point in the discussions in either August or October by the United States?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: As Mr Hansford said, the focus of our discussions has been on biometric data and criminal history.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes, but, you see, I wasn't asking you about the focus; I was asking you a different question. If you'd just answer the question, that would be the quickest way through this.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So no.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: At any point in the discussions in August or October or at any time outside of that has the US raised the question of information in relation to people's political opinions?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No. The requests have been on biometrics and criminal history.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Has there been any discussion about genetic data?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Not to my knowledge.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Mr Hansford?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No. There are two distinctions. It's a matter for the US what they ask of people for the Visa Waiver Program.
