What we have been talking about is how the Australian government could verify some of the information from the US. And the answer, then, to the question about genetics is, no, the Australian government has not been asked to verify genetics or religion or political views of individuals.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I could go through that list, but it might be easier if you just tell us. I assume that they would want validation of the passport number.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's right.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Am I correct in that?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm assuming they would want validation of the name.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Have they asked for documents to help validate the name? That could be driver's licences. That could be birth certificates. Have they asked for documents to validate the name or put forward a proposition that documents could be provided to validate the name?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Not to my knowledge. I think what the US have asked for is, for the passport and name that is on a Visa Waiver Program, is that held in the passport database by Australia, and is it a match?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Does the name match the passport number in the identity document?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's right. That's my understanding.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Is it your understanding that for the EBSP, for the visa waiver, individuals will, when they make the application to the United States, be required to provide biometric data as part of the initial application?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm not aware of the current settings. I understand the request to the EU has been for fingerprint data.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, I'm not asking about the current settings. You're having negotiations about what this arrangement will look like. I'm asking about that. You must know this because, if you're validating biometric data—which is what I understood, Mr Hansford, you were suggesting, validating biometric data; is that correct?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's right. And—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sorry; if you're validating biometric data, they must already have biometric data because you can't validate something that isn't there.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, I think they're asking us to validate whether or not the name and passport number provided—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Whether you have biometric data that connects to that person. And is that—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, we haven't been asked to validate the photo. We've been asked to validate the name and the passport number.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: They do provide their own image in the Visa Waiver Program application or the ESTA application.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Just so I can understand—I wasn't in these negotiations; you were for three days in August, and then you've had the benefit, I assume, of a briefing of further negotiations in October—is what the US is seeking to get that, when the person turns up in the US with their visa, their EBSP, they go through biometrics and you've given sufficient information to the US that they can attach those biometrics to a name? Is that what's intended?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Then explain.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: What is intended is that the name and the passport number that are on the application, which the individual has put there, have been independently validated with the Australian government, so the US can have confidence that the name and passport number match. And then they go through their own process of collecting biometrics both through the form and at the border.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So what are they seeking biometric data from you for?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: They're asking for the name and passport number. One way to get there is potentially providing the biometrics. But that is the subject of the discussions. At the moment, they have asked for the name and passport number to be verified, as I understand.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: If the US doesn't have the biometrics, how do the biometrics assist you in matching the name and the passport number, which I assume sit in a database with name and passport number attached to them? Can you explain to me what you understand the purpose to be of the biometric information that is one of the options the US is seeking? What are they intending it for? How does it work through the process?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: All I can say is that's what we're talking about with the US. I can't really add any more information.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Have there been any discussions about who in the US would hold the biometric data? We know that Palantir, for example, has contracts with the US Department of Homeland Security. We know that Palantir is getting access to vast amounts of US immigration data. Have you had any discussion about whether this information would be passed to Palantir?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: As discussed, we're still talking about the options of whether or not we provide that information or whether we simply provide validation of that information.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So you haven't asked? Have you or have you not asked whether, if the information is given to the United States, it would find its way into the hands of Palantir? Have you asked that question?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I haven't, and I wasn't in the discussions in the US.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Have you, Mr Hansford?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes, certainly have. I've outlined to the US government in the discussions—and, for clarity, the US were here for three days, for a component of which we talked about the Visa Waiver Program. It wasn't a three-day meeting about the Visa Waiver Program. In fact, it was a component of two of the meetings. We outlined that any provision of Australian government data would have to be held securely if that were where it ended up. Our preference, though, is that we would manage it a different way. The US are reflecting on our proposal.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: But what does securely mean? Did you say 'securely, and you can't give it to Palantir'? You said Palantir was raised, so did you make it clear that it would be 100 per cent unacceptable for Australian biometric material to be handed to Palantir through this process?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I've made it clear that we would have to work very carefully through the technology solution.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Was the word Palantir used in your discussion?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Not from me. I think I'd start from a principle of 'secure' before we get to the technology solution.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You say 'not by you'.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Not by me.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Has it been raised at any point?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We will check and take that on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In discussions you were in, was it raised by anybody else during those discussions?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Not from the discussions I was in, no.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The EU is now going through a process of public consultation with their proposed agreement. Will the Australian government go through a process of public consultation, having come to an arrangement with the United States, so that the public can see?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, no agreement has been finalised, and that would be a matter for the government.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Minister?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I would have to take that on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Mr Hansford, do you understand that this is likely to require a legislative response as well?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: They're the issues we're working through.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Is it your understanding it will require a legislative response? If so, what issues are likely to be picked up in a legislative response?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No agreement has been finalised. We're engaging with the US. Before we come to the question about whether or not legislation will be required, we need to come to the agreement about what model is agreed and then whether or not legislation is required. And we're not at that stage yet.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Have you made it an express provision that the US cannot send Australian biometric data or other data to third countries? Is that a non-negotiable starting point?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I don't think we're up to that stage yet either, because it really depends on the model. One model may well be that no data is actually sent to the United States, so it would therefore be a bit of a moot point.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: When does this need to be in place?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The US have said that they would like the agreement to be in place by 31 December. At the 31 December point, the Department of Homeland Security will take a country-by-country view about whether to extend the current visa waiver settings given the negotiations with states—or blocs like the EU—or to make alternate arrangements. The alternate arrangement, of course, is for Australians to apply for a visa, but we are confidently working with the US to try and make sure that we are in a position to see what might be possible, protecting, of course, all of those elements like security of technology, privacy and all of the issues that we've talked about here.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Given how little you seem to know about what the parameters are, what the information is and what the structures are and given you've been having discussions throughout the whole of this year and it's now 27 October, are you saying that, despite all the uncertainty that you've told us about in this hearing, you're aiming for a final agreement resolving all of these issues with the United States by 31 December, in barely two months? Is that your evidence?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We have said to the US and they have accepted the fact that each country comes to the discussions with different systems, different technology, different ways of working and different laws. The decision on 31 December by the US government will depend on the existing cooperation and information-sharing arrangements in place at the time. That's what the US has said. Separately, the US have said that Australia is actively engaging. They were very pleased that we sent a delegation to the US to discuss the issues. And of course, we come to information sharing with the US generally. We've had a longstanding agreement as part of our Protective Security Policy Framework about how data is managed by Australia, so we come to the discussion in that context. We expect to continue discussions between now and 31 December to see how far we can progress, and, of course, the decision by the US government about whether or not the existing Visa Waiver Program will continue is ultimately a matter for them.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Do I read from that—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We're working as quickly as we can.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: that you think the US might think we've been good and we'll get an extension? Is that the summary? It was quite a long way of saying that if that's it.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, we are working as quickly—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We're being cooperative and good, and they may give us an extension on the current arrangements.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Let him answer the question, Senator Shoebridge.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Let me finish the question.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think the answer is we are working as quickly as we can to try and think about where we get to by 31 December. The US are very pleased, though, that we've entered into this in a mature, collaborative approach to try and work through the best outcome for Australians.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: But you haven't even asked some of the most important questions for Australians. You haven't even asked if they're going to give it to Palantir. You don't have an answer about whether they're going to give it to third countries. From what I can tell, you don't even know what information they want. That's the state of play, isn't it, Mr Hansford?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The policy outcome is very clear from our perspective, and we continue to work with the US government.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I would defy anyone who's heard the evidence today from you and Ms Spencer and the secretary to identify the clarity. Is that an appropriate time, Chair? I've got more questions.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I am looking at you encouraging you to move into your next block of questions, if possible.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I have some questions about transnational repression. Is that you again, Mr Hansford?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And Ms Spencer, yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's nice. You would have seen in July, I think the INSLM recommended a specific offence for coerced repatriation. Have you seen that recommendation from the INSLM?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Now we're in October. Has there been any activity from the government in response to the INSLM's recommendation?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Those offences would sit with the Attorney-General's Department.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Notwithstanding the transnational elements of it, you're not engaged in that—it's simply handed over to the Attorney-General's Department?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No. We obviously work very closely with the Attorney-General's Department.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, please tell me what's been happening then.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We have been working through the results of the INSLM report and other work that we have been doing, through the foreign interference issues, and we are developing policy and looking at options.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Working through, developing policy, looking at options—is that what the evidence is?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In terms of proposed offences? Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Has there been an in-principle acceptance of the INSLM's proposal? Is it being progressed positively? It's a matter of very real concern to many members in the community—the fact that coerced repatriation is not currently unlawful and clearly unlawful.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's a matter for the Attorney-General's Department, but we're working very closely with the community to talk about what support we can provide them. We have recently launched a community hub which provides advice, including on transnational repression, and our teams do a lot of engagement with communities to broaden their understanding of the risk and build their resilience and outline the support that the government is able to provide them.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Can you remind me when the National Security Hotline was established. Is that referenced in the hub as a potential response in the face of transnational repression?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The community hub was put in place at the end of last year. The National Security Hotline is a very longstanding hotline, and there is reference to it on that, but the intention of the hub is to provide that for broader community support and guidance.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Are you keeping records of the number of reports of actual or potential transnational repression that are being received by the National Security Hotline?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That information would go through to the AFP, as the law enforcement response.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And they don't provide the information to you? There's no data sharing in that regard from the National Security Hotline?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We work closely together and share information, but I don't have that data. It would be best sought from the AFP directly.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Have you sought from the AFP any update on their numbers of transnational repression inquiries that have been raised?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I haven't directly. I can check with the team and take that on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think we can agree as a starting point that transnational repression is likely to be underreported in Australia because people are self-censoring to avoid upsetting foreign governments. Do we agree on that as a common starting point?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes—and the focus of much of our community engagement is to try and encourage community members to report and to understand that we are a safe place to be able to talk about these issues. We have a number of fora on countering foreign interference and we look at the broad trends in reporting and what we're seeing from the community.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: What are the trends in terms of transnational repression?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Exactly to your point—that there is underreporting. There is fear associated with it, particularly in terms of the potential impacts on family overseas or even within Australia, hence our desire to get more information out and to provide support to the community to encourage their reporting, or at the very least provide them with some tools as to how to take steps.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: What supports are currently offered to an individual who goes to the community hub, comes to Home Affairs and says: 'I'm a victim of transnational repression. I've been making my position clear in relation to the politics in X country, as a result of which threats have been made to my family by the government there,' or 'I've been the subject of attacks and I've got concerns about my family'? What supports are available to someone who comes to Home Affairs and says that?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The first line of direction is to ask them to speak to the AFP or to their local police and report that as criminal offending.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I have, on behalf of a good many individuals who have had situations like this, where they have been outward about their politics in Australia, as they're entitled to be—they've been critical of a third country where they have family connections, and individuals potentially connected with the government in that country have threatened their family. Each time I've referred that to the AFP, the AFP have said, 'Sorry, we can't do anything because those threats happened in another country and it's not a criminal offence'—every time. That's been a uniform response. Sending people to the AFP, in my experience, does not assist in those circumstances. Have you had a different experience? Have people told you a different experience?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: There are also elements where the harassment and interference is occurring within Australia, and we are better prepared—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: They weren't the matters I put to you, though. We're happy to come to that.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Certainly. There is a real challenge when you have that offshore element. The additional support we can provide is referral to support services, guidance on personal security and the steps they can take within government—and this would be a matter for Foreign Affairs and Trade. There are also conversations that are had with representatives from other countries.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: What support services?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sorry?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You said 'referral to support services'. In my experience, the kinds of support services that people are being referred to are services that are already massively overallocated. There are no distinct Home Affairs funded support services that I'm aware of being provided to people in these situations, but I could be wrong. Does Home Affairs fund support services for this, and, in which case, what are they?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, we don't. We refer to broader mental health support services and welfare support services. In the engagement with communities, we work with them on access to community relevant support.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm not blaming you for this, because you operate in the parameters set by the government, but this exchange we've just had probably shows why matters are underreported—because, when they are reported, they get sent to the AFP and the AFP say they can't help. They then get sent to a website, and the website sends them to generic support services like Black Dog, and people don't feel like things have moved one inch and they don't feel supported. This conversation we've just had here, this exchange, is probably one of the reasons why it's underreported—because when people report, nothing happens. Is that your understanding? Is that what you're hearing from diaspora communities?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We are very clear that, while we may not be able to take action in all cases, understanding the environment, the context and the experience helps us build understanding of the threat to take action even at a broader level, if not in direct response to their personal circumstances.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Because of time, would you mind setting out, in answers to questions on notice, what outreach you've done, which communities you've met with, when you've had the meetings et cetera?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Certainly.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: If you could go back until 1 July last year, to get a sense of what's been happening in the space. If you think there's information before that that would be of assistance, I'm not limiting you to—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I have some of that information for this calendar year, if that's helpful now.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That would be helpful, thanks.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: If I go directly to community engagement, we've had 14 engagements with community representatives, 10 with NGO and support organisations, seven with community groups, nine with service providers and one with a faith based peak body. That is the counter-foreign interference team within the Department of Home Affairs. Foreign Affairs and Trade, the AFP and a range of other agencies would also have engagements.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We also have our community liaison officer network in every state and territory, which has regular engagements with communities, not specifically targeting this in the same way the CFI teams do but often covering the same ground. That's another resource we'll tap into when we answer your question.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Thank you; it would be useful if you could get that granularity on notice. Are you aware if there were any visas refused or cancelled in the last financial year, or at any point since, on the basis of the person's involvement or potential involvement in foreign interference or transnational repression?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm not aware.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think we'd need to ask the visa cancellation team that.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Refused or cancelled.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We can do that in outcome 2.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Where we are next.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Has the department assessed any Interpol red notices, extradition requests or mutual assistance requests as politically motivated attempts to reach dissidents in Australia?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That would be a matter for Attorney-General's Department.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That would be a matter for Attorney-General's Department?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Not within Home Affairs.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Is there any support given by Home Affairs to individuals who are facing actual or potential foreign transnational repression, to assist them with their digital security, so they can limit their online exposure and avoid being tracked? Do you offer any of that support?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: As a policy agency, we don't provide individual supports. We provide, including on the community hub, generalised cybersecurity and personal security advice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You don't fund any entity to provide that kind of support for people? I can think of instances where individuals, most often women, are feeling particularly threatened by overseas actors potentially following where they go, knowing what their social connections are and tracking them through social media. But you're saying there's no actual service in place to fund somebody to assist with their digital security and help them in situations like that?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You've raised a number of helpful, practical suggestions today to a problem which is a difficult one. I'd like to take away the things you've been raising today and think about what options we have either within Home Affairs or working with our colleagues in the AFP, the AGD and the states.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Thank you. Minister, is the government considering potential legislative reform to make it very clear that it is an offence under Australian law to seek to coerce somebody in Australia, whether or not the coercion happens in a third country? That would potentially significantly assist in commencing an AFP investigation and also in having an evidentiary base, even if you couldn't ultimately prosecute an evidentiary base, so, as you know, that is a person who can never come to Australia.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm not aware of that personally, but Ms Foster might have something to add there.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I know the Attorney-General's Department is considering those issues. I don't want to speak on their behalf, but I reassure you that that is under consideration.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That concludes the questions we have in outcome 1 this afternoon. Officials responsible in outcome 1 are now released, with our thanks.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We will now move to outcome 2. Senator Duniam, you've got the call.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Back to those questions I foreshadowed under corporate, on the development of the immigration policy ultimately announced by the minister at the Press Club: I was wanting to understand what elements of the department were involved in the construction of that policy—staff numbers et cetera.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: These are issues that have been the subject of much discussion between the department and the minister. I'll let Ms Sharp and her team take you through the detail of how we've been working.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We led the development of the reform package through the division led by Mr Kiley, who leads our immigration policy division. That is a core team that consists of policy officers as well as some officers who specialise in analytics and data. They then, as needed, drew on our program divisions—the divisions that actually run the student visa or the working holiday maker visa—and, also, on our more operational teams in field and immigration compliance in removals, to put together the suite of reforms that Minister Burke announced at the Press Club.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Very good. When did this work commence?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It commenced around November last year.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. In some ways, something like migration, we're always looking at the system—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It's an ongoing thing.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We started the first discussions as shortly after the election, but it really got a head of steam from about November last year.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: When would you say the package was in a broadly final form?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Farmers and working holiday-makers are being unfairly included in a political campaign to cut overseas migration. National agriculture organisations are telling me that they were not consulted ahead of this Labor government promising to cut the rates of working holiday-makers, colloquially called backpackers, by up to 50 per cent over any three-year period. What is the government's justification for applying that cut to backpackers?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text:
Why don't I kick off, and perhaps the officials can follow on. The starting point, is that our government acknowledges that the significant increase that we saw in migration overall to Australia post COVID was simply unsustainable to continue at those kind of numbers. That's why, over the last couple of years, we've taken a range of measures, not all of which have been supported by various parties in the parliament—even those who call for migration numbers to be reduced. We've undertaken a range of measures to reduce migration to a point where we now see the net overseas migration number being roughly half of what it was straight after COVID. Having said that, despite the measures that we've taken, the overall migration numbers remain higher than what we believe is sustainable. They remain higher than the forecasts that we have given for net overseas migration. That's why we've taken a decision to introduce additional measures to further reduce the migration numbers.

The hard bit then becomes: where do you make those reductions? There's a range of people out there who say that we should cut migration numbers, but the minute you say, 'Okay, that means reducing these types of visa applications or these type of visa applications,' then, what do you know? People say: 'No, you can't touch that one. You can't touch that one. You can't touch that one. But we still want you to reduce migration numbers.' That's not how it works. You've got to make the reductions somewhere.

On working holiday-makers, we currently have a record number of backpackers or working holiday-makers in Australia. We have never had more than what we have at the moment. To give you some scale about that, in the 10 years before COVID, the average number of working holiday-makers in Australia was around 140,000. As at 1 September this year, it's over 211,000. So we've seen a 64 per cent increase in the number of backpackers in Australia compared to what we saw pre COVID. It's not as if backpackers are the only group that we have made a decision to reduce the numbers of. You would be aware, I'm sure, of the reductions we've already imposed on international student numbers. We've announced further reductions in international student numbers. Not everyone supports that either. But we do think that it's appropriate that, given we are seeing a record number of working holiday-makers—it's 64 per cent higher than what we saw pre COVID—that has got to be part of the solution. I am very well aware that there are agriculture groups and other groups in the community who don't support that. But you can't say you're going to reduce migration overall without reducing migration numbers in particular cohorts.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text:
Backpackers are tourists. They come here for a holiday with an intention to always go home. They work their way around the country on their holiday, fill regional jobs and return to regional communities the money that they earn. I spoke to one of Tasmania's largest potato farmers a few years ago and I attended his farm. He produces 25,000 tonnes of potatoes every year, and at harvest season 90 per cent of the people who pull the potatoes out of the ground are backpackers. He assures me that, following the promised imminent cuts to backpackers, more than half of his potatoes are going to be rotting in the ground.

Going back to pre-COVID numbers, pre COVID our food production rate was $60 billion a year. Now our food production rates are $101 billion a year. The increase in backpackers is commensurate to the increase in food production in this country. So, if we cut our rates of backpackers to pre-COVID levels, we are not supporting food security and food production in this country. Will the federal Labor government consider pulling this bad idea on using backpackers and using our farmers to decrease overseas migration, when these are people who are helping us, who are helping our farmers and who are always going to return home?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: There are a couple of things there, Senator. For starters, because of the free trade agreement that was signed between Australia and the UK by the former coalition government, it is not the case that every backpacker works their way around the country. There's no requirement for UK backpackers to serve out what's known as the 88 days that are required of backpackers from other countries in regional areas. Of course, UK backpackers is a sizeable part of the overall backpacker numbers. I've also spent quite a lot of time on farms in Tasmania, particularly when I was the Agriculture Minister. I've seen for myself the very large number of Pacific workers who are employed on Tasmanian farms, as they are on farms right across the country, under the PALM scheme, which is a very successful scheme that delivers workers for Australia and delivers important income for people from Pacific countries. That option remains available to farmers to use workers from the Pacific, and no change has been made to that under these recent announcements. We encourage farmers to make even more use of the PALM scheme than they are at the moment. I'm sure the officials have the numbers, but there are tens of thousands of already cleared workers in the Pacific who are wanting to come here and work on Australian farms. I'd encourage that farmer and farmers generally to make even greater use of that program.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: They already do. The farmers who I speak to across Tasmania and across the country tell me they already do access and seek to further access that scheme. So that's not going to help them fill what is, by my calculation, a shortfall of about 150,000 backpackers across the country that we need this summer to harvest our food out of the ground. How are you going to find that many Aussies to do that many jobs, which our farmers will immediately need once harvest commences this summer? Already backpackers have stopped coming here. Already some backpackers who have been here for one year are leaving farmers in Tasmania because they're too scared to pay $1,000 to take the risk and go into a ballot. We're introducing our first visa lotto in this country—to go into a ballot box and hope that their ticket will be pulled out so they have an opportunity to stay on for a second year.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Or third.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: They're going home already. How are you going to help our farmers in this country fill what's going to be an immediate, urgent skill shortage ahead of the next harvest season?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I can't remember what the position of the Greens political party is on migration numbers overall, but there is a widely accepted position—not just in this Parliament but across the Australian community—that despite the efforts that we've made the net overseas migration figure remains too high. As I said, if you accept that we need to reduce migration levels into Australia, then they've got to be reduced somewhere. What we've tried to do is reduce those numbers relatively evenly across a number of different programs—international students, working holiday-makers and other categories as well—and, if we say, 'We'll turn a blind eye to backpackers,' that just means you have to cut even more deeply when it comes to international students or doctors or nurses or aged-care workers. And I reckon you'd tell me that we need more of them as well. It's not a simple solution. You can't just say, 'I'm going to cut migration numbers to 100,000 or 125,000'—or whatever One Nation's policy is today—without saying the numbers have got to come from somewhere. When it comes to agriculture, what I'm encouraging farmers to do is make even greater use of the PALM scheme. It works for farmers all across the country, and there are more Pacific workers who are keen to come here right now.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The Greens aren't joining Labor, Liberal and One Nation in a race to the bottom on migration. We are here to support our farmers, and we urge you to consider pulling the pin on this bad idea that is cutting the rates of backpackers. It will have a devastating impact on food security in this country.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Is there a reason that the farmers that you're speaking to aren't prepared to make more use of the PALM scheme?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: They have been making use of the PALM scheme to the extent that they have been able to access it.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: There are thousands of extra Pacific workers who want to come and work here on Australian farms.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Are there 140,000 to 150,000?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm not sure where you got that figure from, but I'm literally happy to provide you with the contact details for the people who manage the PALM scheme so that you can put those farmers in contact with them.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And I'm happy to put some further questions on notice to you, Minister, and thank you for answering my questions.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No worries.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I note the time, Chair.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Thank you very much for your assistance, Senator Bleyer. We are scheduled to take our afternoon tea break now.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We will now resume from our afternoon tea break, and I will hand the call to Senator Duniam.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I wanted to go back to the Working Holiday Maker program and the set-up of the balloting. I was just trying to get an understanding. We're just on a month before operation of this scheme, and we've allocated $12.9 million—in May—to stand this scheme up and have the capacity to deliver it in whatever way. I'm still seeking to understand what has happened, how much has been spent and—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Ms Goodchild is here to assist you.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Excellent.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I am not sure if my IT colleagues are coming up, but, where Ms Bird referred to the work that Mr Kiley's division does in the policy, my division does the delivery implementation side of it, with my colleagues in IT.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Skilled and Temporary Visa and Capability

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Excellent.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In terms of your other question earlier around how far we are, there's $12.4 million that has been made for the IT build. The $12.9 million included the $500,000 for communication as well, which will be key to these measures.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Skilled and Temporary Visa and Capability

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Who are we communicating with?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: To the Australian public, and the backpackers and everyone, so that they'll understand the program as it develops, and to industry.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Skilled and Temporary Visa and Capability

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We'll come back to that. But, of the $12.4 million, what have we spent so far, and what have we got for it? And are we on track?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I can talk a little bit to that, and then my colleague Ms Walker can do so. Yes, we are on track. We're obviously working with our industry stakeholders on the development of what the ballot will be the final product of. There are already ballots in place for a number of countries, so we are working to add in another two countries. The minister referred to that—Indonesia and Philippines—and that's on track as well. We have a number of regular scheduled system releases, and they are on track for that November release. Then we are also building, within our immigration systems, the capability to do the ballots on a broader sense. We don't have that capability for working holiday maker 2 or 3 as such, so we're building that at the moment, and that is on track.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Skilled and Temporary Visa and Capability

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: My question earlier was: how many people have been employed? We talked about recruitment. We talked about contractors. How many people have been enlisted in this task as part of the $12.4 million piece of work to get us ready by the November launch date of this new ballot program for working holiday makers?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We'll still need to take the exact number on notice. I'll need to get that for you.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm just mildly concerned. We're a month out from the end date, we're five months from the budget provision being set aside for this purpose, and I don't have any detail about how many people have been engaged, even in rough terms. We're talking about designing something, not purchasing equipment or anything like that. We're just literally designing some sort of software, are we, or redesigning something that we have? What can you tell me about how we're spending $12.4 million to do this fairly straightforward task that we've had half a year to do?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The migration reform program has a number of changes within it. Within my tech group, I have lots of people who are working on different projects, delivering different things. We are given the money for these types of changes, from a system perspective, that involve a number of tasks. They involve designing the system and working with our colleagues in Immigration to make sure that it meets the requirements of the policy and the business needs. Then the team do all the normal things that a software engineering group would do. We have to develop it. We have to code it. We have to test it. We have to do user acceptance testing. We have to make sure that it's all working. And then we deploy it. As Ms Goodchild said, we have lots of standard releases through a year where we implement various changes for migration. The ones that we're talking about are for our next release in November.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In terms of consultation with stakeholders—we had some talk about farmers before; I'm sure there'd be people from the hospitality and visitor economy sector as well that would be interested—there's the communication program, but I just want to know whether they are going to see this thing before it's launched. Are we working with them on how it'll work? Have you told them how it'll work?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We are working with them on how it will work. They obviously won't see the IT changes—they're internal to us, and there's a number of systems that get changed—but that is just so that the staff in my division will be able to randomly draw from the ballots once how that will work is agreed with our stakeholders. This month alone, we've had over 14 stakeholder meetings with them.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Skilled and Temporary Visa and Capability

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Who are the stakeholders? Is it NFF and groups like that?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. The National Farmers' Federation is one of them. It's been predominantly with the agriculture sector and the tourism sector, but it's also been with organisations such as BlazeAid and different kinds of industry groups that bring people in to do things like play cricket, to be honest with you. But, largely, it's been with agriculture and tourism, as the two largest sectors that use working holiday maker.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Skilled and Temporary Visa and Capability

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: On notice, could you provide me with the dates on which these consultations have occurred and who has been a part of those consultations?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. I'm happy to do that now, or would you—
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Skilled and Temporary Visa and Capability

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes—maybe just the dates. I'll just assume you can do the other on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force

One was with the National Farmers' Federation. One was with the Australian Tourism Industry Council. The other was with the Tourism & Transport Forum. Then, on 13 October, we hosted two roundtables in the department. One in the morning was with agriculture, and that included all of the National Farmers' Federation's GrainGrowers association, the Fresh Produce alliance and a growers' association. There would probably have been a number of other ones; I can't remember off the top of my head.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Skilled and Temporary Visa and Capability

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: On notice, if you can.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We sought to consult with them on what their concerns were around a ballot process. That also happened with tourism in the afternoon. The three main themes that I would say came out of that was looking for certainty, making sure we had people in the region and simplicity—making sure the process was simple enough that people who were applying for a working holidaymaker visa and the employers who were using it could understand it. That goes to how we will build the system to make sure it's not overly complicated.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Skilled and Temporary Visa and Capability

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You have almost finished building the system, right, given—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, we have not finished building the system.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Skilled and Temporary Visa and Capability

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Almost, though. Surely you're getting close. We're a month away from operation.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We build the basic core operation of our system to enable it to do a ballot, and then, once we have finished our consultations with the stakeholders, we will do the final changes to that system. We have the core capability well underway.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Skilled and Temporary Visa and Capability

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You can't tell me at this point how much of the $12.4 million you have expended that was provided for this five months ago.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, we'll need to take that on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We'll wait and see how that goes. There's no purchase of additional equipment here; it is literally just design and using human resources to get there. Is that correct?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Okay, and you've taken on notice how many staff have been utilised and how many contractors. I was going to ask on this, of course. Moving away from that particular project, what modelling was done on the impact of each of those proposed changes in the 17 September announcement on the eventual NOM?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We did a lot of work looking at a variety of different settings and how, if you were just looking at particular ways—and it's pretty detailed work—to come up with a set of changes that would ensure the government could meet its NOM forecast both this year and into the future.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Has the government released any of that modelling, like how much of the contribution to the trajectory we're on for the NOM is related to the restriction, for example, on student dependant visas or anything like that? How much of the overall heavy-duty—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It hasn't been released yet, but it has been the subject of an order for production.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Ha! Is that one I put in?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: There's so many; you lose track of them.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I've done a handful!

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Those figures are being pulled together.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We'll await the response to those.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Hanson.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Minister, you advocated before that you encouraged farmers to go for PALM scheme workers. Is that the case?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes, I would certainly encourage farmers to make use of the PALM scheme, as thousands of farmers already do.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I was in Tasmania last week, and, apparently, the farmers there were depending on PALM scheme workers—approximately 150—who applied for their visas to arrive out on 22 October. Their visas weren't processed, and they were not able to come out. Then, the process—because there were complaints to the department—meant they won't be able to arrive till 10 November. The farmers are now out of pocket $10,000 for flights. There was no refund, recompense or reimbursement for that cost. Apparently, this has been happening quite a bit. The process is not being dealt with, visas are not being issued on time and now the farmers, who are not having their fruit picked and will lose a lot of it. Can you explain. Why the hold up? Why is the visa turnaround taking weeks? It's been extended, processing these visas, and the farmers are not getting the workers that they've been promised.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I don't know any of the circumstances of that case. I think the only thing that this department would be able to shed any light on is visa arrangements. The PALM scheme is administered by the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations, and so any more general issues about using the PALM scheme in that case would need to be put to them. It might be that some of the officials here can help you on the visa issue. I doubt they'd have individual—I don't even know which farmer you're talking about.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm talking about farmers from the north-west coast around Burnie and Ulverstone, that area.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: With respect, there are a lot of farms in that area.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In general—that's what I'm saying to you—they're not getting their workers. It wasn't only that. It was the tourist industry as well. It's been brought to my attention that they've put in for workers coming from overseas. They are not getting their visas processed in time, and they cannot book these tours and have them out for Christmas time at the height of tourist season, because there's been a hold up in visa applications. Is this because the department is trying to cut back on the numbers coming into the country to make your figures look good?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, far from it. I and other members of the government have encouraged people to make more use of the PALM scheme, so we'd hardly be trying to stop people coming in. Have you raised this concern with the department or the minister's office already?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes, it has—last week. That's why they weren't going to be out until 20 November. Now they've processed it to be 10 November. That also has been from a complaint from one of your own lower house members of parliament, who also put in a complaint to the department.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Again, if there are any officials here who have any information on that, I'm happy for them to share that. What I would say is that, if there are things that can be done to assist that particular farmer, we should do so. But right now there are tens of thousands of PALM workers working on farms, in abattoirs and elsewhere around the country. It may well be the case that there's been a problem in that instance. That doesn't mean that the program is a problem overall. It's actually supporting farmers to stay afloat right across the country.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I said there's been $10,000 out of pocket. Would you consider the department reimbursing for those flights that were booked and paid for? Due to the department and your failure to process those visas that were put in months beforehand, they are out of pocket—plus other businesses and their accommodation as well.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think Ms Goodchild or Mr Willard might have some information about that.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I don't have any information on that specific instance you've mentioned, but I thought it might be useful to give you some figures around the PALM scheme more generally. There are around 32,000 PALM visa holders in Australia at the moment. Last year we granted 26,389 visas. In terms of processing times, 75 per cent of those were processed within 14 days. Because I don't know the specific details of the case you raised, I can only speculate as to why they might be taking longer. There can be a range of reasons to do with health checks or other checks that we need to do that can delay processing. We do generally give advice not to make arrangements or book tickets before the visa is granted, but, if there are specifics in respect of that case that you've provided to the office, we'd be happy to look into the specifics.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We actually do have a little bit of information about this specific case. Ms Goodchild knows something about this.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: As Mr Willard said, we are processing PALM visas quite quickly. We did resolve the particular cases that you mentioned that did get escalated to us, but there was actually in fact another issue that related to the labour hire company. So I think your questions are in fact for the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations, because there was not a delay with the visa processing.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Skilled and Temporary Visa and Capability

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Minister, you actually spoke about the migration numbers that have to come back. Do you admit that it is under the Labor government that the highest recorded number of migrants in a single year have come to this country?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I already acknowledged that, after COVID, we saw a huge spike in migration numbers into Australia. Of course, that all occurred under the settings for the migration system that we'd inherited from the previous government. We then went about making changes to those settings: reducing international students, reducing the number of hours that international students could work and a range of other changes that we undertook which have now seen the net overseen by overseas migration figure nearly halved compared to what we saw straight after COVID.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You got elected in 2022. Between 2022 and 2023, approximately 739,000 people came into the country. Net migration was around about 512,000, the highest on record, under your government. You've had 2.2 million students and postgraduate visas in the last four years under your Labor government, and 385,000 of these have been to family and partners of temporary visa holders. Why haven't you gone after the temporary visa holders and partners of students, not the backpackers?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Before you respond to that, Minister, though I understand that there is some context sometimes required in leading into some questions, I do encourage senators to get to the questions, noting that we are running short of time. You've got about one minute left, Senator Hanson. Minister?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Just before I throw to Ms Sharp—we have made changes and are continuing to make changes across a range of different visa categories, including international students. Ms Sharp might have something further to add there.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's right, Minister. Earlier this month, the government announced and put in place new regulations that will prevent most students and temporary graduates from having secondary dependents in Australia attached to the primary student or temporary graduate holder, which will restrict the dependents coming with them while they're temporarily in Australia.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's only because One Nation has put out the policy to actually pull back on students' family members accompanying them. Otherwise, nothing would have been done about it at all. But you're going after the backpackers. That is actually going to be critical for rural and regional areas—to those workers in Australia—and you're targeting them, which is going to cause a shortage of workers in this country.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, Senator Hanson, as I said before, if we don't reduce the record number of backpackers that we have in this country at the moment, then that means cutting even more doctors who work in regional and rural hospitals. That means cutting—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: They are not backpackers. The doctors are not backpackers, so don't tell me that.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, that's exactly right.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You talk about nurses. Only one per cent of the people coming to this country are nurses.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's exactly right—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So you are exaggerating the figures here and you're saying it about those aged-care workers and nurses.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: For once in my life, I agree with you.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Hanson, please let the minister respond.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text:
For once in my life, I agree with you, Senator Hanson. Doctors are not backpackers. That is correct. My point is: you more than anyone say that we need to reduce migration numbers in this country and, if we don't reduce the record number of backpackers that we have in this country at the moment, that means reducing a whole range of other migration categories. It means international students, which we're reducing. It means doctors out of hospitals in rural areas. It means childcare workers out of childcare centres in the outer suburbs. You can't just pluck a figure out of the air and say that you're going to cut migration and say, 'Oh, but we're not going to touch that group, not going to touch that group and not going to touch that group.' Your numbers don't add up if that's the case. You've got to make the reductions from somewhere.

We think it is reasonable to reduce the record number of backpackers that we have in this country at the moment. We also think it's reasonable to further reduce the number of international students that we have, the partners of international students and a range of other categories as well. But what we don't want to see is doctors ripped out of rural hospitals and childcare workers ripped out of suburban childcare centres—and that would be the result of your policy.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Actually, wrong.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Thank you. Minister, I am going to take this opportunity to share the call. Senator Pocock, you've got the call.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Thanks again for your time this afternoon. I've got some questions about the healthcare checks that Bupa do for migrants, refugees—a whole range of people arriving in Australia. Is it just Bupa that does these health checks?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Onshore, yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And why is it just Bupa?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: There have been longstanding arrangements with the department to have a single provider do that. From my perspective and from a clinical governance perspective, having a single provider means you can achieve a certain level of consistency against the policies that we—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Do we pay Bupa anything?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: They don't receive any money from Home Affairs?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No. The way the contract works is that they charge the applicant for the health assessment.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: How much do they make a year? What's their revenue from this?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I don't have that detail with me. I'd have to take that on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Do you know a ballpark?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No. I don't want to speculate.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: How do they set their fees?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It's codified in the contract and in the key performance measures that we assess them against each year to determine whether or not they can increase during the life of the contract.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Home Affairs has no contracts with them? We don't pay them any money? They just get to charge?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: There is a contract, but it's not a contract where the department pays the provider any fee.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Every person getting a health check, regardless of who they are—I remember getting a health check when we moved to Australia. You obviously pay for that yourself. But are there any cohorts where the government assists with the payment?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That might have to be a question for some other colleagues.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The humanitarian caseload—if you're talking about people moving to Australia within the assisted passage program, there are health checks provided for that caseload.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: For the humanitarian cohort, do Bupa do theirs as well?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No. Overseas it's a different set of arrangements. But we have what are called panel doctors who do the checks, and Dr Pegg could talk more about how that works.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Overseas—so that's before people arrive here?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes, this is the health check they do before they come to Australia, before they're granted their visas.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: What about people who are being assessed onshore for a humanitarian visa?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Where a medical is required, then they go to Bupa.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And they have to pay that?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm not completely certain whether there are any circumstances where they don't have to pay, so I might have to take that on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Has the Department of Home Affairs ever denied protection for someone with a well-founded fear of persecution on health grounds? Does that happen?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, I don't think that's a ground, but Mr Kiley may be able to assist.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's not a ground for refusal.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Migration, Citizenship and Humanitarian Policy

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: If that's not grounds for refusal, why are we shovelling this money to Bupa?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'll have to take that on notice. Mr Willard was talking before about humanitarian applicants and health checks for those individuals. For offshore applicants for a humanitarian visa there is a health check. It's not a ground for refusal in that visa process, but there's a health check so we understand the health needs of the individual before they arrive in Australia. For onshore protection visas, my understanding is that there is not a health check, but I'll correct the record on that, if that's incorrect.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Migration, Citizenship and Humanitarian Policy

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That would be good. I want to check one example. I heard about a person seeking asylum who was experiencing homelessness and was admitted to a Sydney based hospital. They were invited to undertake their visa health checks by the Department of Home Affairs, but they weren't allowed to undertake these health checks in the hospital. They had to go to Bupa. Why is that the case? Surely a hospital is fairly well placed to do a health check.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'd have to look at the particular circumstances, but, if you're looking for an answer in the broad as to why we have an arrangement with Bupa as opposed to any medical practitioner, it could be one that Dr Pegg could take.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The visa health screening is obviously for a very dedicated, particular purpose and has to be carried out according to certain policies. It's not the case necessarily that any health practitioner would be aware of those policies to carry it out with the fidelity that we require.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: On the Bupa contract, is it a rolling contract? How often is it reassessed or renewed?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The current contract commenced on first of July 2022. We exercised the first of two contract extension periods of two years from 1 July 2025, with the revised contract end date of 30 June 2027.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: What happened before 2022?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I believe it was a different provider, but I'd have to take that on notice. It was before my time.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Okay.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I can correct my evidence earlier. Onshore protection visa applicants do need to undertake a health check. They have to pay for those health checks themselves, but I can confirm that is not a ground for refusal.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Migration, Citizenship and Humanitarian Policy

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I assume someone who is trying to get a humanitarian visa probably doesn't have a lot of spare cash. How much are they having to pay for their health check, given it's not grounds for refusal? It's just a nice to know. What does that cost them?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Unless Dr Pegg has the details—
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Migration, Citizenship and Humanitarian Policy

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We'll have to take that on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You don't have that figure? No-one up the back's got that figure? This seems like a pretty strange set of circumstances where we're forcing people who have been assessed as genuine refugees to pay Bupa hundreds—potentially thousands of dollars for a family—to get a health assessment that is not grounds for refusal just so we can know that there might be some health needs when a doctor gets 70 or 80 bucks to do an extended consultation through the MBS. Why are we throwing money at a multinational insurance company rather than having a more sensible solution where they go to a local GP who can bulk-bill?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You will have seen I've been speaking with the official, Senator Pocock. We've just been trying to clarify the policy rationale, and I think Ms Foster or Ms Sharp might have something to say here.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It's not dissimilar to the rationale for doing a health check for offshore so we understand the health needs. This health check allows us to target the settlement services to ensure that appropriate health care is provided during that period. It's actually focused on caring for the person as they transition, not any other reason.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The thing I don't understand here is, when my family was moving here, the health check was important because there are certain exclusions for different health conditions, and that was made very clear. This is something where you've just said it's not grounds for refusal. Why on Earth don't we just send them to the local GP and have some sort of MBS item where they can do a full health check? First, we are shovelling money at a multinational that, the last time I checked, is questionable on some of the tax paid and, second, we're forcing people who probably don't have much cash and who may not even have work rights to pay hundreds of dollars—thousands of dollars for a family—for a medical exam that's not grounds for refusal so we know what's wrong with them. Send them to a doctor. Minister, surely there's a better way to do this.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Obviously, as the representing minister, I don't have the knowledge of this content to the degree you're looking for. If the officials have got anything further they can add—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: One further reason for having a centralised system in the way we do is that it allows us to have confidence that every person has had the check done, and that ensures we do know the health conditions of people who are coming to Australia and we can have confidence that, if somebody does happen to have a communicable disease, we know that.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sure.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: If, in the way you suggest, it was done in a very individual led way, we wouldn't be able to give any assurance around the system that's in place to have confidence.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Ms Sharp, you've just talked about an overseas example. I totally get that. But what if someone's here? They've probably been here for many years. The processing takes—well, you know better than all of us that people here decades long have been here on some sort of limbo. Finally, if you can't afford the health check, can you get your humanitarian visa, or is it no health check, no visa?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
