text: I would need to take it on notice. I would imagine that we have hardship circumstances or there would be an arrangement, but let me take on notice the arrangements if a person cannot afford the health check.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Roberts.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Thank you for appearing. Before we start, Ms Foster, thank you for the briefing on Friday, I think it was, last week. We've heard via the media that there is currently a 'go slow' practice occurring in the processing of some visa applications. Which types of visas are currently being processed slowly?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Minister Burke, in his Press Club address, made it clear that there was slower processing being applied to the working holiday-maker visa. That has stabilised now at around a three-month processing time for all working holiday-maker visa applications where there's a specified work requirement, which is that every everyone is required, if they want to do a second year, to work in a regional area. For working holiday-maker visa applicants from the UK, who do not have the specified work requirement, those are still being processed more slowly.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: How many such applications have had delayed processing?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Mr Willard might be able to help you with that.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I might be able to give you some numbers in terms of numbers of visas on hand—the number of visas processed in the working holiday-maker visa space—if you'll bear with me. In 2026-27, to 31 August, we've granted 22,377 working holiday visas. When we look at the active applications on hand, there are 48,752 on hand.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: How many was that?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Applications on hand?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Why are they being delayed again?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Ms Sharp just outlined.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We have got historically high, very high, levels of working holiday-maker visas in Australia currently. The purpose of slowing the processing and stabilising the processing time with that three-month delay is to moderate the growth rate of working holiday-maker numbers in Australia. Longer term, we're moving towards managing that number so that it's not completely demand-driven through the use of ballots going forward.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It's an official policy. It was directed by Minister Burke.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It's certainly something we've worked on with Minister Burke to manage the number while we've been working on the longer term solution that will involve the use of ballots.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It's an attempt to temporarily limit numbers of persons entering Australia and to smooth out the application processing.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. It's—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You've got a varying load, by the sound of it, and you want to smooth it out.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. The challenge with the Working Holiday Maker program, prior to the government taking action this financial year, is that it is completely demand driven, which means that we've seen very rapid growth over several years, which led us to the situation where we had these historically high levels. The actions we've taken are seeking to moderate that growth and bring that level down somewhat, in the way that the minister has also talked through today. We're looking at every visa class; it's not just the Working Holiday Maker visa. That's probably been the one most publicly commented on in the media, but there are other changes being made to student visas. We're making changes to visitor visas. We're making changes to the way our permanent program is allocated, all with the sole goal, if you like, of ensuring that the government has much better control over the number of people coming to and staying in Australia.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Thank you. You want to restore control to immigration entry?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We want to maintain control and, for some of these programs that have historically been completely demand driven, provide government with some levers to have control over numbers. In something like the Working Holiday Maker program, it has historically been a program where, however many people applied, if they met the criteria, they would be granted a visa.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Does this apply to international students and their dependants and families? Does it apply to illegals and the unskilled?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Certainly we are making changes. There have been a number of steps taken in relation to students over several years, and another round of changes was announced earlier this month. The most significant of those is restricting dependants accompanying students and temporary graduates—for most students, not all, but most. So, yes, certainly we are, as I said, looking across the system to make changes where they are sensible, moderate, and ensure government has levers to manage the volume.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: What about graduate students?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Temporary graduates?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Temporary graduates will be subject to similar controls to those we're applying to students. Most temporary graduates will not, going forward, be able to have dependants attached to their visa.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It sounds like One Nation policy that you're adopting. Could we have a copy of a listing of the numbers, please, and the cuts in each area?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'd love to see one of those from One Nation.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We've shown it. I'll get it to you.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Is that your version, Senator Hanson's version or Mr Farley's version?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It's the party's version.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: But I've seen about four or five. Which one should I look at?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The one that was finalised.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Is that your version?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'll send it to you. No, it's the party's version. Ms Sharp, I'm very pleased to hear this, but I won't endorse it until I see the actual numbers, because the Labor Party has been frightened to address the numbers.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator, we can take on notice the NOM effect of these measures.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: What effect? I'm sorry.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The net overseas migration effect. What impact do we think these measures will have on net overseas migration? I would note that Senator Duniam also asked something similar, and there is an order for production seeking similar information as well. That's currently being processed through our system.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Could I have the existing numbers and the reduced numbers expected in future for each of the visa categories: main visa applicants, students, graduate students, dependants of students, dependants of graduate students, illegals, the unskilled and graduates?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. Illegals are a little different.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes, that will be different.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In that we don't control—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You know they're there, but you haven't chased them. Okay.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's correct.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Have applicants been notified of potential delays in the processing of visas?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes, Senator. There is information on our website that applicants receive that indicates they should expect three-month processing times.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: This policy is contributing to enlarging the backlog of visa applications waiting to be processed, I take it?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I gave you the figure for the on-hand number, which has risen over the last three months.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Minister, will this mean the Labor Party will start to use the word 'no' and refuse people entry?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We already do that where someone seeking a visa doesn't pass security tests or meet a range of other requirements.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: What is the number of backlogged initial applications and currently known appeals awaiting a decision? Do you have those numbers, or is that a question on notice?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Across all visa types?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sorry, could you ask the question again, Senator?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: What is the number of backlogged initial applications and currently known appeals awaiting a decision?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Across all visa classes? We would need to take that on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That will be fine. Shifting slightly, how common is visa hopping? It sounds pretty common from Ms Foster's nodding.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Visa hopping, as it's referred to, is one of the practices that the changes that have been introduced are seeking to address. It refers to a circumstance where students, in particular, shift from visa to visa but never achieve completion of a course. In addition to the changes to dependence that Ms Sharp has outlined, there are also changes to the way in which people can apply for student visas onshore. That requires completion of a course and progression to a more advanced course. Those measures are designed to deal with that practice of visa hopping. In addition, the minister has announced that the visitor visas will be subject to a condition known as a 'no further application' or 'no further stay' condition, which means that only in exceptional circumstances would people be allowed to shift from a visitor visa to another visa while they're onshore.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Thank you. You may not know the answer to this one. What is the current number of non-citizens in Australia with no valid visa?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Mr Thomas could probably come to the table and assist with that.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Noting these are estimates because, by the nature of that cohort, we're not managing them on visas.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's right. At a point in time, 30 June this year, we estimate approximately 79,400 non-citizens were here without a visa. That cohort is very fluid; it includes people that have been unlawful for a day, an hour, a week, a year. That cohort continuously changes as people become unlawful and subsequently leave the country as well.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, that's remarkable. It gives me confidence because we've been saying there are 80,000 people here illegally, and that's pretty much the target. What measures—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You are at time for your 10-minute block. Are you almost done, or is now a good time to rotate the call?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Now would be a good time to rotate.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Excellent. Thanks so much. Just indicating I'm going to share the call.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: If I could just add one more to that—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sure.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: How many non-citizens are currently here illegally? Is that different from the number who are here with no valid visa?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, Senator. The number I gave you is the number of non-citizens that are here without a current valid visa.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Can I just add one thing on that. The government's position is that, if someone doesn't have a valid visa, they shouldn't be here. That is why one of the other measures that's just been announced by Minister Burke is an increase in what's called compliance activity to remove people who don't have a right to be here. Under the former government, funding was removed from that function.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You've been here for half a decade.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I know.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Roberts.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I know you don't like hearing things about your Liberal mates, but the truth is that, under the former government, funding to remove people who didn't have a valid visa was wound down. We are putting that funding back in to remove people who don't have a valid visa.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And you're chasing us because we introduced all these policies.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We're not chasing you.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes you are. We're setting the agenda, Senator Watt.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We are not chasing you.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Roberts, thank you very much. I will take the opportunity to share the call. Senator Duniam.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Could I ask about direction 119, which commenced, as I understand it, on 25 July this year, which established the new processing priority framework for skilled visas, which was then replaced not two months later by directions 121 and 122. Can I understand why there was a change.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Certainly, Senator. In the budget this year, the government announced, when it was announcing the Permanent Migration Program, that it would retain it at 185,000 places. It also announced that it would shift the focus of the program so that 70 per cent of places went to people who were already onshore in Australia and 30 per cent could go to those who were offshore. Ministerial direction 119 was put in place to give us the best chance of ensuring we could achieve that 70-30 split, because it involved shifting our priority quite substantially to get more of our cases from the onshore cohort. It worked very effectively. And we'd always intended that it wouldn't be a direction that needed to be in place for more than a few months. After about 10 weeks of operation, we were in a position where we could say to the government, 'Yes, we're pretty confident you can get to the 70-30 split, but you can free up more space for some more high-priority industries.'

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Hence, 121 and 122.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. So 121 and 122 came, and the big difference between them is in 119. The only specified industry that could sit above onshore applications was defence and law enforcement. When we could move after that 10-week period to a wider group of industries, we were able to pick up industries like agriculture, aquaculture, construction, mining, health care, teaching—a wider group of priority industries.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That explains that. If I can go to the matter of housing. In the minister's Press Club address, he did reference the need to address migration as a means of dealing with housing—in a sense, slow down the numbers to catch up and allow houses to be built so that we can accommodate. I'm just wondering what modelling was used to inform the numbers that we have ultimately arrived at, or the government has arrived at for its NOM. Is there any information on what housing modelling input there was?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The NOM figure that we're working towards, which is 245,000 this year and 225,000 next year, is NOM modelling that was produced by the Treasury. It was really forecasting where it thought NOM would get to. The measures we're taking are really to ensure that we've had a shift—I think the government's been pretty open about that—from thinking of that as an economic forecast to treating it like a target. They're not numbers that were set based on housing like an analysis of housing demand. It's a NOM forecast.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I understand the point you make there. That being said, it is more an assumption, then, in this speech, that you reduce numbers here. It enables us to catch up on housing as opposed to there having been a formal input into the numbers that either Treasury or Home Affairs undertake.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think very much you need to direct questions about the rate at which homes are being built and the like to Treasury.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sure. Insofar as it relates to their projections on the NOM, is that what you mean?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Insofar as what level of NOM and how fast housing is being constructed and the like. We worked very closely with Treasury on the migration reform package and on the NOM modelling, and also on settings around how we get more construction workers and the like in as a higher proportion of the program.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: But, in terms of that partnership you've just explained, there was no range of housing construction numbers for a 12-month period that Treasury might have brought to the table and said, 'Here's how we think we might be able to deal with this issue the minister talks about in his speech.'

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We're trying to be helpful in terms of what inputs we make, but the actual modelling really needs to go to Treasury. It would be a brave Home Affairs department that gave an opinion on Treasury modelling.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Venture forth where others may not. I'll return to working holiday makers, then. There are specific caps for the second- and third-year visas. How did we arrive at 45,000 and 5,000 for the two respective years?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We looked at the numbers last year, and we looked at the kind of non-reduction or the effect we needed to achieve. For example, the working holiday maker ballot number that Minister Burke announced of 45,000 represents about 80 per cent of the number of working holiday maker 2 people who were actually here last year. Essentially, it was a combination of looking at what kind of reduction or tapering of growth we needed to achieve, along with what we expect demand would look like. Also, Minister Burke was very keen to ensure that, particularly in working holiday maker 2, we kept enough places available, as many as we could, to create a strong incentive for people to do their regional work in year 1, which is why, at 80 per cent, you've got a four in five chance if you go in the ballot of getting a place.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: A range of options were considered when it comes to numbers, I assume, on the way through, but 45,000 for working holiday maker 2 was decided the best one to achieve the ultimate outcome here.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's correct. We looked at a range of options.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And the same for 5,000 in year 3.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The calculation is a little different. I don't have that off the top of my head.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: But also a range of options were considered.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: With those numbers, obviously the government retains the capacity to, in any given year, despite this being the stated aim, go beyond that.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's right. Where the government decides to set a ballot level is very much up to the government, and it could change during the course of a year based on economic need or demand or society. We would be running the ballot with some frequency. The ballot mechanism itself is just a control lever, if you like, that allows government to manage volume. It can also set some criteria around it. But the number is very much a choice of government of the day.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Going back to operations of the program, when will registrations open? On what date are we looking to commence that?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I don't think we've settled a precise date yet.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I assume early December, given the program will be up and running in November, or the necessary—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I do not know the date, Senator, so I'll need to take it on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Can I understand from, for example, the point of view of a farmer who is looking to obtain a workforce for harvest or a hospitality business looking for workers seeking to have someone in the month of January next year, are they able to apply now? If so, are they treated under the normal arrangements, or would they be under a go-slow, we've talked about previously, or is there a complete hold on things until this new scheme is up and running?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Applications continue to be open for working holiday maker 1, 2 and 3 at the moment, within the constraints that we described, with that three-month processing time.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'll come back to that other issue, but, on the process time, while we're on it, how did we determine three months was the workable period to process in?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Again, that was a decision we took based on looking at the need to temper that rapid growth, alongside what we thought was a reasonable amount of time for somebody to wait.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We did some analysis that showed that, typically, working holiday makers take just over three months between the time they get their first visa overseas and the time they actually arrive in Australia?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Okay. So it was set for that reason. Going back to this certainty issue and the scheme being up and running, we're on track to have the balloting system working for year 2 and 3 working holiday makers, and their visa might be coming to an end sometime over the Christmas-New Year period. How do they operate in this void or vacuum? Is it just business as usual?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In the case of somebody who's here, they've completed their specified work in their first year and they could apply now, and they are, and we are processing those, albeit with that three-month wait. The ballot doesn't apply yet.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So it only then applies after a point in time when you've stood it up, and we don't know quite what date that will be yet.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. Minister Burke has said November, and we've said today it will be towards the end of November.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: For those who pay a fee and miss out—to some questions Senator Bleyer was asking before—$1,000, I think it is, is that for year 2?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, the fee for participating in the ballot is not the visa application fee. It will be a lot lower than that.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Do you know what it will be?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Where we have ballots in place already, it's $25. It's a nominal fee. It's designed to stop bots and the like clogging up the system.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Roberts.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: What measures are being taken to send the illegals out of Australia?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator, Mr Thomas will no doubt come up and join me at the table. The government has announced that it's funding an additional 250 beds in immigration detention. That is going to assist us to much more actively target people who have no right to remain—visa overstayers, predominantly. We have also received additional funding for around 100 additional officers, predominantly for our field removals and detention capability. That will allow us to have the additional people to go out and do the work to identify individuals who are overstaying their visas. We will also be communicating much more proactively with people as they approach the end of their visa period, and immediately after, to ensure they understand that, when their visa expires, they either need a new visa or need to leave and that, if they don't leave, the immigration detention system is there and it will be used.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: As Ms Sharp said, it's really maximising the engagement with this cohort to encourage self-departure as much as possible. Where people do not self-depart, we look at detention and removal. But we aim to maximise the number of unlawful non-citizens here leaving the country at the end of their migration pathway.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Thank you for your answer. Would it be fair to say that there are two problems here? One is you're addressing 80,000 people who are here illegally with 250 beds. So there are two aspects. One is stopping the future illegals and one is getting rid of the current illegals. Is that fair?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's right, Senator, and I think there are a number of amplifying factors. Depending on how quickly we can turn people over from detention to removal, obviously, those beds can produce a lot more than—it's not 250 a year, for example. It's rotating.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It's rotating. I get it.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: If, on average, for example, it took us a month to prepare all the papers and get someone involuntarily out, then that's still 250 by 12. What we're finding is that some people are leaving more quickly than that. So that's one factor. The second is that our historical data shows us that, for every person we remove, there is a flow-on effect of people who understand what might happen to them. It's not advantageous to be removed. It affects your future visa prospects. So there's a factor of somewhere around six or seven per cent of people who leave voluntarily in relation to the number of people that we remove.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Six or seven times.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sorry, six or seven times.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We've covered that.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And then there is the impact of the communications activity and the knowledge that will get around in communities about what's happening to people that we think will also add to that number. This has been a sticky problem for many, many years. We believe that this combination of measures will allow us to start to make a real impact on that number.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You should contact Senator Hanson's office, because our policy comprehensively addresses this, but we'll move on. What measures are being taken to stop preachers of hate within the Islamic community?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm very glad you asked, Senator Roberts, because—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Good. I hope you've got news—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You might remember my mentioning at a previous estimates hearing that earlier this year, when we introduced legislation to make it easier to deport hate preachers, you, Senator Hanson and every other One Nation senator voted against that legislation.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Because of your poison pills in your legislation! You've got to get out of this habit.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Roberts, let the minister answer.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: As I've pointed out, the other major aspect of that legislation was also cracking down on Neo-Nazis, so I'm still waiting to hear what it was about that legislation you didn't like. Was it that it was taking on—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm happy to sit down in discussion with you.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Neo-Nazis or deporting hate preachers? I think this is the third or fourth time I've made these points.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So when do you expect Islamic preachers to be sent out of the country?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, it would help to have your support for the legislation that we passed. We actually got support from the coalition. I'll acknowledge that. But you voted against the legislation—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Because of the poison pills in the bill.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: that makes it easier to deport hate preachers.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You can't get honest legislation through without blackmail, and we're not going to fall for blackmail.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You voted against deporting hate preachers.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Correct.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It couldn't be clearer than that.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We voted against the poison pill in your—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: What was the poison pill?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: There were many poison pills.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Can you give me an example?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You've put it in industrial relations. You've put it in immigration. You've put it—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Can you give me one example?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No. How many persons on skilled worker visas in Australia are working in their identified skilled professional field?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text:
Senator, in terms of temporary skilled visa holders, it's a requirement of their visa that they work in the role for which they were recruited. So most of those temporary visa holders are working in their field. In terms of permanent visas, there's a recent release from the Bureau of Statistics which is 'Migrant settlement outcomes', which talks about permanent skilled entrants. It has some figures in comparison to the Australian population around how those permanent skilled entrants are tracking.

In terms of employment rate—and this is the employment to population ratio—the figure for permanent skilled entrants is 82 per cent and the figure for the Australian population is 74 per cent. There are a couple of other key figures there. English proficiency is 91 per cent for permanent skilled entrants and 92 per cent for the Australian population, and a non-school qualification is 80 per cent permanent skilled residents and 36 per cent for the Australian population. This is a Bureau of Statistics publication that was released in September.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Thank you. What is the extent of people entering Australia as skilled workers who hold worthless or forged qualifications? Do you check qualifications on their application?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We do check qualifications. Any instance where there's a fraudulent qualification submitted in an application would result in visa refusal. The vast majority of skilled migrants are highly skilled people who hold high-level qualifications.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: When do you envisage the backlog on visa appeals to be resolved by the Administrative Review Tribunal?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: There was some very useful legislation passed by the parliament earlier this year that will assist the Administrative Review Tribunal to get through the student backlog. That was a large group of student visa applications that had built up there. They are in the process of now rolling out that change, which is allowing them to dismiss matters on the papers without holding a hearing. You would need to directly ask them about how many months they think it will take to clear that backlog, but they are making some positive progress.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So you wouldn't be able to give me an idea of how long it'll take?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, I really think that's a matter for the Administrative—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: What are the numbers in the ART appeals process?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I've got the ART report. These are their figures, but the figure I have here—this is a case-load report for 1 July to 31 August 2026. I'm reading the 'On hand at period end' figure. There are 54,000 student visas, or just under that figure.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Then there are other categories as well.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: There are other categories.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: What's the total backlog that the ART is facing at the moment?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Again, I'm reading their figure to you. I haven't been able to verify all of this, but the figure is 83,847 under a heading 'Migration'.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Are you aware of the massive current rort of the maritime crew visa subclass 988 for domestic trade and the active abuse of the subclass 400 short stay specialist and subclass 482 temporary skill shortage visas, to flood domestic waters with cheap foreign mariners doing the work that hundreds of highly skilled Australian mariners are qualified and willing to do?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: There are a range of safeguards and measures, in respect of all of those visas, that are designed to prevent misuse of the visas. There are always some instances of noncompliance in respect of visas, but, for the large part, it's very high levels of compliance that we record.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Multinational companies are falsely claiming, we've been advised, that they cannot find local employees and then hiring low-cost foreign mariners under visa subclasses 400 and 482. There is no skills shortage in this field in Australia. There are many captains, mates and engineers seeking work in Australia.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: If you have specific examples, you're very welcome to send them through to us and we can have a look at them. If there are businesses that should be on our radar, we'd welcome you sending those through.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Is this rort currently being investigated? Are you aware of it?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Where there are instances of concern raised then we do look into them, and we do engage with employers where there are concerns raised about their practices.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's encouraging, because the foreign workers' wages go straight out of our country.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Roberts, to give you an indication, you are at your 10 minute block.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. This will be my last question. Minister, what are you doing to target the huge number of students currently here in Australia—way in excess of the numbers of beds at universities for international students? They, and their families and dependants, are taking up beds and houses that could be filled with Australians. What are you doing about their dependants, their families? What are you doing about people who are here with no real skills? What are you doing about graduates? One Nation has an answer for all of these.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And you'll have a chance to put your answers to the public.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We look forward to that.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We have already taken action to reduce international student numbers, over the last couple of years, but the recent announcements by Minister Burke involved further action around student visas. To give you a couple of examples, we're cracking down on what's referred to as 'visa hopping', so student visa holders will not be able to apply for another student visa onshore unless they fit a small number of categories. Most temporary visa holders will be prevented from applying for a student visa onshore. Most international students and temporary graduates will be prevented from bringing family members with them to Australia. So there are a range of new measures that we're taking in addition to ones that we've already taken.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In addition to that, from 1 July 2026, the visa application charge for new student visas and temporary graduate visas was increased by 25 per cent. The government allocated $19.8 million to extend the student visa cancellation team to ensure that we can identify and cancel visas of students who are not doing the right thing. Finally, the government is also applying a higher degree of scrutiny over particular providers that are offering courses that are not doing what they're saying—what they should be doing. So, recently, Minister Hill issued three notices of intention to suspend particular courses and providers.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Minister, I must say it's very, very pleasing and gratifying to see that the current government is taking tiny steps to catch up with One Nation. But when are you going to start acknowledging that you are the government—you've been the government for almost half a decade—instead of blaming the previous lot?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The fact is that, when we came to office, we had a broken migration system—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Half a decade ago.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. Let me finish. The fact is: when we came to office, we had a broken migration system that was full of rorts, that led to what you've described as the highest migration numbers that we've seen. Since that time, we've taken a whole range of measures that have almost halved net overseas migration—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You've come down to the second-highest and the third-highest! Well done!

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It's well below that now, because of the action that we've taken.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: They were the highest—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yours were the highest, by far.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I am now going to take the opportunity to share the call. Had you concluded, Minister?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sure.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Duniam.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Back to the Working Holiday Maker matter, in terms of the slowdown, as it's been referred to, who from industry was consulted in proceeding with that?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That was a decision of the government. It was consulted within the government.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: There was no consultation with farmers, hospitality or tourism stakeholders?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Not prior to it being implemented. As Ms Goodchild was outlining, there has been extensive consultation—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: After it was implemented.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: after and as we run up to how we implement the ballot arrangement.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I appreciate the consultation on the forthcoming changes that have been announced, which is good practice, but there was none on the first ones. On 24 September, it was reported that the government and National Farmers' Federation put in place an arrangement allowing urgent farm related Working Holiday Maker cases to be put forward for priority processing. Whose suggestion or idea was this proposal?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The National Farmers' Federation approached the government.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Has an arrangement like this ever been put in place before, to your knowledge?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We routinely consider requests for expedited processing for a wide range of reasons. It could be compassionate circumstances. It could be instances such as this, where particular individuals needed to be in particular locations to help with harvest. The broad practice of considering expedited processing requests is something that we do across a lot of our caseloads.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Is partnering with a third-party non-government organisation to facilitate these approaches something that's been done before?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I would have to take that on notice. I have vague recollections that in the past we have done so, but I wouldn't be confident answering the question definitively.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Is that arrangement still in place?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think we still engage with the NFF and a number of other organisations who choose to bring urgent cases to attention. We then make a determination about whether or not we're in a position to expedite it.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You mentioned other organisations that bring urgent cases, but that's not in the same way we're talking about this formalised NFF arrangement that was advertised as such by the NFF.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think the NFF arrangement is a more organised approach, but we certainly get reps from a whole lot of organisations.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Is this more organised approach and partnership with the NFF still in place today?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes, in that we're still engaging with the NFF.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: To extinguish it, there will have to be some communication with them saying, 'Okay, team, we're not going to take any more, in the same way we have been'?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I think it might be just reverting to the normal approach we take in respect of any requests for expedited processing.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You'll tell them when that time comes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes, we will.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So there would be a formal extinguishing of the arrangement. Do we know how many applications have been received by the department through this formalised arrangement?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I don't have that. If Ms Goodchild has it, she'll approach the table. Otherwise, she'll take it on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: There are around about 749 that have been processed under that arrangement.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Skilled and Temporary Visa and Capability

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And granted?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Skilled and Temporary Visa and Capability

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Okay. And how many applications are there all up?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: All of the applications are still subject to our normal visa processing, but all of the ones that have been escalated have actually been granted. So it was still the same number.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Skilled and Temporary Visa and Capability

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Alright. And do you know on what date this arrangement kicked off? It was announced on the 24th, but what date was it actually instituted?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I would have to take the actual date on notice.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Skilled and Temporary Visa and Capability

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Alright. I presume the minister was satisfied that this arrangement was needed to deal with some of the issues that stakeholders were facing.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It was predominantly to deal with harvest.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Skilled and Temporary Visa and Capability

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. My question ultimately is going to be: did the minister sign off on this arrangement, or was it something that the NFF just came to the department about, saying, 'We'd like to do this because we have a problem with the way things are tracking and being processed,' with the department saying, 'Yes, we can do this'?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We were working at that point in time most closely with Assistant Minister Hill, but also Minister Burke was aware and had no concerns with the approach. As Mr Willard was saying, it's not at all uncommon. We do our best to make sure that, when there are urgent, extenuating circumstances in different contexts, compelling and compassionate, we can move around the system. When you operate a system as large as ours, you need to always have safety valves or escape valves to deal with cases. So this is one example of us being able to flex the system a little bit.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. I do think there are many well-documented cases of being able to expedite. But, when you say it's not unusual, my point here is that because of a set of circumstances that, frankly, stakeholders were screaming about and about which saying, 'This is not working for us,' one group of stakeholders has said, 'We want to enter into this arrangement.' The arrangement is not usual, is my contention here.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Probably not at the level of formality that we have here. But, in principle—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You will have expedited.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: we do get cases escalated, and we do act on those, where there are reasons to do so.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Assistant Minister Hill, then, was more involved in this. Did he sign off on the arrangement, or was it one that didn't require ministerial agreement or sign-off?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It doesn't require ministerial agreement for an organisation to approach us and say, 'Here is a set of cases we'd like you to look at.'

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Okay.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Some of this has now come out, but Minister Hill agreed the arrangement with the NFF, having discussed it with Minister Burke.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Very good. Thank you very much. On the ballots, was any modelling commissioned around the economic impact of these changes by the department and done by external agencies—Treasury or a private sector consultant?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: There were no private sector consultants used for any modelling by us in relation to migration reform—so 'no', to that part of your question. On the economic modelling, we did do that NOM analysis modelling, which I think I've taken on notice to provide.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. Can we talk to the impact of those changes in terms of the number of working holiday-makers here in a full program year. What's the number of working holiday-makers we expect to be in Australia once the two caps come into effect. From December or whenever it kicks off, in the following year, do we have a projection on how many working holiday-makers we expect to be in Australia?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Because we're trying to manage NOM, and it's about the flows, not stock—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes; of course, it's flows. But that flow reduction has an impact on stock, generally, noting, though, the fact that these are temporary visa holders, and they should leave at the end of their visa if they haven't got an extended one.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. And the complicating factor is that not all of the working holiday-makers will 'NOM in'. Some of them just come for a relatively short period—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes—two months.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: and then leave. At the other end, the rate at which they're 'NOMming out' is also a factor. We're seeking to have, if you like, a system that allows us to manage the NOM impact more than a system that focuses on particular stock levels. If the flows allow, a stock level could be higher, if that makes sense. If you've got enough coming in, balanced by the number coming out, then that's the impact we're seeking to have.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: This might be a conversation for the pub or something, I think. I'm going to move on. In terms of the—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sorry; I was distracted for a second. Are you about to move on to a new topic, or are you just going to wrap this up?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Look, how about I wrap these up, and then I'm done with the bulk of this outcome.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. Wrap that up, then I'll go—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: To Senator Hanson? Yes. Under these arrangements, it is the case, though, isn't it, that if you meet those requisite levels of regional work—your 88 days and 179 days—you could still lose the ballot because it is truly randomised? That's the intention, isn't it, that, having satisfied year one and year two, if you intend to go into year three, this program could mean you—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That's the design work we've been doing with those stakeholders that Ms Goodchild referred to. We've been working through how can we design the ballot to reduce the likelihood of that occurring. A range of ideas are being worked through, like if people can enter the ballot before they do their regional work so they know when they start your regional work, if they do my regional work and complete it successfully, they've got their place. Yes, we're working our way through that.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Roberts asked before if we have looked at how many additional PALM workers would be required to offset the reduction in working holiday-maker visas. Does this scheme have capacity to cater to that gap if it should exist in terms of economic need?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In a lot of the discussion today, there has been an assumption that every single working holiday-maker is working in agriculture, which isn't true, so it's not right to think that if we reduce working holiday-makers by 20,000, we would need 20,000 more PALM workers in the region. It's not one-for-one like that. Working holiday-makers work in a whole range of industries, so we have been talking with our colleagues in DFAT and DEWR about what a sensible growth pathway for PALM would be.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So that implies that a growth pathway is required for PALM to offset. I agree with you. It's not all of the working holiday-makers are going to be out in the regions, but a portion will be; therefore, there will be a reduction. That assumption you refer to, which is a growth pathway required for PALM, have we done any analysis on what that looks like?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The other point to make in terms of PALM, of course, is the working holiday-makers are in a region for a short period of time in a year, whereas the PALM worker is dedicated to that particular work. We are certainly keen to work with the partners that Ms Sharp mentioned to grow PALM. We don't have a particular formula that we're working to in terms of how much it needs to grow versus the working holiday.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You're considering. You're looking at that because it's deemed not a necessity, but it is something you have in contemplation?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: There's a range of reasons why the government's really supportive of PALM. In addition to the agricultural workforce, it's really important as part of the government's overall approach to working with the Pacific. They're part of our neighbourhood, so there's a very deliberate approach, not necessarily to say, 'Australia says we need X thousand farm workers', but actually talking to the countries about what they need and what kind of arrangement would work with Pacific countries.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator Hanson.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'd like to go back to the multicultural grants. We've established that in 2022-23 you actually handed out approximately $5,900,000 in multicultural grants and then, in 2025-26, it was approximately $325 million, which is an increase of 5,400 per cent. Eighty-seven per cent of multicultural grants have been awarded through a closed non-competitive selection. Why was it that hundreds of millions of taxpayers' dollars were handed out without transparency or competition? Did the department provide any advice to government about the size of this program and the fact that closed tenders present corruption risks? If so, what did you raise in your advice to government about multicultural grants?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: A significant proportion of the multicultural grants were election commitments. In relation to election commitments, the department does not provide any advice on the government's decision to make that commitment. We do administer the grant process, so we do provide advice. If the government says, 'We want to grant $X million to this organisation,' we will run checks and make sure that the grant guidelines can be met by that organisation, that they have the financial capacity to do the work and that they meet kind of base requirements, but we don't provide a separate view on whether the government's election commitment is a good idea from a policy perspective or not.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So the department has no say in tendering for this. The government comes to you and says: 'We want a grant for this. We want this work done. So you just do it without any tender process of why we're handing out taxpayers' dollars.'

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Ms Sharp was being specific to election commitments, which are a large portion of the funding. I also want to make sure that we've got the correct figures on the record for you. The $5.9 million related to multicultural grants, not to election commitments, whereas the second figure for last year combines both. Ms Chatterjee can update you on the figure for 2022-23.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes. The figure for 2022-23 was $6.3 million. Election commitments were administered in the following financial year.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office for Multicultural Affairs

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: In total, under this current government, you've handed out $386 million for multiculturalism grants in Australia. Did the department receive any correspondence from, or was the Labor Party headquarters involved in the selections for this program in any way?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: For the election commitment grants? Is that what you're referring to?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: For all these grants—the $386 million that has been issued. Did the department receive any correspondence from, or was the Labor Party headquarters involved in the selections for this program in any way?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Senator, we've made a distinction between multicultural grants programs and election commitments. The department has no role in advising the government on—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: That wasn't my question. Did the department receive any correspondence from the Labor Party?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: We monitor election commitments as they're made, and then, after the election, Prime Minister and Cabinet typically pulls together a full list of election commitments, and they are then apportioned out to departments to deliver. As Ms Sharp said, we go through a process of ensuring that the organisations so nominated by the government can actually deliver.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'll go back to my question. Did you receive any correspondence from the Labor Party headquarters?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, Senator. There's a process—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes or no? That's all I'm asking. That's my question. Did you receive any correspondence from the Labor Party headquarters with regard to these grants?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, Senator.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Minister, I'll ask you directly. Were the Labor Party headquarters involved in the selection of these grants, like they were for the infrastructure program? I would like a yes-or-no answer.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I don't have any knowledge of that, so I'm happy to take it on notice.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You'll take it on notice?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Last year, 94 per cent of the $325 million in multiculturalism grants went to Labor seats—94 per cent. This is a flat-out rort. This is taxpayer money being used as a slush fund for Labor Party seats. Tony Burke's seat has received $45 million from this program alone. Please explain why this is not a rort or pork-barrelling.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I haven't seen those figures before, Senator Hanson. I can only take you at face value. For that reason, it's probably not wise for me to speculate about that.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Alright.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And we don't record expenditure by electorate, so we are unable to help.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Alright. Then I'll ask anyone here from the department if you can answer that question. You've got your advisers here. I'll ask the question. Is there anyone here with the information? Did $45 million go to Tony Burke's electorate? I'll ask the question again. Did 94 per cent of the multiculturalism grants go to Labor seats? Now, under this, I have every right to ask you these questions. I suggest, if you don't have the answers, please go to anyone who's sitting outside. If you can hear this question, please bring the information to the minister, and let us know the answer to this question.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I was trying to explain the reason we were unable to help with that question and that none of my staff will be able to is that we don't record by electorate.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Then why can I get the figure of 94 per cent of it that went to Labor seats?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, I'm not sure where those figures came from. Have you calculated that yourself?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm not answering your questions. I'm asking you the questions here.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You just said that you were able to come up with those figures.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: The question here is—you don't have any indication. You're telling me that you hand out grants to these areas and to seats, and you can't tell me where they went?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I don't have that information with me, no.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Well, I'm asking the department.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And what Ms Foster has twice told you is that the department doesn't break down these grants by electorate. Presumably they break them down by the name of the organisation that receives the grant—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And by state.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: and by state.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Sometimes by local government area.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Or postcode. You could do Sydney.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: It might be possible to give you some figures about the proportion that have gone by state or maybe by local government area, but they don't do it on the basis of an electorate. That's what Ms Foster has said.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Right. Well, I'll put it on notice then. If you put it on notice, can you establish if $45 million went to Tony Burke's electorate? We know the Prime Minister's got $6 million for his grant in his electorate for the golf club—Marrickville Golf Club.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: As did dozens of other clubs, yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So there you are. You know where that money went.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I can take on notice for you the figure you've quoted that you say went to organisations in Minister Burke's electorate. I don't think it would be a very big surprise if a reasonable number of multicultural grants went to a very multicultural electorate like Minister Burke's. That would not be strange.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So you've got to be of multicultural background, so it's not for Australians to apply for these grants. It's a multicultural grant, isn't it? So it's divisive.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I happen to think that multicultural Australians are Australians.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: So it's divisive. So why call it multiculturalism? Why don't you open it up for all Australians to actually apply for these grants and not just what you want to—

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: You just said these grants are only open to multicultural people, not Australians.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Just the heading: multiculturalism. That's what it is. Everyone should have the opportunity to apply for these grants. But it wasn't for everyone to apply for it.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: How do you know that?

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Because you've admitted it. It's election commitments by the Labor Party.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And your party right now is making election commitments in Victoria.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: No, I'm not talking about my party, so don't put it back on me.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: But you just talked about what Labor has been doing.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: I'm asking you the question. It has been admitted here that it was election commitments.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Home Affairs Australian Border Force
text: And it was verified by Madeleine King that it went through the Labor Party headquarters.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism
text:
Last week the nation was shaken by the tragic attack on Helen Haines. It is now a matter for the police and the courts. But, as has been consistently pointed out, it is another example of a symptom of our fraying social fabric. The Governor-General reflected the views of, I'm sure, all of us when she said this is a moment for us 'to pause and to choose to be better'. Many of our leaders across the political spectrum have called for the temperature of dialogue to be turned down.

Obviously, the temperature has been rising for some time. ASIO told a parliamentary inquiry only last week that the climate has become more permissive of violence. And, clearly, we saw this when antisemitism alighted on 14 December last year, when 15 innocent people were murdered and 40 wounded at a Hanukkah celebration at Bondi, in our nation's worst terrorist attack.

Antisemitism and hatred do not begin with violence. They start with words and grow when that hatred is executed. Antisemitism across our society, especially online, surged after 7 October 2023 and has never returned to prior levels. In some institutions we now risk it becoming normalised.

However, in the 27 months since ASECA's inception, we have also made real inroads. We have worked constructively with government, institutions, regulators, law enforcement, other major sectors of society and the royal commission to assist them to define, identify and meaningfully tackle antisemitism. The government has adopted the ASECA plan in full, and work is underway in many areas.

This experience has shown the value of a sustained focus on addressing antisemitism as a major societal issue, not simply a consideration that arises urgently after major incidents. We must believe that modern antisemitism can be responsive to education, and this requires a long-term strategy.

Over the coming period, ASECA will continue to pursue its priorities, address the royal commission's findings, advise government institutions and policymakers as needed and work with others to push antisemitism to the margins of society, where it must remain.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: I now call the Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia. Mr Malik, would you like to make an opening statement?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text:
I do. Thank you very much. Since this committee last met in May, Muslim Australians have kept confronting the same question: can they take part fully in Australian life, practise their faith and keep their children safe without being held collectively responsible for acts they had nothing to do with? There has been real progress in addressing this. On 18 July the government responded to my national response to Islamophobia with commitments across education, community safety, social cohesion and accountability. The Islamophobia Education Taskforce has met three times. In June my office has launched the Australian Muslim Poll, a major new research project to better understand Muslim Australians' own sense of wellbeing, identity and belonging. In September my office also launched the National Islamophobia Index, which will build the first national evidence base on attitudes towards Muslims and Islam.

But announcements are not outcomes. The test is whether the lives of Muslim Australians measurably improve. In the past two months, events overseas and nationally have brought two words to the fore: terrorism and extremism. Terrorism and violence are unacceptable, including when committed by Muslims. These acts must be condemned unequivocally and without excuse. That condemnation also applies to words. In a sermon given in July and reported last month, a Melbourne preacher told his congregation not to take Jews and Christians as friends and spoke of an obligation to take arms against enemies. He has since explained that he did not advocate for harm to befall anyone. There is no place in Australia for inciting hatred or sowing social disharmony from the pulpit in any faith.

In September the co-pilot of flydubai flight 1073 allegedly attacked his captain mid-flight. United Arab Emirates authorities alleged that, in addition to reading extremist literature and following extremist online content, he was radicalised while he was studying in Melbourne and was acquainted with people linked to a Melbourne mosque almost a decade ago. Events abroad now land at home. If anyone in Australia played a part, they must be held to account.

When we talk of radicalisation, we must do so responsibly. It means recognising that radicalisation has multiple pathways and not treating religion as its only cause. It means not stoking fear or creating a moral panic over how Muslims may choose to dress or where they worship or partake in communal activities. It means seeing ordinary Muslims as Australians and not as suspects. Laws must target offenders, not isolate or interrogate all Muslims. Political leaders must not generalise about Australian Muslims. Media coverage must not scapegoat Muslims or Islam. When these lines are crossed, the result is suspicion, marginalisation, disenfranchisement and, most dangerously, a licence to abuse people because they are Muslim.

Children bear the heaviest cost. Consider the experience of Jannah, a year eight student who only last month was subjected to a frightening and hateful Islamophobic assault while on a bus in Sydney, defending another student. Jannah was called a terrorist and immigrant dog by a 50-year-old man. This is by no means an isolated event.

Islamophobic abuse includes Muslim children being called terrorists at school and teachers being verbally abused by random members of the public. It's facing harassment and intimidation from your neighbour. It's being physically attacked, threatened with rape and being spat at. It's pregnant Muslim women being called ISIS bombers. It's being abused on public transport and having your hijab forcefully pulled off. Cemeteries are desecrated, worshippers threatened and violent, hateful messages are sent to mosques and schools. Islamophobia can strike when you're driving your car or parking it, when you are shopping or taking a stroll on the beach or at the park. These all highlight that Islamophobia isn't just an abstract political debate. It is a real, physical threat targeting ordinary Australians for who they are and not what they have done. As Derya Iner and Linda Briskman have recently shown, children internalise this all and, rather than developing a sense of identity, some are learning to conceal who they are and feel shame instead.

To close: we must hold two responsibilities at once and recognise one fact, condemn violence and hatred without hesitation and protect innocent people from discrimination and intimidation while acknowledging speaking about this wrongly fuels anti-Muslim prejudice, hatred and discrimination.
witness_organisation: Office of the Illicit Tobacco and E-Cigarettes Commissioner

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: And they said that that was a significant gap in the government's response. What do you say to the position put by the Alliance of Australian Muslims and the National Imams Council?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: I can answer that. Before I answer that, I think it's really important to understand where we are today. My office is unprecedented. It does not exist anywhere else in the world. There is no national office that is established by a national government to solely tackle Islamophobia. The fact that out of the 54 recommendations, the government has responded to 35 does not mean that I'm resting on my laurels. For the remaining responses that I'm looking for, I'm petitioning the government to respond. And amongst the most important reside around legal protections because you cannot tackle Islamophobia piecemeal. It needs to be a holistic approach. This is how I wrote my report. Each element that constitutes my report is very important, but it's only by the whole that you can truly, effectively, tackle Islamophobia holistically and comprehensively.
witness_organisation: Office of the Illicit Tobacco and E-Cigarettes Commissioner

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
