agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text:
Finally, Mr Malik, I recognise the incredibly difficult task in front of you. I recognise the discrimination that the Muslim community is facing and what a monumental task is in front of you. I'm not pretending it's easy, and having responses to your report from the government that are opaque only adds to the difficulties with your talk. I don't hold you accountable for any of that. I just want to acknowledge the scale of the task in front of you. But in their concluding remarks in response to the government's partial acceptance of your report, the Alliance of Australian Muslims and the Australian National Imams Council said:

… Muslim hate must be confronted with the same seriousness, urgency and determination as every other form of hatred, racism and religious discrimination. Achieving this will require clear commitments, adequate resources, effective accountability and the timely implementation of measures that deliver real and lasting change.

Do you agree with that position?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text:
I do, and I think the statement you just read was the summary of my first recommendation, which is:

Confront Islamophobia with equivalent urgency to other discriminatory practices, and provide it with the same rights, protections, and legal recourse.

This is my first recommendation.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: We will resume with outcome 2. Senators have indicated they've got further questions here—hopefully, not too much longer. The committee has agreed to release the ACIC from the program this evening. You go with our thanks. We will now go to questions and to Senator Duniam.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: I wanted to confirm that, with regard to the second- and third-year working holiday-maker ballot program, there was no modelling undertaken, including projected loss of workers across the various sectors that that impacts—a reduction in visitor spending perhaps or economic outputs and all of the flow-ons. Was there any modelling of that nature undertaken in the lead-up to making that decision?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Not analysis that I would call modelling. One thing to understand about the working holiday-maker, and it builds on what I was saying earlier, is that it's a demand driven program. We don't know how many there will be in a given year at the moment. It's not a planned number. The number has been rising over the past few years, as you've heard. The other thing about it is that people do come with work rights, but they're not tied to a specific employer; they're not required to work in a specific industry. There are specified industries, and there are quite a number of those, but they're not—

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: But you'd attribute some nominal value, economic value, surely, to any of these visa holders.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Yes, an average.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Yes. And so, with a projected growth in numbers and then a capping as a result of a policy—at least, even if it was static across the forwards at that point in time, when the new policy comes in, there is a reduction. So my question is: did the government undertake any assessment, whether it's a form of analysis, modelling in partnership with Treasury or back of the envelope in the department, prior to the decision being made?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: There was certainly, through the costings process, an assessment of the impact on revenue.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Government revenue, not economic impact?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Yes, government revenue.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Okay. That makes that clear. How many second- and third-year working holiday-maker visas have already been granted, and how many valid applications are already in the pipeline under existing arrangements this financial year, the assumption being that there will be no third- and potentially no second-year visas left to issue, the cap having been reached with those applications already made? It comes back to those questions I asked earlier. You've got people who have got applications in right now. Let's say the new process starts. Are those people who have applications in now—under the three-month, or slowed-down, treatment—grandfathered through or do they get caught up under this new cap once it's enlivened?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: People who have already applied are assessed under the criteria that were in force when they applied.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Okay. So I could apply today, new criteria come in, and anyone who applies from that day is treated differently to me?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Yes.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Alright. Thank you.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Now we're over to Senator Shoebridge to get us through the rest of outcome 2 reasonably swiftly.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Indeed. I'm sure I'll be assisted in that by pithy and direct answers, which is how we'll get there! I was asking questions about parent visas and the impact of ministerial direction 117 on parent visas. What do you understand, Mr Willard, will be the impact of ministerial direction 117?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: For parent visas, there's another factor, which is the queuing system that we have for parent visas. There's also a ministerial direction in effect that relates to queue dates. The broad impact is the same, in that onshore is prioritised, but the existing queue dates still remain in effect. So, if you already have a queue date, that determines your priority. But, for people applying and entering into the system, then their onshore applications are prioritised.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: This is the retention of ministerial direction 103—is that right?—which is a carve-out of 117.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Yes.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: So the queue date is retained, but in terms of the ability to make an application onshore—if a parent is visiting, they won't be able to make an onshore application because, going forward, there will be a no-further-stay condition. Is that right?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Correct.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: How many onshore applications have been made by parents in the last 12 months? When I say the last 12 months, perhaps it might be the last financial year, to make it easier—prior to this directive.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: We might take that on notice. If we can find it now, we'll give it to you. Otherwise, we'll take it on notice.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: I appreciate that. But the effect is that parents, who can be elderly, who have gone through the process of flying to Australia—that can be quite arduous for some. Often they put the parent application in while they've been here on a visitor visa and then they've had bridging visas granted. That's no longer going to be available because of this ministerial direction. Now even elderly parents, even frail parents, will have to fly back overseas and make an application offshore and, because they're making the application offshore, they'll be put at the back of the queue. That's the reality, isn't it?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: If they're making a parent application—there are a couple of points I'll make for completeness. One is that there are waiver provisions that exist in respect of the 'no further stay' condition that exists on visitor visas. That goes to circumstances that have come up since the visa was granted and that are out of the control of the applicant, that are compassionate, compelling—

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Yes—compelling or compassionate, or they may need to have urgent medical treatment or something. But, save for that, the 'no further stay' condition will send them off?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Ordinarily, the 'no further stay' condition will mean they can't lodge a parent visa application onshore. They can continue to access visitor visas, and, for parents, there's a facility for an up-to-12-month stay on a visitor visa. Mr Kilner also mentioned the temporary parent visa—

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: But this is often quite frail people having a maximum 12-month stay going forward and bouncing back and forth on often long-haul flights, with all the expenses and all the disruption that that causes. That's going to be the practical effect for many parents, isn't it?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Yes. The visitor visa is not intended to be used to remain in Australia permanently.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: And the same analysis applies for partner visas, doesn't it? Again, if someone has come here on a visitor visa and they have fallen in love and may want to start a family, until ministerial direction 117, they could, in those circumstances, put a partner visa application in, seek a bridging visa and retain the family or start building the family. But that will no longer be available, because the 'no further stay' condition will mean that they have to leave and go back overseas, and, again, they'll be put at the back of the queue and they could be waiting years and years before they can come and make the family here. That's the reality, isn't it?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: The 'no further stay' condition will mean they can't lodge an application onshore. In terms of where they sit when they lodge their application, that will be a function of the direction that's in effect at the time they lodge.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: If you have the data, how many of those onshore partner applications were made in the last financial year prior to direction 117 coming in place?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: I think we'll have to take that on notice, if it's prior to direction 117.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: I might have last year's figure, but you want the figure prior to direction 117—
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Citizenship, Humanitarian, Family Visa Programs and Support

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Given that the direction happened only in July, I'm more than happy, if you've got last year's figure, for you to give us last year's figure. Rather than have you flick through now, we'll come back to it whenever you get the figure, because there are a couple of other questions. Minister, do you believe that, if an Australian citizen falls in love with somebody from another country, they have a right to complete the family here, to bring them to Australia to complete their family, and to commence living together? Do you believe that's a basic right that an Australian citizen has?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Subject to our immigration requirements. Anyone who wants to come to Australia for whatever purpose needs to meet Australia's requirements.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Subject to character tests and those matters that are standard across the board—if they meet those standardised tests across the board, do you believe that an Australian citizen, if they fall in love with somebody from another country, has a right to complete their family and bring them here and have that family? Do you think that's a right?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: As I say—subject to all of the procedures and requirements of Australia's immigration laws and systems.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: But your government has now put all these additional barriers in place. Your government has now said that, if an Australian citizen falls in love with somebody from overseas while they're here, they can't put their partner application in here, they'll have to be separated, the application will have to come from offshore and the application coming from offshore will be radically deprioritised. They'll be waiting, from the evidence we've had, for more than two years. Your government has made that decision, taking away that right, hasn't it?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: The reality is that there are vastly more people living overseas that wish to migrate to Australia than we can possibly accommodate in any one year.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: But, Minister, I'm only asking a question about partner visas.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: We have to make decisions around what is a sustainable number of people to migrate to Australia, whether it be on partner visas or any other visa. If we were to allow our migration program to be either completely or mostly swallowed up by one category, that would be to the disadvantage of all the other categories of people who want to come here as well—skilled migrants, parent visas, backpackers. I had one of your colleagues here earlier saying that we should be letting more backpackers in. There are more people who seek to migrate to Australia than we can accommodate. We have to ensure that there's a reasonable spread of categories, but, of course, a partner of someone in Australia, provided they meet all of the requirements within the limits of what we can absorb, of course.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: What we have heard, the evidence has now established. When your government came in there was a nine-month delay for partner visas. Now, four years into Labor, there's a 23-month delay for partner visas. Now we've heard that, in terms of offshore applications, which your government is now making mandatory in many circumstances, the delay is going to be well north of 23 months. You're effectively taking away the right for Australian citizens to complete their family, to have the person they love come and complete their family and for them to get on with their life. You've effectively taken away that right.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: It might assist to give you some context, if I get the officials to talk to you about the growth in partner visa applications that we've seen over that period of time. That might help you understand why it can't be an automatic yes to every single person.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: So that's your position: there is no right.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: I didn't say that—

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: This is a question about policy—

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: You go back and have a look at what I said, rather than what you'd like me to have said.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: This is a question about policy, not about numbers. Do you believe that, if an Australian citizen falls in love with somebody from another country, that, subject to meeting the standard immigration requirements of character et cetera, that Australian citizen has a right to complete the family, to bring the person they love here and to get on with their life as a couple? Is that a right that you believe Australians have?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: I've already answered that question at least twice, and I'd like the officials to be able to give you the figures that demonstrate the growth that we've seen in partner visa applications as part of my answer.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Mr Willard, you'd recall I asked for that data previously.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: I'll read those figures now. I've got them in front of me. In 2021-22, lodgements of partner provisional was 44,408; the following year, it was 51,800; the following year, it was 65,160; then 68,105; and then last year, it was 66,916.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: So there's been an increase of, what, 22,000 over the course of five years.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Nearly 50 per cent.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: An increase of 22,000 over five years.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Yes, which is nearly 50 per cent.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Minister, is your position that Australia can't absorb 22,000 partners coming in, completing a family—that that is too much? You've put the cap in processing numbers at just over 40,000.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: So far today, what I've heard from Greens senators is that we should increase partner visa numbers, increase parent visa numbers, increase backpacker numbers. We'll probably get to other categories that you'd like us to increase as well.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: I think what you heard from Senator Bleyer was that your proposal to radically reduce the number of backpacker numbers is something that she doesn't support, and, indeed, she's not on an island on that. There's widespread anxiety about your proposal to reduce those numbers. That was the conversation, and you should fairly characterise the conversation you had with Senator Bleyer.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: That is what she was calling for, more backpackers than we are proposing to allow, despite the fact we are at record backpacker numbers.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: I've had these conversations with Senator Bleyer. I know what her position is, and you're mischaracterising it. She says that your proposal, to radically reduce the number of backpackers, will cause significant harm, and, indeed, she's not alone in that. Your government made this decision without any consultation, and you've been told, from multiple sources, the harm it will cause.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: What I said 30 seconds ago was that Senator Beyer is saying that we need more backpackers than what our government is proposing to allow. As I say, we've gone through several categories of visa applicants now, all of which the Greens say we should increase. Our government's view is that to continue seeing the sorts of numbers accumulatively across every category that you're talking about is simply unsustainable.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: I want to be clear. My party, the Greens—

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Is it your party now?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: believes that, if an Australian falls in love with somebody from another country, they are entitled to complete their family in a timely fashion. If Australians are living here and their parents are overseas, they have a right to complete their family. Parents provide enormous benefits to families, to look after kids and to pass on culture. Our party believes that your position of putting a 43-year delay for parent visas is unsustainable, to be clear. It is unfair and it's inappropriate, to answer your question.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Thank you for the statement.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: I might just move on to Naoero. Who's in a position to answer that?

text: I don't have that detail in front of me. They're younger than 18 years old. But I could take that on notice and try to get you a more granular breakdown.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: In July, the Asylum Seeker Resource Centre released a research report called Hungry for freedom: food deprivation among people seeking asylum on Nauru, which found that 99 per cent of people seeking asylum in the Naoero community could not afford to purchase sufficient food with the limited financial support they have. agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: It's right, isn't it? Australia sends people to Naoero, and the people they send to Naoero have chronic hunger. That's part of the system, isn't it?

text: They're provided with an allowance that is calculated to ensure they have sufficient financial means to provide necessities in Naoero.

text: Since these transfers have ramped up and since the financial stipend has been set, have you undertaken any assessment of the adequacy of food and living conditions of the people Australia has been sending to Naoero?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Did it conclude that the payment was adequate, and did they have access to people on Naoero to determine whether or not they were going hungry, like the Asylum Seeker Research Centre found?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: My recollection is that that review resulted in an increase to the fortnightly payment. It essentially looks at it, effectively, a bit like a CPI test. agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Can you please provide that review to the committee? If there's a previous review, can you provide that previous review as well?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text:
Thank you, Chair, and thank you, senators. I really appreciate the opportunity for a brief opening statement. Australia's border environment is evolving rapidly as travel and trade grow, organised crime becomes more sophisticated and emerging threats require new approaches. The ABF is responding with modern capabilities, stronger partnerships and a more secure, efficient and connected border.

Last financial year, the ABF enabled the safe passage of 49 million passengers, a five per cent increase from the previous year. Working with government and industry, we are delivering a more secure, streamlined and technology enabled border. By the end of 2027, paper incoming passenger cards will become part of Australia's border history—

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Hear, hear!

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text:
replaced by a digital process. Of the 4,805 detainees who entered the immigration detention network last financial year, 88.4 per cent had a criminal history, demonstrating a larger and increasingly complex immigration detention cohort.

The ABF disrupted illicit tobacco and vape supply chains at unprecedented scale across the border continuum. In addition to the 2.2 billion illicit cigarette sticks, 590 tonnes of loose-leaf tobacco and 13 million vape devices, as highlighted by the secretary this morning, we also seized 7.2 million nicotine pouches, exposing the scale and determination of organised criminal syndicates seeking significant profits from Australia's tobacco market.

The illicit drug threat is also changing. ABF officers detected seven tonnes of methamphetamine, almost seven tonnes of cocaine, 380 kilograms of heroin and 2.5 tonnes of ketamine at the border. Cocaine detections increased by 76 per cent and ketamine by 193 per cent compared with the previous financial year, demonstrating that organised crime groups are diversifying the drugs they seek to import.

In the maritime domain, sustained surveillance, enforcement and regional partnerships continue to protect Australia's borders. The ABF achieved 2,458 on-water days and 15,476 aerial surveillance hours, the highest levels in five years.

These outcomes reflect the professionalism and dedication of our people, on the front line and behind the scenes, who work every day to keep Australia safe, secure and prosperous. Thank you, Chair.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Thank you very much, Commissioner. We will now proceed to questions and begin with Senator Duniam.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia

I will have a crack now. Excellent. Thank you very much. I am very pleased about those incoming passenger cards. They had the tiniest boxes, which you could never actually write in—or at least I couldn't, with my messy handwriting.

I want to go to the unauthorised maritime arrival at Weipa if I can. I just want to get an understanding from ABF about the nature of this arrival. What happened for this to occur? It's obviously a failure. It's the nature of a big border, I accept, but what led to this being the case? I think it was 10 unauthorised arrivals who were able to travel from Indonesia, arriving at Pennefather Beach in Queensland at 3 am on 30 June this year.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Senator, the commander of Operation Sovereign Borders, Rear Admiral Sonter, will be able to provide that response for you.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: To your point, the ABF's role—and certainly our expertise—is to fundamentally prevent the illicit firearms, firearm parts, ammunition et cetera from entering Australia. So we turn what we detect at the border into intelligence and enforcement opportunities that we work on with our partners. Certainly, from an ABF perspective, officers are trained to identify when there are false declarations, where goods are misdescribed to try to smuggle them through the border, as opposed to legitimate declarations where firearm importers are openly declaring what the goods are and potentially may not have hit the threshold in terms of what the permit requirements are. And it is a pivot point for us. As with my title, Assistant Commissioner, Customs Compliance and Enforcement, a large proportion of my division is focused on compliance activity, where importers will enter into the import system with the information that they have, and our teams within the ABF will work with the importers to validate that information and make sure that they've addressed all of the necessary requirements. text: No, but we do work very constructively and continuously with the contracted service provider, Secure Journeys, to ensure that all of their commitments with regard to the safety and security of Australia's immigration detention network are met. That includes the number of detention security officers required to ensure that safety and security.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: What is the number required to ensure minimum standards of safety and security? Can you just give us that?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: We're working with the contracted service provider.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Do you determine that or do they determine that?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: We work with them. We conduct the assurance to ensure that they're meeting our standards.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: So it is your standard. So what is your standard with regard to that?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: We set the standard with regard to safety and security of immigration detention.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Where could I find that standard?

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: That standard is in a series of policy documents.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Yes, it's in a series of policy documents. What I would say, too, is that the network, in terms of its capacity and the numbers of detainees within the network, fluctuates. Therefore, the staffing requirements have to also flex with the flexible nature of the network, which is the inflows and the outflows. Of course, we have a standard that Secure Journeys personnel must meet, and that includes training qualifications. Some of those measurements are in the contract. We explicitly ask that Secure Journeys personnel meet particular requirements of training and qualifications. When we talk about standards—that encompasses their training and their qualifications to ensure that they're meeting the safety and security requirements of the contract.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: Thank you.

agency: Office of Australia's Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia
text: That does conclude the time that we've got now, as I indicated when we resumed. Thank you very much for your succinct answers this evening in the shorter time that we had. I appreciate it.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: I call officers from the Australian Federal Police. Thank you very much for joining us later in the program than you were scheduled. We have your opening statement tabled, but I understand there are a couple of things that you want to say before we proceed to questions.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text:
Thank you, Chair. Given what's occurred over the last week, there are some important messages that I'd like to read this evening.

Good evening. Tonight, the AFP provide our ongoing thoughts for the member for Indi, Dr Helen Haines, and her family, who have chosen strength and bravery over anger and despair. There is a heaviness that hangs across Australia after the horrifying event last week. The alleged offender accused of attacking Dr Haines is before the court, facing a number of charges. I am limited in what I can say about this Victoria Police led investigation. However, I can reaffirm that the alleged offender was unknown to the AFP.

Across the world, we are witnessing a trend where violence emerges with little or no warning, particularly where individuals do not have a protection intelligence footprint. Lone actors are being motivated by a convergence of personal grievances, mental health vulnerabilities and ideological concerns. What helped keep us safe in recent times, such as our geography, analogue systems and faraway criminals, has been impacted by fully integrated technology, social media and artificial intelligence. Tech has enabled an instant pipeline of hate. This pipeline of rapid rage, often unhinged and violent, is being home delivered—or to the places we work—because of the devices we use. The threats are instant, and they're voluminous, and they instantly shock and cause legitimate fear. Perceived or real anonymity has given cowards courage. When I'm asked what has changed in recent years, this is what has changed. The vector of tech and social media is converging with the angry, the haters, the unstable and the amoral, who wrongly believe threats and violence are tolerable if their cause is noble.

The contagion of online hate has breached the digital compound and is spilling into the physical world. This is corroding our communities and has normalised violence, and it continues to impact on many, most notably the Jewish community. Antisemitism is often the early warning sign of a decay in our society and the poisoning of our compact with each other. History shows us this. Words can become deeds that forever change our country's values and moral compass. Our collective consciousness must be awake to this threat and acknowledge there will always be another target group of hate if we do not recognise where it can start. This is why, in October last year, I announced the National Security Investigations teams, which I call flying squads of hate disruptors. These NSI teams target high-harm antisemitic individuals, and they help ring fence our democracy by investigating those who threaten Commonwealth parliamentarians and high-office holders. Our investigators are charging almost one person a week for targeting Commonwealth parliamentarians or high-office holders.

From 1 January to 1 July this year, the AFP received 785 protective security reports that contained adverse content about federal parliamentarians. Adverse content does not always meet a criminal threshold. However, the AFP takes all reports seriously. When adverse content does not meet a criminal threshold, it is used to inform our assessment of threat, risk and vulnerability. Of those 785 reports, 50 per cent were directed at male parliamentarians and 47 per cent were directed at female parliamentarians. The remaining three per cent were generic threats to politicians. Female parliamentarians were three times more likely to report receiving offensive or threatening contact that was sexualised or gender based in nature. Female parliamentarians from culturally and linguistically diverse communities were also more likely to experience frequent and varied offensive contact. The threat themes directed at male parliamentarians also include threats generally gendered in nature, with accusations of weakness, femininity or subordinate masculine traits.

Our case load shows that threats to parliamentarians generally relate to four key aspects: policies, perceived performance, profile and personality. It would be wrong to think only inflammatory comments are creating the flood of threats. In some cases, just the debate causes the hate. In some cases, parliamentarians are being targeted because of their accent, what they look like or their political party. The fact is this: at times there is an almost immediate link from a policy announcement or comment to a threat being sent.

But that should not be taken as veiled advice. I am providing this information to explain what we are recording in our case load and to highlight there is not one single measure alone that will stop the threats, because this goes to a wider societal problem Australia is facing. The AFP is not here to make judgement on how parliamentarians do politics, but we are here to help keep federal parliamentarians and high-office holders safe. We work closely with the Department of Home Affairs and the Department of Finance, which are responsible for the security of electorate offices and the homes of parliamentarians.

I want to thank every member within the AFP who keeps parliamentarians safe. However, we will do better in showing you how we take these threats seriously, and we will introduce better training and consistency in this approach. I will also raise the issue of democratic and parliamentarian security with state and territory police commissioners at an upcoming meeting.

Chair, I'll leave it there. But, just before I finish, just very quickly, I will this evening pay tribute to Deputy Commissioner Ian McCartney who, after more than 30 years of service with the AFP, will retire in the coming weeks. Ian has often been at the forefront of combating the worst of humanity while maintaining his own. Ian retires with enormous gratitude from myself and the 8,000 members of the AFP.

Finally, I acknowledge the service of shadow home affairs spokesman, Jonno Duniam. Senator Duniam, you have asked the AFP tough questions, and you have rightly held us accountable to the public, and you have done this with respect and with the graciousness of a politician with the best interests of Australia in your heart and in your mind. Thank you.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: That is a lovely way to finish an opening statement. Senator Duniam, you've got the call.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text:
Our best wishes to Deputy Commissioner McCartney as well on retirement. I'll be shortly out the door after you! But I will indicate that, given time, there is a likelihood that the opposition will need a spill-over hearing for the agencies we haven't—counter to previous advice, it's just now become unsustainable.

I do want to go to, as best as can be dealt with at this point in time, the Bondi royal commission and the witnesses that were provided by the AFP to the commission. Commissioner, you did not attend as a witness, but I think your deputy did. Is that right?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: There were a number of AFP members who attended as witnesses, but I might pass to our chief operating officer.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: The point of my question is: Who determined which witnesses attended from the AFP. Was it something that the AFP had discretion over? Could they say, 'Well, we would like to send Commissioner, Deputy Commissioner et cetera,' or was it entirely up to the royal commission?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: We didn't receive specific summonses in relation to specific AFP witnesses. What we did receive from the royal commission was a range of questions and issues that they wanted covered, which flowed from the material that we had provided on notice. We responded to 20 notices to produce. On the basis of those questions, we worked through with counsel assisting in terms of who was best placed to answer the questions that were put in front of us. What was obvious in the questions was that the royal commission was after specificity. They were after direct evidence, so we determined that, in terms of our contemporaneous counterterrorism expertise, Assistant Commissioner Stephen Nutt, who was assistant commissioner of counterterrorism at the time, was nominated as our primary witness in that aspect, but we did have a range of other witnesses that went to the specific questions and the direct evidence at the royal commission sought. Some of those witnesses provided witness statements. Some of them were called to appear in hearings. Some of those hearings were open hearings to the public that you would have seen them appearing at and some of them were closed, confidential sessions that you wouldn't have seen.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: No, definitely not. Obviously, there was a high degree of interest at previous hearings and in commentary as well about whether or not you would attend. You have counterterror experience. Was it determined that Assistant Commissioner Nutt would attend instead of you because of his more relevant recent experience? What was the rationale to send Assistant Commissioner Nutt instead of the commissioner?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: It was because of the specific questions that the royal commission was asking. So they were after specificity, so an operational level expertise, not necessarily from a commissioner or even a deputy commissioner. The assistant commissioner was determined to be the best person who could provide both strategic and reflective input in terms of actual operational expertise in and around the Bondi incident.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Thank you for that. With regard to the interim report recommendations of the royal commission, obviously, there are some that are confidential, and I don't want us to breach any of those confidences, but, insofar as the recommendations relate to the AFP, have all steps been taken to implement, respond to and deal with those recommendations?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Yes. The AFP isn't the lead on any of the recommendations, but we certainly are working with the department and our state and territory colleagues in relation to our input into those recommendations. My understanding is that all recommendations from the interim report, both the public and the confidential versions, are on track to be completed by the end of December.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: I will quickly move to FOIs and refusal rates. As I understand it, the rate of refusal has risen from 22 per cent to 40 per cent from 2021-22 to 2024-25. Is there a driving reason for that increase in refusals of freedom of information requests?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: There is not a driving reason per se. We continue to receive, year on year, substantial increases in the number of FOIs that we do receive. Last financial year, the 2025-26 year, we received 1,162 FOI requests. That was a nine per cent increase on the previous year. We continue to, despite this increase in the number of FOI requests received and the increasing complexity of them, see an upward trend in relation to our compliance rate for completing those FOI requests on time. In regards to refusals, my comment would be that the complexity of the matters that we're having subject to the FOI requests—we balance the legislation. We're pro transparency and pro release but have to balance the national security considerations, particularly when there's a current criminal matter or a current royal commission. Those matters obviously impact what we're able to release under the legislation. Given the interest because of the Bondi attack and other matters, we are seeing an increasing number of requests around those types of things that have complexities in what can be released.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Thank you.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Senator Shoebridge?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Commissioner, first of all, I'd like to acknowledge the professionalism of the SPDL team in the engagements that I've had with them. If you could pass that through to them, that would be appreciated. In the short time we have over, there are two basic questions I'll put to you. The first is: what has the AFP done, if anything, with the referral from Amnesty, APAN and AMAN—APAN being the Australian Palestinian Advocacy Network, AMAN being the Australian Muslim Advocacy Network—about Australians who are alleged to have committed crimes under Australian law while serving as members in the IDF during hostilities in Gaza? Has that referral been assessed? Has it been progressed? Are there resources attached to it?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: First, I'll pass to Deputy Commissioner Hilda Sirec. We also have Acting Assistant Commissioner Matt Gale at the table, who can speak to this.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: We are aware of those referrals, and we have taken that information forward in regards to undertaking reliable inquiries. In terms of the specificity on relation to those investigations, I'll pass on to Acting Assistant Commissioner Matt Gale.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: What I can advise is that on 20 May 2026 the AFP received correspondence from Amnesty International Australia, the Australian Palestine Advocacy Network and the Australian Muslim Advocacy Network. This matter has been referred to my special investigations command, and we're reviewing the material that has been provided. We will provide an update in an appropriate time.
witness_position: Acting Assistant Commissioner, Cyber and Special Investigations

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: You're not able to identify how that's been staffed or how many officers have been attached to that investigation?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: It's been referred into my command. In relation to how we actually resource that, it is part of our day-to-day workflow. We treat that with the appropriate level of priority. These are actually quite complex and voluminous referrals that we have received. There is quite a process of actually going through and giving the due diligence to the reports that we have received. They do take time though.
witness_position: Acting Assistant Commissioner, Cyber and Special Investigations

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Which is why I was asking about staffing. How many staff are attached to it?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: We have a number of teams. I have two dedicated teams in Canberra. I have a team in Sydney and also a team in Melbourne that support matters that come into the special investigations command. War crimes is one of those responsibilities that the command tends to.
witness_position: Acting Assistant Commissioner, Cyber and Special Investigations

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: How many of those staff have been attached to this particular investigation?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Senator, we won't go into specifics in terms of how many numbers of members are part of the team, because as you can appreciate any investigation, depending on the inquiries, will wax and wane in terms of requirements. We have dedicated individuals involved.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Given the time, could I ask you to provide on notice whatever details you can about the hours that have been devoted to it so far and what the expectation is going forward.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: We'll do what we can.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Commissioner, in May you announced an international joint investigations team in Bogota. Five months later, Colombia's antinarcotics police say they have no record of any agreement. Inquiries that have been sent to Colombia have come up with nothing. Is there an agreement? Who in the Colombian national police has the AFP actually signed this agreement with? What is the state of cooperation with Colombia?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Yes, indeed. The announcement was made in May at the conference in Fiji. Present at that conference were also representatives from the Colombian national police. Since then, going from the announcement of the concept, I travelled to Bogota myself and signed an annex to our agreement with the Colombian national police on how we cooperate in Colombia. That was done on 21 August 2026. Since then, and even during that trip, I met with officials from the Colombian national police. Present at the signing was Major General Pena, who I signed the agreement with. I also met with officials from the Direccion de Investigacion Criminal e Interpol, or DIJIN, who are the responsible authority in Colombia who are working with us with establishing the international joint investigation team.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: I've run out of time. Can you put on notice how many AFP staff are in Colombia under that? Can you also put on notice if you have had any engagement with Colombian police given their public statements that they knew nothing of these agreements?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: We are of course working very closely with the Colombian national police. Yes, we'll take it on notice.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Yes, thank you.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Senator Blyth.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: I'm going to be very direct and brief. In relation to Mr el Matari, which was transferred from the Attorney-General's Department to Home Affairs and the AFP, are you able to let the committee know if there is any application for his continuing detention?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: I'll pass to Deputy Commissioner Sirec for that answer.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: The AFP considers interim control orders. I can advise that we do have an interim control order that has been applied to the Federal Court and that is our responsibility in regard to engaging and mitigating the threat that relates to the release of Mr el Matari.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Is it fair to say he will be released on 1 November?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: That is the end of his head sentence.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: So you haven't applied for any continuing detention of him?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: We don't apply for continuing detention orders in the AFP. That is a matter for the Department of Home Affairs. But we do apply for interim control orders.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Has the department of Home Affairs instructed you that they will be doing that? Because the Attorney-General's Department and Home Affairs have all said to speak to the AFP.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Yes, and that's appropriate. Because we have a treatment measure coming in, we do have the interim control order through the Federal Court system.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: But that's it; there's been no instruction for a continuing detention?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: That's correct.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Thank you.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Senator Roberts.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: My office has been contacted by AFP members who say that musters were held in AFP offices recently indicating that the AFP is in a dire financial position and that voluntary redundancies are being considered. I've heard recently that the undercover program had only a 15 per cent staffing footprint and the counterterrorism program had vacancies of nearly 30 per cent. Are these true?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: I'll pass to our chief operating officer to give you a detailed response to that, but I would just say that, as part of our budget management for this current financial year, we are going through an organisational realignment to ensure that we have resources in the positions where we are budgeted for and in alignment with government priorities. I will ask the COO to elaborate further on that.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: I can confirm the specific statements you said are not correct. The AFP does continue to receive additional funding. We do continue to grow year on year. We received an additional $316.6 million in the 2026-27 budget. As the commissioner flagged, we are also running a business, and we are subject to increasing costs in terms of a range of business costs. Internally, in the AFP, despite our significant growth and the investment in the AFP, we are doing a bit of a realignment to make sure the resources we have are focused on the priorities as defined by government and our agency, and to make sure we can deliver against those. We've applied a tiered approach to our budget implementation, which means we're considering, in terms of our legislative responsibilities, risk appetite et cetera so that the majority of reductions in terms of where we're realigning from is from our back-end areas, not our frontline staff. Overall, our FTE continues to grow, though. We're not reducing FTE. You mentioned redundancies before. I confirm that at this stage redundancies are not being considered at all by the AFP. We're currently in a realignment process in terms of moving our staff across the commands.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Thank you.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Senator Antic has just one very quick final question before we wrap up.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: In relation to your announcement about the national security investigations team, Commissioner, what I want to understand is what sort of oversight, accountability and transparency you're able to put on that to ensure that this doesn't become a searching out, seeking out and distinguishing between political speech, free speech and what you're describing as social-cohesion or anti-social-cohesion behaviours. What's the AFP going to do to make sure those boundaries aren't crossed?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: I have publicly stated a number of times in the last week that we are not here to police free speech; we are not here to intervene in political discourse; we are here to enforce the law. So, in terms of your question about what oversight exists, it's pretty straightforward for us. We investigate. If there are offences that have been committed, then we will charge and we will prosecute in conjunction with the CDPP. For us, our guiding light is always that we investigate alleged offences; if we have the evidence that an offence has been committed, then we will arrest and charge if appropriate.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Senator Payman has one quick question. We will be wrapping up after that.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Two hours ago, we received an email saying, 'Watch your back, c— .You're going to die very, very soon, you dog c— .' That's something we receive daily. But this weekend we were due to hold a community stall at a local market. We have had to cancel it because my staff told me they don't feel safe after the AFP advised us, 'An assessment of all available information has been undertaken, and unfortunately at this stage the AFP won't be in attendance to assist.' Can you please tell me how this assessment was made and with what rationale?

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: I will pass to Deputy Commissioner Scott Lee, but can I just say I'm horrified that this is the type of abuse and threats that a number of you are receiving and, as I called out in the opening statement, in relation to female parliamentarians in particular. So I'm very sorry to hear that you've received so recently examples of what I've been talking about this week.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text:
I just want to reiterate what the commissioner said earlier. The AFP is absolutely committed through our dedicated and professional staff to the safety and security of all federal parliamentarians. Our thoughts are with you all because, obviously, with the terrible events around Dr Haines, we understand the impact that this has had on all of you in terms of your critical role to our democracy and also on your families, your loved ones and your staff.

The AFP undertakes a range of assessments based on threat, risk and vulnerability. In terms of your particular matter, I'll just focus my answer on that, if I can, in the interests of time. Certainly, I am aware of your matter. I spoke to our assistant commissioner who is responsible, in Western Command, who has been speaking to your staff to seek a meeting to discuss that assessment and the rationale behind that assessment.

It's a difficult situation for me to go into in a public forum such as this, around the nature of that assessment and the information behind that assessment and also the assessment process that determines the response that was provided by the AFP, simply because it goes to the operational methodology around our protection. We're happy to talk to you and your staff around that in the meetings we do, and certainly our SPDL teams do that regularly with federal parliamentarians. But I know our team is looking to talk to your office and your staff as a matter of priority on that assessment.
witness_position: Deputy Commissioner, Community Policing and Protection

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Thank you, Chair.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Thank you to each of you for the very quick whip-around of questions from senators. I do thank senators for their assistance at the back end of the program. Thank you to the AFP for the work that you do and all the work that you've done, particularly this week, in keeping us safe in doing our jobs. Thank you very much. I join with your comments about Senator Duniam and his final estimates with us.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Good lord, yes!

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: I'm sure he'll be thinking of us when we are back in the new year!

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Maybe not!

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Thank you very much for all your time and all of your work. Thank you to the secretariat and to Hansard for all the things you did to make the last two days run smoothly. Senator Polley's indicating she wants to speak.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: I just want to thank Deputy Commissioner McCartney. Since I've been on this committee at estimates, he's always been grilled. Thank you very much for what you've done over three decades. It's been fantastic. Also, as Chair of the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Law Enforcement, I thank you for your contribution.

agency: Australian Federal Police
text: Hear, hear! Thank you very much.
